tools.desc: Self-hosted TypeScript agent runtime with durable approvals and verifiable run records. Own it, approve it, audit it.

cls.summary: Open Multi-Agent (OMA) is a self-hosted TypeScript runtime for coordinating LLM-based agents with durable human approvals, verifiable run journals, and pluggable model providers.
cls.what_it_does: OMA lets teams run, inspect and govern multi-agent workflows: you can run a single agent, an explicit task pipeline, or let a coordinator plan a team from a goal. It provides durable approval gates, an offline verifiable run journal, and adapters for many hosted and local model providers so organizations keep keys and data on-premise. Notable features are its self-hosted, no-telemetry design and built-in governance/inspection primitives for auditable agent runs.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, well-starred (7k+ stars), documents real users/integrations and provides examples, but it is only ~231 days old (<1 year) so it lacks the multi-year track record for TRL7+; evidence supports a beta-level TRL6.
prerequisites: Familiarity with LLM providers and API keys (OpenAI/Anthropic/etc.)
student_project_ideas: Build a supervised PR-review assistant that runs a multi-agent review team using OMA, integrates with GitHub webhooks, and records verifiable run journals for audit.

Create an experiment comparing coordinator-planned vs hand-coded task pipelines for a security analysis workflow using local quantized models (e.g. Ollama or vLLM) to measure throughput and approval latencies.

tools.name: Oldcircle/geo-sleuth
tools.desc: An agent skill that finds where a photo was taken — OpenStreetMap geometry, elevation skylines, satellite imagery and street view — and shows its work. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot.

cls.summary: geo-sleuth is an open-source agent skill that estimates the exact camera location and heading from a single photo by combining OpenStreetMap geometry, elevation-derived skylines, satellite tiles and street imagery and it produces reproducible evidence for its claims.
cls.what_it_does: geo-sleuth automates image geolocation: given a photo, it runs many specialised scripts to scan candidate map features (e.g. bridges), synthesise horizon/ridge-line views from elevation data, compare skyline fingerprints and other geometric cues (pier spacing, shadows) and returns coordinates, heading, an error radius and an evidence image. It is packaged as an Agent Skill so it is invoked by agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, etc.) and is notable for producing explicit files and commands that explain each step of its reasoning.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has many stars and a substantial README with case records and scripts, indicating early adoption and real examples, but it is only 60 days old so it lacks the long track record and stable releases needed for TRL 6+.
prerequisites: an Agent runtime that supports SKILL.md (e.g. Claude Code/Codex/Gemini CLI/Cursor)
access to elevation/satellite tile sources and optionally street-view APIs (may require API keys)
student_project_ideas: Reproduce one of the README case studies: run geo-sleuth on a withheld photo, document the pipeline outputs, and compare the tool's estimated coordinates against the ground truth while measuring runtime and failure modes.

Extend geo-sleuth to add an alternative evidence source (e.g. use a different global DEM or substitute Mapillary street imagery) and evaluate how the different data source affects localisation accuracy across a curated photo set.

tools.name: google-ai-edge/LiteRT-LM
tools.desc: LiteRT-LM is Google's production-ready, high-performance, open-source inference framework for deploying Large Language Models on edge devices.

cls.summary: LiteRT-LM is an open-source, production-grade runtime and orchestration layer for running large language models efficiently on edge devices and desktop platforms.
cls.what_it_does: LiteRT-LM provides a cross-platform inference framework that runs LLMs on CPUs, GPUs and NPUs across devices (desktop, mobile, web and IoT), supporting multimodal inputs, function-calling and performance features like speculative and multi-token prediction. It is used as a drop-in runtime/CLI/SDK to deploy models from common model repositories and to maximize on-device throughput and latency.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively maintained, has many stars/forks, and the README states it powers Google products (Chrome, Pixel Watch, etc.), indicating production use; repository is ~1.6 years old with regular releases and demos, consistent with a mature, widely adopted project but not a universal standard.
prerequisites: C++ development and native build toolchains (cmake, bazel or similar)
familiarity with LLM concepts and model formats (Hugging Face / model files)
GPU/NPU toolchains if targeting hardware acceleration (CUDA, Vulkan, vendor SDKs)
student_project_ideas: Benchmark and profile a small LLM (e.g. a 7B model) running with LiteRT-LM on Raspberry Pi vs a desktop GPU, then present optimisation recommendations (measure latency, memory, power).
Build a privacy-preserving local assistant: integrate LiteRT-LM into a mobile app (Flutter or native) to perform on-device question answering over a local document store using embedding search.

tools.name: graphhopper/graphhopper
tools.desc: Open source routing engine for OpenStreetMap. Use it as Java library or standalone web server.

cls.summary: GraphHopper is an open-source, Java-based routing engine that calculates routes, turn-by-turn directions, isochrones and supports map-matching using OpenStreetMap and GTFS data.
cls.what_it_does: GraphHopper computes shortest and fastest paths on road networks and returns distance, travel time, turn-by-turn instructions and many road attributes; it can run as a Java library embedded in applications or as a standalone web service. It also supports map-matching (snapping GPS traces to roads), isochrone analysis and importing GTFS for public-transport routing, making it notable for performant, production-ready routing on OSM data.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository created in 2012 with continuous development, numbered stable releases and published service jars, many stars and forks, and documented production use; this indicates a mature, widely adopted project (TRL 8).
prerequisites: familiarity with web services (REST) for the server mode
student_project_ideas: Build a multimodal route planner combining GraphHopper with GTFS feeds to compare car vs public-transport travel times across a city and visualise isochrones on a web map (Leaflet/Mapbox).
Create a map-matching pipeline that takes smartphone GPS traces, uses GraphHopper's map-matching module to infer travelled routes, and analyses route choice behaviour or network coverage gaps.

tools.name: uber/h3
tools.desc: Hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing system

cls.summary: H3 is an open-source geospatial indexing library that maps Earth coordinates to hierarchical hexagonal grid cells for efficient spatial analysis and aggregation.
cls.what_it_does: H3 provides a hierarchical hexagon-based spatial index: it converts lat/lon coordinates to compact cell identifiers, computes cell boundaries, neighbours, and performs region/aggregation operations. It is used as a C library with mature language bindings (Python, JavaScript, Java, etc.), making it notable for fast, consistent spatial partitioning and aggregation in mapping, analytics and operational digital-twin pipelines.
cls.trl_rationale: H3 is a long-lived (created 2017), actively maintained project with thousands of stars, multiple language bindings, documentation site and production use at Uber and others; this indicates a mature, widely adopted library (TRL 8).
prerequisites: C build tools (cmake, make) for building from source
experience with chosen language binding (Python/JS/Java) for application use
student_project_ideas: Use the Python H3 bindings and PostGIS to build a spatial aggregation dashboard that ingests vehicle telemetry and visualises hex-binned traffic density and temporal trends.

Compare clustering and routing performance by implementing a heatmap-based anomaly detector that converts sensor locations to H3 cells, then fuses results with a simple simulation (e.g., agent-based mobility) to study spatial sampling effects.

tools.name: gonglei007/GameDevMind
tools.desc: 最全面的游戏开发技术图谱(Game Development Map)。帮助游戏开发者们在已知问题上节省时间，省出更多的精力投入到更有创造性的工作中去。

cls.summary: A large, well‑maintained, open knowledge map and handbook covering game development topics, code examples, case studies and an AI-for-games resource.
cls.what_it_does: This repository collects structured documentation, practical code snippets and diagnostic case studies for game development across rendering, physics, networking, pipelines, production and operations. It is used as a reference and learning roadmap (with indexed markdown, interactive navigation and example code) and is notable for its breadth, practical examples and an AI-for-games subsection.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is mature (created 2022, 1600+ days old), widely used (6.6k stars), actively maintained with many documents, example code and cases; this indicates broad adoption and stable content suitable for teaching and practice.
prerequisites: basic familiarity with game engines (Unity/Unreal) and game-engine concepts
student_project_ideas: Use the repo's quadtree code to build and benchmark a simple 2D collision subsystem and compare performance against a brute-force approach.
Implement the provided network sync examples to create two small multiplayer prototypes (lockstep and state-prediction) and evaluate latency, bandwidth and reconciliation strategies.

tools.name: koharu-rs/koharu
tools.desc: ML-powered manga translator, written in Rust.

cls.summary: Koharu is an open-source, local-first application that automates manga translation using object detection, OCR, inpainting and local LLMs, with a WebGPU-based editor for manual cleanup and typesetting.
cls.what_it_does: Koharu detects and segments text and speech bubbles in manga pages, runs OCR, automatically translates text (locally or via hosted providers), and performs generative inpainting to remove source text and reconstruct artwork. It provides a WebGPU canvas for manual cleanup, text placement and layered export, and supports local GGUF model inference and multiple hardware backends for acceleration.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is >1 year old, has many stars and forks, active pushes and published documentation and hardware guidance; that indicates production-ready maturity and real user interest rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: up-to-date GPU drivers (CUDA/ROCm/Metal/Vulkan) for hardware acceleration
basic understanding of OCR and inpainting workflows
student_project_ideas: Create a pipeline that compares Koharu's OCR+translation results with a cloud-API translation (e.g. Hugging Face or Google Translate) and evaluate accuracy and artefact quality across a labeled dataset of scanned pages.
Extend Koharu to generate bilingual layered PDFs by integrating its detection and typesetting output with a simple web viewer, and measure editing workflow time-savings for translators.

tools.name: OpenDroneMap/ODM
tools.desc: A command line toolkit to generate maps, point clouds, 3D models and DEMs from drone, balloon or kite images. 📷

cls.summary: OpenDroneMap is an open-source command-line toolkit that converts aerial drone images into orthophotos, DEMs, classified point clouds and textured 3D models.
cls.what_it_does: ODM processes collections of aerial images (JPEG/TIFF/DNG or video) to produce georeferenced orthophotos, digital surface/elevation models, point clouds and textured meshes; it is typically run via Docker or native installers and can be scripted or served over the network via NodeODM. It is notable for being free, cross-platform, GPU-accelerated for some steps (SIFT extraction), and widely used by the mapping and photogrammetry community.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository created in 2014 and actively maintained with many stars, forks, releases and a user forum; the project has production use and integrations (NodeODM, Docker images, GPU builds), indicating broad adoption and maturity.
student_project_ideas: Build an automated pipeline that ingests drone imagery, runs ODM in Docker to produce orthophotos and DEMs, and visualises results in QGIS to measure volumes or area change for a civil engineering site.

Compare point-cloud quality and DEM accuracy from ODM versus a commercial photogrammetry package (e.g. Agisoft Metashape) across multiple flight altitudes and camera settings, and report effects on derived measurements.

tools.name: openMVG/openMVG
tools.desc: open Multiple View Geometry library. Basis for 3D computer vision and Structure from Motion.

cls.summary: OpenMVG is an open-source C++ library and set of command-line tools for performing structure-from-motion (SfM) and building 3D reconstructions from images (photogrammetry).
cls.what_it_does: OpenMVG implements the full pipeline for multiple-view geometry: feature detection and matching, robust estimation, camera modelling, and SfM reconstruction to produce sparse 3D point clouds and camera poses. It is used as a library (C++ API) or as standalone binaries that can be chained into pipelines and exported to dense reconstruction tools; it is notable for being research-driven, well-documented and widely used in academic and applied photogrammetry workflows.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is long-lived (created 2013), actively maintained with CI, documentation and many stars/forks, and is widely cited in the literature; it has a stable codebase and ecosystem of tools that integrate with dense MVS packages, supporting a TRL of 8.
prerequisites: familiarity with image processing libraries (e.g. OpenCV) and linear algebra
student_project_ideas: Build a pipeline that uses OpenMVG to reconstruct a small urban scene from drone images, then post-process the sparse cloud with OpenMVS to produce a dense model and evaluate reconstruction accuracy against surveyed control points.
Integrate OpenMVG with a ROS-based platform to localise a mobile robot by matching live camera frames to a pre-built SfM map and report pose drift during loop closure experiments.

tools.name: LibreCAD/LibreCAD
tools.desc: LibreCAD is a cross-platform 2D CAD program. It can read DXF/DWG, and write DXF/DWG/PDF/SVG files. It supports point/line/circle/ellipse/parabola/hyperbola/spline primitives. The GUI is highly customizable, and has dozens of translations.

cls.summary: LibreCAD is a mature, open-source 2D CAD application for creating and editing technical drawings and exporting/importing DXF, DWG and common vector/raster formats.
cls.what_it_does: LibreCAD provides a desktop GUI and command-line converters for 2D CAD drafting, supporting primitives (lines, arcs, splines, ellipses, etc.), layer management and export to DXF/DWG/PDF/SVG/PNG. It is used to produce technical drawings, convert between CAD formats and import GIS shapefiles, and is notable for being cross-platform, GPL-licensed and built on Qt with long-term community development.
cls.trl_rationale: The project began in 2011 and shows long-term development, many stars and forks, regular releases and CI; it is a mature, widely used open-source 2D CAD tool rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: familiarity with DXF/DWG concepts for advanced use
for building from source: C++, Qt and CMake toolchain
student_project_ideas: Create a set of standardised manufacturing drawings for a small mechanical part in LibreCAD and export DXF/PDF files suitable for laser cutting or CNC, documenting layers and tolerances.

Build a conversion pipeline that takes ESRI Shapefile geometry, imports it into LibreCAD, and produces annotated PDFs for site-layout drawings, combining Python scripting for file handling and LibreCAD command-line converters.

tools.name: vasturiano/3d-force-graph
tools.desc: 3D force-directed graph component using ThreeJS/WebGL

cls.summary: A JavaScript/WebGL component that renders interactive 3D force-directed graphs in the browser using Three.js and a physics layout engine.
cls.what_it_does: It visualises graph data (nodes and links) in a 3D scene with an iterative force-directed layout, supporting custom node/link rendering, interaction (drag, zoom, focus) and large graphs. It is used as a web component or via bindings (React) and notable for combining Three.js rendering with d3-force-3d or ngraph physics engines and many built-in examples.
cls.trl_rationale: Active repository since 2017 with many stars, forks, published examples, React bindings and regular updates; widely used in web visualisation projects which supports a mature TRL (8).
student_project_ideas: Build an interactive network-visualisation dashboard that reads telemetry or dependency data and highlights critical components using 3d-force-graph and a backend (Node.js) for data ingestion.

Compare performance and readability of different layout engines by visualising the same large network with d3-force-3d and ngraph.forcelayout3d using the 3d-force-graph component and report on scalability and interaction latency.

tools.name: melonjs/melonJS
tools.desc: A modern & fully featured HTML5 game engine (2D & 3D) for JavaScript/TypeScript, with WebGL/WebGPU rendering, built-in physics, Tiled map & glTF support and WebAudio.

cls.summary: melonJS is an open-source, browser-based 2D/3D game engine (JavaScript/TypeScript) with WebGPU/WebGL/Canvas renderers, physics, Tiled and glTF scene support, and a small dependency-free runtime.
cls.what_it_does: melonJS provides a high-level game engine API that handles rendering (WebGPU, WebGL2, Canvas2D), input, audio, physics, tilemaps and scene loading so developers can build interactive 2D/3D experiences for the web without managing low-level GPU plumbing. It is used by importing the engine into a web project or using its loader to load Tiled maps or glTF/GLB scenes; notable features are its unified renderer abstraction (automatic backend fallback) and compact, dependency-free distribution.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is mature (created 2011), actively maintained, large community (6.5k stars, many forks), recent activity and stable feature set (WebGPU/WebGL2/Canvas support) indicating wide adoption and production readiness.
prerequisites: familiarity with 2D/3D concepts (cameras, transforms) is helpful
student_project_ideas: Build an interactive physics-based demonstrator (2D tilemap level) that visualises control inputs and sensor data from a small robot simulator and runs in the browser using melonJS for rendering and Box2D-style physics.

Create a simple digital-twin-style scene by exporting a glTF model from Blender, loading it into melonJS, and layering telemetry visualisation (animated overlays) to explore interactive visualisation techniques for system state monitoring.

tools.name: pshenok/server-survival
tools.desc: Tower defense game that teaches cloud architecture. Build infrastructure, survive traffic, learn scaling.

cls.summary: Server Survival is a browser-based 3D tower‑defense simulation that teaches cloud architecture and operational concepts by having players design and scale infrastructure under traffic and failure conditions.
cls.what_it_does: The project is an interactive web game where you place cloud services, tune autoscaling and resilience, and respond to traffic patterns (including DDoS and inference workloads) to keep services healthy and budget-positive. It is used in the browser (three.js) as a learning simulator with campaign levels, sandbox mode and live metrics dashboards that model real cloud behaviours like autoscaling, circuit breaking and multi-region failover. Its notable aspect is mapping many real cloud operational trade-offs into an accessible game loop for hands-on learning.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, popular (many stars and forks) and provides a complete playable web application with campaign and sandbox modes, indicating a mature beta. However the project is under one year old (created 361 days ago), so by the provided rules its TRL should be capped at 6 despite strong community interest.
prerequisites: familiarity with three.js or WebGL concepts
basic cloud concepts (VMs, autoscaling, load balancing) for deeper use
student_project_ideas: Extend the sandbox to log telemetry from each service and implement a data pipeline (export to CSV or a time-series DB) to evaluate different autoscaling policies using recorded traces.

Create a new campaign level that models a real-world outage scenario (e.g. region failure + cold‑start model) and measure how different architectural decisions (multi-region, CDNs, circuit breakers) affect uptime and cost.

tools.name: ARahim3/DigUp
tools.desc: Search your computer by what's in your files: photos, PDFs, documents, recordings, videos and code. On-device on Mac, Windows and Linux, built on Google DeepMind's EmbeddingGemma 2.

cls.summary: DigUp is a free, on‑device desktop app that indexes files (images, PDFs, audio, video, code and documents) and lets you search them by meaning using Google DeepMind's EmbeddingGemma 2.
cls.what_it_does: DigUp reads and indexes selected folders on your Mac, Windows or Linux machine, producing multimodal embeddings so you can search by natural‑language queries and jump to the relevant page, timestamp or code line. It runs the embedding model locally, supports many file formats, and provides a menubar/tray quick shortcut for instant semantic file search across languages.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is very new (created 39 days ago) but already provides platform installers/releases and detailed install instructions and has many stars, indicating early adopters; because of its short age it fits TRL 5 (alpha in use) per the guideline.
prerequisites: basic familiarity installing desktop apps (DMG, .exe, .deb or AppImage)
sufficient disk space for the model download (~865 MB)
student_project_ideas: Build a small tool that uses DigUp's indexed output to cross-link course lecture notes, lab reports and student code so students can quickly find related resources across formats.
Create an extension that exports DigUp search results to a course LMS or a git repo as citations (e.g. auto‑generate a reading list of PDFs and timestamped podcast clips relevant to an assignment).

tools.name: hyperknot/openfreemap
tools.desc: Free and open-source map hosting solution with custom styles for websites and apps, using OpenStreetMap data

cls.summary: OpenFreeMap is an open-source production-ready vector-tile hosting and deployment project that serves custom OpenStreetMap-based maps without running a traditional tile server.
cls.what_it_does: OpenFreeMap generates, packages and hosts vector map tiles from OpenStreetMap and related data and provides deployment scripts to set up Ubuntu servers that serve tiles directly from Btrfs partition images. It is used by running the provided tile generation and linux host deploy scripts (over SSH/Fabric) and is notable for using Btrfs images + hardlinks to serve hundreds of millions of tiny tile files without a separate tile server.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo runs a public production instance and has been the basemap service for MapHub since mid‑2024; it is actively maintained with many stars and weekly automated updates, indicating production readiness rather than a prototype. The README documents deployment and benchmarking and the project is older than one year.
prerequisites: knowledge of OpenStreetMap and vector tile concepts
student_project_ideas: Set up a mini self-hosted OpenFreeMap instance on a cloud VM and benchmark tile-serving performance using the repository's benchmark tools, comparing Btrfs image serving against a simple tile server.

Create a web map viewer using MapLibre that consumes OpenFreeMap vector tiles and implements a thematic overlay (e.g. infrastructure assets) sourced from GeoJSON or Wikidata to demonstrate map styling and data integration.

tools.name: michidk/Unity-Script-Collection
tools.desc: A maintained collection of useful & free unity scripts / library's / plugins and extensions

cls.summary: A curated, long-lived list of free Unity scripts, libraries, plugins and editor extensions for game and real-time development.
cls.what_it_does: This repository collects links and short descriptions for many free Unity assets (scripts, shaders, editor tools and small libraries) so users can find reusable components for Unity projects. It is used as a reference directory rather than a single library — notable for its breadth, maintenance history and community popularity.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository was created in 2016, has many stars and forks and has recent activity, indicating sustained community use as a curated resource rather than early experimental code; it is broadly adopted as a reference list rather than a single production library.
prerequisites: familiarity with Unity (editor and project structure)
student_project_ideas: Use a pathfinding script listed in the collection to implement NPC navigation in a Unity-based robotics simulation and evaluate performance in different scene topologies.
Assemble several free shaders and post-processing assets from the list to build a small visualization demo showcasing rendering techniques and measure their runtime cost on different platforms.

tools.name: PlotJuggler/PlotJuggler
tools.desc: The Time Series Visualization Tool that you deserve.

cls.summary: PlotJuggler is an open-source interactive time‑series and multimodal data visualiser used to inspect, compare and transform recorded or live sensor and message streams.
cls.what_it_does: PlotJuggler loads time‑synchronised recordings or live streams (CSV, ROS/ROS2, PX4 ULog, MQTT, MCAP, video, pointclouds and more) and displays them in linked time‑series, XY plots and 2D/3D views. It provides interactive exploration (zooming, alignment across runs), signal processing (filters, FFT, derived series via Lua/Python) and a plugin/marketplace system for custom loaders and streamers. Notable points are GPU‑accelerated rendering, multimodal synchronisation (video, pointclouds, maps, URDF) and an SDK for extending integrations.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has a long public history (created 2016), many stars and forks, active recent development, packaged releases and an ecosystem of official plugins and a plugin SDK, indicating maturity and real‑world adoption consistent with TRL 8.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of time‑series data and signal concepts
familiarity with ROS/ROS2 or other messaging systems for integrations (optional)
comfort installing desktop applications or building from source for custom plugins
student_project_ideas: Build a ROS2 data logger and use PlotJuggler to visualise, align and compare sensor recordings from multiple runs, then implement Lua/Python transforms to compute and plot derived metrics like drift or latency.

Create a PX4 flight data analysis pipeline: convert flight logs to MCAP, visualise vehicle states and video in PlotJuggler, and develop a plugin that flags anomalous flight behaviours using basic signal processing/FFT analysis.

tools.name: amagine-ai/Amagine3D
tools.desc: Amagine3D: From hardware requirements to editable 3D designs

cls.summary: Amagine3D is an open-source tool that generates editable CAD designs (STEP/STL/3MF) for printable hardware enclosures from natural-language requirements, images and key dimensions.
cls.what_it_does: Amagine3D converts product requirements, reference images and component dimensions into multipart, 3D-printable enclosure and assembly geometry while preserving editable Python/build123d source and exporting STEP, STL and 3MF. It includes an agent-driven workflow that arranges internal mounts, checks clearances and collisions along motion paths, and produces a semantic scene that captures parts, features and interfaces.
cls.trl_rationale: The README documents substantial features (editable Python/build123d source, STEP/STL/3MF export, collision and thickness checks) and the repo has many stars and active pushes, indicating interest and functionality, but the repository is only ~90 days old so it lacks the longer track record or stable release history required for TRL 6+.
prerequisites: understanding of 3D printing constraints and CAD export formats
student_project_ideas: Use Amagine3D to generate an enclosure for a Raspberry Pi-based sensor module, then modify the generated build123d source to add mounting features and export STEP for 3D printing and assembly testing.

Compare automated text-to-CAD results from Amagine3D with a manually modeled design: evaluate wall thickness, printability, and assembly clearances, and report modifications required to meet a set of mechanical requirements.

tools.name: RodZill4/material-maker
tools.desc: A procedural textures authoring and 3D model painting tool based on the Godot game engine

cls.summary: Material Maker is an open-source Godot-based application for creating procedural textures and painting 3D models.
cls.what_it_does: Material Maker provides a node-based editor to author procedural textures and brush assets, and to paint those textures onto 3D models. It is used as a desktop tool (Windows/macOS/Linux) and is notable for its Godot integration, GLSL-based shader nodes and exportable texture outputs suitable for real-time rendering pipelines.
cls.trl_rationale: The project was created in 2018, has a large star count, active recent commits, published builds (itch.io, Steam) and user documentation, indicating a mature, widely used tool rather than a small prototype.
prerequisites: familiarity with Godot or desktop 3D tools
student_project_ideas: Create a set of procedural material libraries (metal, paint, concrete) in Material Maker and apply them to a mechanical part model exported from CAD, then evaluate how texture variations affect perceived surface defects in a visualization pipeline.

Integrate Material Maker textures into a Godot scene: author PBR textures in Material Maker, export them and build a small interactive scene in Godot to demonstrate material reuse, LODs and runtime performance impacts.

tools.name: RediSearch/RediSearch
tools.desc: A query and indexing engine for Redis, providing secondary indexing, full-text search, vector similarity search and aggregations.

cls.summary: RediSearch is a Redis module that adds secondary indexing, full-text search, aggregations and vector similarity search to Redis to enable fast queries over documents and vectors.
cls.what_it_does: RediSearch provides compressed inverted indexes, an expressive query language, aggregations and vector KNN search as a module for Redis, so you declare indexes on Redis data and run full-text, numeric, geospatial and vector queries. It is used by loading the module into Redis (or using Redis 8+ where the query engine is integrated) and is notable for combining text search, geospatial and vector similarity within the Redis ecosystem and for cluster/distributed support via Redis Enterprise.
cls.trl_rationale: RediSearch is a mature, long-lived project (created 2016) with thousands of stars, active development (integrated into Redis 8, recent pushes) and production deployments (Redis Enterprise / Redis Cloud), which supports a TRL of 8.
prerequisites: familiarity with database querying and indexes
student_project_ideas: Build a small IoT telemetry pipeline that stores device telemetry in Redis, creates a RediSearch index over recent telemetry and implements real-time alerts and aggregated dashboards using RediSearch aggregations and geospatial queries.

Implement a prototype semantic search for engineering documents by storing document embeddings in Redis and using RediSearch vector KNN to retrieve similar documents, comparing retrieval quality against a baseline keyword search (e.g., Elasticsearch).

tools.name: Azgaar/Fantasy-Map-Generator
tools.desc: Web application generating interactive and highly customizable maps

cls.summary: A mature open-source web application for procedurally generating and interactively editing fantasy maps in the browser or via desktop installers.
cls.what_it_does: Fantasy Map Generator creates procedurally generated world maps (terrain, biomes, political borders, cities, etc.) and provides interactive editors and export options for customization. It runs in the browser (and as desktop apps) and separates world data, generation, editing and rendering into distinct layers, producing SVG/WebGL visuals and exportable .map files. It is notable for a large user community, many features for map customization, and active long-term development.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is long-lived (created 2017), has large community interest (6k+ stars, many forks), regular activity and published releases with installers for Windows/macOS/Linux, indicating broad real-world adoption and a stable codebase.
prerequisites: familiarity with TypeScript recommended for code contribution
understanding of SVG/WebGL for rendering customisation
student_project_ideas: Integrate FMG export with a GIS or mapping library (e.g. convert FMG exports to GeoJSON and display them in a Leaflet/Mapbox demo) to explore coordinate transforms and map projections.
Build a plugin or script that converts FMG map data into assets for a simple game engine (e.g. Godot or Unity) to investigate procedural world generation and asset pipelines.

tools.name: Redot-Engine/redot-engine
tools.desc: Redot Engine – Multi-platform 2D and 3D game engine

cls.summary: Redot Engine is an open-source, cross-platform 2D/3D game engine (a community-driven fork of Godot) for building and exporting interactive applications to desktop, mobile, web and consoles.
cls.what_it_does: Redot provides tools and APIs to create interactive 2D and 3D real-time applications and games from a unified editor, with one-click export to multiple target platforms. It is used to build interactive visualisations, simulations and games, notable for being a mature, community-driven open-source fork of Godot with multi-platform export and documented build instructions (including Nix support) and AI integration via MCP.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is long-lived (created 2017), actively maintained with many stars and recent pushes, provides binary downloads and build docs, and is used to export real projects — evidence of production readiness though not a de-facto industry standard.
prerequisites: build tools (SCons, Nix) for compiling from source
student_project_ideas: Create an interactive digital-twin style visualiser for a small mechatronic device (e.g. robotic arm) using Redot for the real-time 3D UI and connect it to a ROS/ROS2 simulation for controls.
Develop a physics-based interactive simulation (2D or 3D) of a control system (e.g. vehicle dynamics) and build a UI and data-logging/export feature to evaluate controller performance.

tools.name: cactus-compute/engine
tools.desc: 2bit quants, kernels and runtime for consumer devices.

cls.summary: Cactus is an open-source C++ engine that runs quantized large language and multimodal models efficiently on mobile and edge devices using custom kernels, a zero-copy computation graph and rotation-based quantization.
cls.what_it_does: Cactus provides a local inference runtime, computation graph API and optimized CPU/GPU kernels to run quantized LLMs, speech and vision models on smartphones, tablets and desktops. It is used via a C API/CLI (and conversion tools for HuggingFace models) and is notable for its custom low-bit quantisation formats (CQ2/CQ3/CQ4), device-specific kernels and mobile-first benchmarks.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository has existed >1 year, active commits and many stars/forks, provides CLI, brew package and benchmarking which indicates production-readiness and real users; not a de-facto standard but shows clear real-world use and stability.
prerequisites: understanding of quantisation and model inference
student_project_ideas: Benchmark and compare on-device inference latency and memory of a small LLM converted to Cactus versus llama.cpp on an Android phone, and produce a report analysing trade-offs of different quantisation levels.
Integrate Cactus into a simple mobile robotics demonstrator to run a small on-device model for voice command recognition and decision-making, measuring end-to-end latency and resource usage.

tools.name: dialogic-godot/dialogic
tools.desc: 💬 Create Dialogs, Visual Novels, RPGs, and manage Characters with Godot to create your Game!

cls.summary: Dialogic is an open-source Godot plugin that provides a visual editor and runtime for creating dialogues, visual novels and RPG-style conversation systems inside Godot games.
cls.what_it_does: Dialogic supplies an in-editor dialogue/character manager and playback system so game developers can author branching conversations, cutscenes and visual-novel style UI without building the systems from scratch. It is distributed as a Godot addon (requires Godot 4.5+) and is notable for tight integration with the Godot editor, an auto-updater, documentation and a class reference for runtime APIs.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository created in 2020 and actively maintained through 2026 with many stars (6k+), documentation, unit tests and an auto-updater; these indicate a mature, widely used Godot plugin though not an industry-wide standard.
prerequisites: basic GDScript and Godot editor familiarity
student_project_ideas: Build a short visual-novel style prototype in Godot using Dialogic to author branching dialogues and integrate simple gameplay mechanics (e.g., inventory or choices that affect state).
Create an RPG conversation system that uses Dialogic for dialogue flow and Godot signals to trigger quests or state changes, then evaluate usability and state-management patterns.

tools.name: CGAL/cgal
tools.desc: The public CGAL repository, see the README below

cls.summary: CGAL is a mature, open-source C++ library of reliable computational-geometry algorithms used for meshes, triangulations, point clouds and other geometry processing tasks.
cls.what_it_does: CGAL provides implementations of core computational-geometry algorithms and data structures (triangulations, convex hulls, mesh processing, boolean operations, Voronoi diagrams, etc.) as a C++ library so developers can use them directly in engineering and research software. It is header-only since version 5.0 and is used by projects that need robust geometric primitives, mesh manipulation and exact geometric predicates. CGAL is notable for its breadth, rigorous implementations and active release cadence and test infrastructure.
cls.trl_rationale: CGAL has a long track record (repository created 2014, active development and biannual releases), thousands of stars and an extensive manual and testsuite; these indicate a mature, widely-adopted library rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: modern C++ (experience with templates and C++17+)
student_project_ideas: Implement and compare Delaunay triangulation and mesh refinement for a 2D/3D geometry and visualise quality metrics using CGAL and a plotting library.
Use CGAL to perform boolean operations and repair on STL meshes produced by a 3D scanner, then export results for 3D printing or FEM preprocessing (combine with MeshLab or an FEA preprocessor).

tools.name: CadQuery/cadquery
tools.desc: A python parametric CAD scripting framework based on OCCT

cls.summary: CadQuery is a Python library for creating parametric 3D CAD models and exporting them to engineering formats like STEP and STL.
cls.what_it_does: CadQuery lets you write Python scripts to build parametric 3D CAD geometry using high-level operations (extrudes, lofts, fillets, assemblies) and export lossless CAD formats (STEP, DXF) or meshes (STL). It is used as a headless library (and via Jupyter/CQ-editor) for automated model generation, integration into servers or pipelines, and includes built-in visualization via trame/vtk.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is mature (created 2018), has many stars and forks, extensive documentation, companion projects (OCP, CQ-editor) and Docker/Apptainer images, and active recent commits — evidence of real use and a stable user base.
student_project_ideas: Create a parametric bracket generator in CadQuery that exports STEP and STL and integrates with a simple stress analysis workflow (e.g., export to an FEA tool or use a Python FEA library) to study geometry-driven changes in stress.

Build a small parts library and web preview: use CadQuery scripts to generate parameterised components, render previews in Jupyter/Trame, and provide a JSON-driven web API for selecting and exporting CAD files.

tools.name: dograh-hq/dograh
tools.desc: Open source voice AI platform. Self-hosted alternative to Vapi and Retell. On Prem, BYOK across  Speech to Speech or LLM/STT/TTS, with a visual workflow builder, MCP native and telephony support.

cls.summary: Dograh is an open-source, self-hostable voice AI platform for building and running conversational voice agents with a visual workflow builder and telephony integrations.
cls.what_it_does: Dograh provides a self-hosted platform to design, test and deploy voice agents using a visual workflow builder, integrated STT/TTS/LLM providers, and telephony connectors (Twilio, Vonage, Asterisk ARI, etc.). It is used via a Docker quickstart or self-hosted deployment, supports MCP for coding-agent integration, and emphasises on-premise control and BYO LLM/STT/TTS providers. Notable points are the MCP-native support for AI-assisted coding of agents and wide telephony provider support.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is over a year old, has a large community (6k+ stars, many forks), active recent development and public docs, and positions itself as production-capable (self-host Docker quickstart and telephony integrations), indicating production-ready maturity rather than an early prototype.
prerequisites: basic Linux command-line and networking knowledge
(optional) familiarity with telephony providers (Twilio, Vonage) and MCP clients
student_project_ideas: Build a simple inbound voice assistant for appointment scheduling using Dograh, integrate it with Twilio for telephony and a small backend (Flask) to store bookings in a database.
Create an evaluation lab where students compare STT/TTS provider quality by swapping providers in Dograh and measuring response latency and recognition accuracy on a curated audio test set.

tools.name: DeanChensj/jiangshan-map
tools.desc: 江山时序 · 中国历史交互地图时间轴 (403 BCE – Present) | Interactive Historical Atlas of China across 18 dynasties, 198 territory snapshots, ancient-to-modern place genealogy & classical poetry routes

cls.summary: An open-source, browser-based interactive historical atlas of China (403 BCE–present) that lets users scrub a timeline to view territorial snapshots, cities, rivers and events on an annotated map.
cls.what_it_does: jiangshan-map is a JavaScript web application that renders multi-era historical territorial maps, place genealogies and timeline-driven map animations so users can explore how borders, cities and geographic features changed over 2,400+ years. It is used in a browser (live demo available) and is notable for a polished timeline UI, multi-stage territorial diffs, place tracing and rich historical annotations tailored to Chinese history.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is an actively maintained, popular web application with a working live demo and many stars, indicating a usable beta-level product; however the repository is only ~4 months old so it lacks the longer track record and releases needed for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with GeoJSON/TopoJSON and mapping libraries for development or extension
student_project_ideas: Build a lab assignment where students extend the map with a new time-slice (e.g. a local region) by adding GeoJSON boundaries and metadata, then present how administrative boundaries change across that period.
Create a web visualization that overlays historical flood events or river course changes from external datasets onto the atlas and analyse spatial correlations with historical population centres.

tools.name: mob-sakai/ParticleEffectForUGUI
tools.desc: Render particle effect in UnityUI(uGUI). Maskable, sortable, and no extra Camera/RenderTexture/Canvas.

cls.summary: A Unity package that lets standard ParticleSystem effects render directly inside Unity UI (uGUI) so they can be sorted and masked like other UI elements without extra cameras or render textures.
cls.what_it_does: The package bakes particle meshes (using MeshBake/MeshTrailBake) and renders them through CanvasRenderer so ParticleSystems can appear as native UI elements. It supports masking, sorting, multiple materials, trails, and works with overlay/camera/world canvases and SRPs (URP/HDRP). It is notable for avoiding extra cameras or RenderTextures and for production-ready performance optimisations.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2018), actively maintained with many stars/forks, documented installation options and demos (WebGL), and explicit support for multiple render pipelines, indicating broad adoption and maturity beyond beta.
prerequisites: understanding of Unity UI (uGUI) and ParticleSystem
student_project_ideas: Create an interactive HUD in Unity for a robotics simulation that uses UIParticle to display sensor events and system alerts as particle effects, integrating with ROS or a mock sensor stream.

Build a WebGL demo that overlays particle-based UI feedback on a digital twin scene (Unity) to visualise runtime telemetry and test performance/scalability of UI particles under different canvas modes and render pipelines.

alternatives_to: Unity Particle System rendered to RenderTexture

tools.name: Michael-A-Kuykendall/shimmy
tools.desc: ⚡ Pure-Rust WebGPU inference engine — OpenAI-API compatible, GGUF native, runs on any GPU. No Python. No llama.cpp. Single binary.

cls.summary: Shimmy is a pure‑Rust, local GPU inference server and CLI that runs GGUF LLMs on WebGPU and exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API.
cls.what_it_does: Shimmy runs GGUF-format language models on GPUs using a Rust + WebGPU (wgsl) execution engine and provides a CLI and HTTP server with OpenAI‑compatible endpoints for chat and text completions. It is notable for being a single‑binary, no‑Python implementation with verified native downloads, explicit model support/certification and focus on correctness across platforms.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is over one year old, has many stars and forks, and ships versioned releases (2.6.7) with verified native binaries, documentation and a certification matrix—evidence of production readiness rather than a fragile prototype.
prerequisites: GGUF-format models and familiarity with LLM model files
student_project_ideas: Build a small local chatbot for a lab instrument by hosting a domain‑specific GGUF model in Shimmy and connecting it to a simple web UI to demonstrate edge deployment and API compatibility.
Integrate Shimmy with a ROS 2 node (or a robotics testbed) to evaluate using a local LLM for natural‑language operator commands and log latency/throughput under different GPU configurations.

tools.name: srizzon/git-city
tools.desc: Your GitHub profile as a 3D pixel art building in an interactive city

cls.summary: Git City renders each GitHub profile as a 3D pixel-art building in an interactive, fly-through web city.
cls.what_it_does: Git City converts GitHub profile metrics into procedurally generated 3D pixel-art buildings rendered in a browser; users can fly around an instanced city, view profile pages, claim and customise buildings, and share snapshots. It is used as a Next.js + react-three-fiber web app with Supabase for backend/auth and LOD/instancing for performance, notable for its polished demo, social features and easy local dev with a Supabase local stack.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is active, popular (many stars and recent commits) and has full dev instructions, but the repository was created ~270 days ago (<1 year) so it lacks the longer track record and broad production adoption required for TRL 7+. Documentation and local backend support justify a Beta (TRL 6).
prerequisites: GitHub personal access token (for some features)
student_project_ideas: Build a classroom dashboard that maps students' GitHub classroom activity to a private Git City instance and add filtering/leaderboards for teaching analytics.
Extend the building generation rules to visualise repository-level metrics (e.g. test coverage, CI pass rates) and integrate an automated pipeline that updates the city from GitHub Actions.

tools.name: newton-physics/newton
tools.desc: An open-source, GPU-accelerated physics simulation engine built upon NVIDIA Warp, specifically targeting roboticists and simulation researchers.

cls.summary: Newton is an open-source, GPU-accelerated physics simulation engine (Python) aimed at robotics and simulation research with support for NVIDIA Warp, OpenUSD and differentiable simulation.
cls.what_it_does: Newton provides high-performance, GPU-based physics simulation for robots and articulated systems, exposing Python APIs and example scenes to run and inspect simulations. It extends NVIDIA Warp's simulation primitives, integrates MuJoCo Warp as a backend, and emphasizes differentiability, OpenUSD scene support and extensibility for research and development.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is over one year old, has many stars and examples, active pushes and backing/initiatives from organizations (Disney Research, DeepMind, NVIDIA) and is a Linux Foundation project; these indicate production-ready maturity and community adoption consistent with TRL 7.
prerequisites: familiarity with simulation concepts and rigid-body dynamics
NVIDIA GPU/CUDA knowledge for accelerated use (driver and compute capability requirements)
student_project_ideas: Build and evaluate a GPU-accelerated controller for a simulated quadruped in Newton, comparing training speed and control performance versus a CPU-based simulator (e.g., PyBullet).
Use Newton with OpenUSD scene importing to create a simulation-driven digital twin of a conveyor+manipulator cell and validate pick-and-place trajectories under varying payloads.

tools.name: galacean/engine
tools.desc: A typescript interactive engine, support 2D, 3D, animation, physics, built on WebGL and glTF.

cls.summary: Galacean Engine is an open-source TypeScript real-time 2D/3D graphics and interaction engine for web and mobile that supports animation, physics and glTF assets.
cls.what_it_does: It provides a lightweight component-based runtime for building interactive 2D and 3D applications on the web or in mobile mini-game platforms, including scene, camera, lighting, animation and physics subsystems. Developers use it either via an editor or by importing the @galacean/engine npm package and writing TypeScript code; it is notable for being high-performance, WebGL-based and oriented toward web-first deployment with glTF support.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is several years old (created 2020), has a large community (≈5.9k stars), active recent commits and a published npm package and editor; these indicate maturity and real-world adoption consistent with a mature, widely used engine.
student_project_ideas: Build a web-based interactive physics demo (rigid body collisions and simple joints) using Galacean Engine and glTF models to demonstrate dynamics concepts and visualise results.

Create an interactive virtual prototype of a robot arm where students implement kinematics controls and visualise trajectories in the browser, integrating Galacean Engine for rendering and a simple inverse-kinematics solver in TypeScript.

tools.name: cnr-isti-vclab/meshlab
tools.desc: The open source mesh processing system

cls.summary: MeshLab is an open-source desktop application for processing, editing and converting large 3D triangular meshes and point clouds.
cls.what_it_does: MeshLab provides interactive tools to clean, repair, simplify, inspect, render and convert unstructured 3D triangular meshes and point-cloud data typically produced by 3D scanning and reconstruction workflows. It is used as a desktop application (with plugins) for manual and scripted mesh-processing pipelines and is notable for supporting large models, many file formats and an extensible plugin architecture built on the VCG library.
cls.trl_rationale: MeshLab is a long-lived, actively maintained project (repository since 2016, sources and binaries available, regular releases and nightly artifacts) with many users and citations; this indicates a mature, widely adopted tool (TRL 8). The README and repo show established foundations (VCGlib) and cross-platform binaries rather than a prototype.
prerequisites: basic experience with 3D file formats and scanning workflows
C++/Qt knowledge only required for building plugins or compiling from source
student_project_ideas: Build a pipeline to clean and simplify photogrammetry-derived meshes using MeshLab scripts, then compare geometric error and file size before and after simplification using CloudCompare or a custom Python tool.
Develop a MeshLab plugin or script to detect and repair common mesh defects (holes, non-manifold edges) and integrate it with a small 3D printing workflow to evaluate printability of scanned parts.

tools.name: godotengine/godot-docs
tools.desc: Godot Engine official documentation

cls.summary: This repository contains the source (reStructuredText) for the official Godot Engine documentation used to build the online and downloadable manuals.
cls.what_it_does: The repo provides the authored manuals, class references and build configuration for Godot Engine documentation, intended to be processed with Sphinx to produce HTML, EPUB and offline copies. It is notable because it is the canonical, community-maintained documentation for a mature open-source game engine commonly used for real-time 3D, simulation and interactive visualisation.
cls.trl_rationale: Godot is a long-established, widely adopted open-source game engine (repo created 2015) with many stars, frequent pushes and a maintained documentation workflow; the docs repository is mature and actively updated, supporting stable releases and offline builds.
prerequisites: basic understanding of 3D graphics and game-engine concepts
familiarity with Sphinx/reStructuredText if editing docs
student_project_ideas: Create an interactive vehicle dynamics visualization in Godot that reads CSV telemetry from a simulation and visualises states in real time.
Build a small robot simulator in Godot that integrates ROS2 or recorded sensor logs to prototype perception and path-planning visualisation.

tools.name: nerfstudio-project/gsplat
tools.desc: CUDA accelerated rasterization of gaussian splatting

cls.summary: gsplat is an open-source, CUDA-accelerated library that renders 3D Gaussian splats for fast neural scene rendering and reconstruction.
cls.what_it_does: gsplat implements high-performance rasterization and optimization primitives for 3D Gaussian splatting, enabling fast real-time and inference rendering of radiance fields and LiDAR/camera sensor models. It is used as a Python library with CUDA kernels (PyTorch operators) and notable for its optimised CUDA paths, multi-GPU support, and integrations (e.g. NVIDIA 3DGUT, LiDAR sensor models).
cls.trl_rationale: The project is multi-year (created 2023) with many stars, active development through 2026, versioned releases, integrations (NVIDIA 3DGUT, NCore) and pre-built wheels, indicating wide adoption and production-grade performance optimisations consistent with a mature, widely-adopted tool.
prerequisites: CUDA-capable GPU and matching CUDA toolkit
Python and typical scientific Python stack (NumPy, SciPy optional)
student_project_ideas: Build a pipeline that reconstructs and renders a small real-world scene by combining photogrammetry captures with gsplat for real-time viewing and compare visual quality and performance against an instant-ngp baseline.
Integrate gsplat with a simulated LiDAR sensor and evaluate sparse Gaussian splatting for scene representation and downstream object-detection performance in a robotics perception experiment.

tools.name: gboeing/osmnx
tools.desc: Download, model, analyze, and visualize street networks and other geospatial features from OpenStreetMap.

cls.summary: OSMnx is a mature Python library for downloading, modelling, analysing and visualising street networks and other OpenStreetMap geospatial data.
cls.what_it_does: OSMnx fetches OpenStreetMap data (streets, building footprints, POIs, transit stops, elevation, etc.), converts them into routable graph and geospatial data structures, and provides analysis and plotting utilities for routing, network metrics, and spatial queries. It is used as a scripting library in Python and is notable for its ease of use, integration with geopandas/networkx, and extensive examples and documentation.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2016), actively maintained with many stars, forks, documented examples and a formal user guide and citation — evidence of wide adoption and production use, supporting a TRL of 8.
student_project_ideas: Use OSMnx to extract a city's street network, compute and visualise accessibility metrics (e.g. travel time to nearest hospital) and combine with census data to analyse equity of access.

Build a bicycle-routing planner by extracting bike-suitable network from OSMnx, computing shortest-paths with networkx, and deploying a simple web map (e.g. with folium) to visualise routes and travel-time isochrones.

tools.name: maziyarpanahi/openmed
tools.desc: Local-first healthcare AI: clinical NER and HIPAA PII de-identification on hardware you control. 2,200+ medical models, 35 model-backed PII languages, and Python, MLX, Android and browser runtimes. Apache-2.0 SDK.

cls.summary: OpenMed is an open-source, local-first NLP toolkit that performs clinical named-entity recognition and HIPAA-style PII de-identification on-device across Python, mobile, and browser runtimes.
cls.what_it_does: OpenMed extracts clinical entities (medications, diseases, procedures, etc.) and detects/redacts personally identifiable information from clinical text using local model runtimes; it provides Python, Android (ONNX Runtime Mobile), Apple MLX, and browser workflows so processing can run on hardware you control. It is notable for a large catalog of prepackaged medical/PII models, cross-runtime parity tests, and tooling for exporting ONNX and mobile-ready artifacts.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is >1 year old, has many stars (5.8k), an explicit release (v3.3.0 referenced), PyPI packaging, multi-platform runtimes (Python, Android, Apple MLX, browser) and a research paper, indicating production-ready code and real-world adoption rather than a tiny demo.
prerequisites: platform-specific skills for mobile (Android/Kotlin) or Apple MLX for iOS
student_project_ideas: Build and evaluate a local de-identification pipeline using OpenMed on a synthetic clinical notes dataset, measuring precision/recall of PII redaction and comparing Python vs ONNX Mobile runtimes.
Create an Android app that performs on-device OCR → OpenMed de-identification → FHIR export, and report latency, memory use, and privacy benefits compared with a cloud-based pipeline.

tools.name: qybaihe/bla
tools.desc: 🛡️ BLA (bla-agents / Blind LLM Agents) — Open-source Blue Defense MCP server & CLI protecting JS/TS, Electron ASAR, WASM, Python, Native Binaries, SQLite, GGUF/Safetensors & Android DEX against AI reverse-engineering agents (REA).

cls.summary: BLA is an open-source CLI and MCP server that hardens compiled and source software artifacts against automated AI-driven reverse-engineering agents by inserting format-native traps, decoys and source weaving.
cls.what_it_does: BLA automates audit → protect → verify workflows to defend JavaScript/TypeScript, Electron ASAR, WASM, Python, native binaries, SQLite, GGUF/Safetensors and Android DEX from autonomous reverse-engineering agents. It is used as a CLI, bundler plugin or MCP server that instruments source/artefacts with deceptive canaries, resource exhaustion triggers and verification checks to force costly or incorrect analysis by LLM-based REA pipelines. Notable features include integration points for coding agents and build systems, multi-format coverage and an included benchmark/verification suite.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is feature-rich with extensive README, website, benchmarks and many stars, indicating active interest, but it was created only 23 days ago so there is not yet a long track record; age limits the TRL to ~5 despite good documentation.
prerequisites: software reverse-engineering / binary formats awareness helpful for advanced use
student_project_ideas: Integrate BLA as a bundler plugin in a small Electron app build pipeline and measure how hardened artifacts affect an automated decompilation/analysis script (e.g. instrumented Ghidra headless runs).
Create an experiment comparing REA pipelines' success on unprotected vs BLA-protected WASM and SQLite artifacts, quantifying analysis time and token-cost amplification using the provided benchmarks.

tools.name: liangxiegame/QFramework
tools.desc: Godot/Unity3D System Design Architecture

cls.summary: QFramework is a small, MIT-licensed C# framework that provides a layered, SOLID-friendly architecture (MVC/DDD/CQRS style) for Unity and Godot projects to organise game systems, models, commands and utilities.
cls.what_it_does: QFramework supplies a lightweight application architecture for Unity (and Godot) projects implementing layers (View/System/Model/Utility), Commands and Events to encourage modular, testable game code. It is used by copying a single core script or installing provided Unity packages and by structuring game code to follow its interfaces and rules. It is notable for being compact (the core under 1000 lines), broadly adopted in the Unity community and supporting multiple example projects and toolkits.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2016), actively maintained with many stars (5.6k) and shows real game projects and examples that use it, indicating production-ready maturity rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: knowledge of C# and common architectural patterns (MVC, DDD, SOLID)
student_project_ideas: Build a small Unity game (e.g. a simple 2D platformer or counter app) using QFramework to structure View/System/Model layers and demonstrate command/event flows.

Refactor an existing student Unity project to apply QFramework's MVC/Command/Event conventions and measure resulting changes in modularity and testability (compare before/after with simple unit tests).

tools.name: gpuweb/gpuweb
tools.desc: Where the GPU for the Web work happens!

cls.summary: This repository holds the W3C Community Group specification for WebGPU and the WGSL shading language, which define a modern GPU API and shader language for web browsers.
cls.what_it_does: The project develops and publishes the WebGPU API and the WGSL shading language specifications so web developers can run GPU-accelerated rendering and compute in browsers. It is used as the authoritative spec and reference material for browser implementers, graphics library authors and developers targeting high-performance web graphics and GPU compute. Its notability comes from being the community-driven W3C work-stream that defines the successor to WebGL with a modern GPU programming model and a typed shading language (WGSL).
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2017), has many stars, active recent pushes and is the W3C Community Group source for a specification that browsers are implementing; this shows maturity and broad adoption though it is a spec repo rather than an application.
student_project_ideas: Create a browser-based real-time viewer that loads a 3D model and applies a custom WGSL shader to visualise simulation-derived scalar fields (combine with a simple CFD/FEA dataset).
Implement a GPU-accelerated particle or fluid simulation in the browser using WebGPU and WGSL, and expose controls to compare performance against a CPU implementation.

tools.name: ExpressLRS/ExpressLRS
tools.desc: High Performance Open Source Radio Control Link

cls.summary: ExpressLRS is an open-source high-performance radio control link firmware and ecosystem used to provide low-latency, long-range RC links for drones and RC vehicles.
cls.what_it_does: ExpressLRS implements firmware for transmitters and receivers that use LoRa-based radios (SX127x / SX1280) with Espressif or STM32 MCUs to provide low-latency, high-rate RC links and telemetry for FPV racing and UAVs. It is used by flashing supported hardware and configuring parameters via the ExpressLRS Configurator and integrates with flight-stack protocols like CRSF and MAVLink. Notable aspects are its optimisation for very high packet rates (up to 1000 Hz on 2.4 GHz), wide hardware support, and an active community maintaining features and updates.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is mature (created 2018) with large community adoption (5.5k stars), active maintenance (recent pushes), broad hardware support and a dedicated configurator and ecosystem, indicating production-ready firmware used in real projects and hardware.
prerequisites: basic embedded C and firmware build toolchain
understanding of radio communications (LoRa/ISM bands) and RC protocols
ability to flash hardware and basic soldering/electronics skills
student_project_ideas: Build and evaluate a small quadcopter link using ExpressLRS hardware to measure latency and packet loss across different environments and compare performance against an alternative RC link (e.g. TBS Crossfire).
Modify ExpressLRS firmware or configuration to add a custom telemetry payload (e.g. battery + IMU data) and integrate it with a ground station using MAVLink for monitoring and logging.

tools.name: Adam-CAD/CADAM
tools.desc: CADAM is the open source text-to-CAD web application

cls.summary: CADAM is a browser-based open-source text-to-CAD application that generates parametric OpenSCAD models from natural-language and image inputs and provides realtime previews and exports (STL, SCAD, DXF).
cls.what_it_does: CADAM converts plain-English descriptions and image references into parametric 3D CAD models (OpenSCAD) in the browser using WebAssembly and AI, with interactive sliders for parameters and realtime Three.js previews. It is notable for producing editable parametric OpenSCAD output, supporting common libraries (BOSL, BOSL2, MCAD), and exporting to STL/SCAD/DXF without server-side rendering.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, >1 year old, has a public live demo, many stars and forks, export features and integration with OpenSCAD libraries; these indicate production-ready capability and real user interest rather than a small prototype.
prerequisites: familiarity with OpenSCAD or parametric CAD concepts
web development tooling (Node/npm) for local runs
student_project_ideas: Use CADAM to generate parametric parts from specifications and evaluate manufacturability by exporting STL and running automated slicing/printability checks with a slicer API.

Integrate CADAM-generated OpenSCAD models into a digital thread: build a simple web workflow that takes a text prompt, generates a CAD model, runs a structural/simplified FEA (e.g. using a Python FEA library), and visualises results in the browser.

tools.name: DavidHDev/canvas-ui
tools.desc: A library of creative canvas components. Real HTML with WebGL effects running over it. React, Vue, Svelte, vanilla.

cls.summary: Canvas UI is an open-source library of framework-agnostic canvas components that layer WebGL/WebGPU shader effects and small 3D scenes over live HTML content.
cls.what_it_does: It provides ready-made visual components (liquid, glass, fire, cloth, ripple, etc.) that render GPU effects on top of real DOM using WebGL or WebGPU, and ships builds for React, Solid, Preact, Vue, Svelte and vanilla. It is notable for using the experimental HTML-in-canvas approach so text and links remain live and interactive while the page is used as a texture, and for offering both GLSL/WebGL and WGSL/WebGPU renderers.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively maintained, framework-agnostic, ships dual WebGL/WebGPU builds, and has substantial community interest (many stars and forks), but the repository is younger than one year (created ~124 days ago) so it fits a beta-level maturity rather than long-term production status.
prerequisites: experience with React/Vue/Svelte/etc. to integrate components
basic GPU shader concepts (GLSL/WGSL) helpful but not mandatory
student_project_ideas: Create an interactive web dashboard for a small cyber-physical system prototype that uses Canvas UI glass or liquid effects to visualise sensor status and overlays clickable live content for control, integrating with a simple MQTT backend.

Build a small UX experiment comparing readability and interaction on pages with and without Canvas UI effects (HTML-in-canvas vs GPU overlays) and measure accessibility and performance across browsers, producing recommendations for using GPU effects in engineering web apps.

tools.name: godot-rust/gdext
tools.desc: Rust bindings for Godot 4

cls.summary: godot-rust provides Rust language bindings to build Godot 4 game engine modules, allowing developers to write engine classes, scripts and plugins in Rust.
cls.what_it_does: godot-rust exposes Godot 4's GDExtension API to Rust so you can implement engine classes, signals and methods in safe, idiomatic Rust and call them from GDScript or other Godot systems. It is used as a library/crate in Rust projects that target Godot and supports building games, editor plugins and tools with optional targets like WebAssembly and mobile.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is mature and long-lived (created 2022, >1500 days), has large community interest (5.4k stars), active maintenance with recent pushes and CI/testing mentioned in the README, and is used for real projects (editor plugins, games); these indicate a mature, widely adopted library though not an industry standard.
prerequisites: Familiarity with Godot engine concepts (nodes, scenes, GDScript)
student_project_ideas: Build a simple robot simulator in Godot where the robot controller is implemented in Rust (godot-rust) and use the simulation to test control algorithms and sensor models.

Create a physics-based interactive visualization of a mechatronic mechanism in Godot, implementing computation-heavy components (path planning or collision checks) in Rust for performance and exposing results to a Godot UI.

tools.name: sacridini/Awesome-Geospatial
tools.desc: Long list of geospatial tools and resources

cls.summary: A long-running, curated index of geospatial tools, libraries, data sources and resources useful for GIS, remote sensing and spatial analysis.
cls.what_it_does: This repository is an 'awesome' curated list that collects links to geospatial databases, libraries, applications, cloud services, datasets and learning resources. Lecturers and students use it as a discovery index to find software (e.g. PostGIS, GDAL, Cesium), data sources and workflows for mapping, remote sensing, LiDAR and spatial analysis. Its value is the breadth and long-term maintenance rather than being a runnable tool.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2016), widely starred and actively maintained, showing stable community value as a curated resource rather than experimental code; therefore it is mature as a reference (TRL7-level evidence) though it's not production software itself.
student_project_ideas: Build a week-long lab sheet where students pick a dataset and a stack (e.g. PostGIS + Leaflet or GDAL + QGIS) from the list and produce a reproducible spatial analysis and web map.
Create a course-specific curated toolkit (subset of links and install scripts) and demonstrate a small end-to-end pipeline: ingest (PostGIS), process (GDAL/Python), visualise (Cesium/Leaflet).

tools.name: ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D
tools.desc: The fastest and most memory efficient lattice Boltzmann CFD software, running on all GPUs and CPUs via OpenCL. Free for non-commercial use.

cls.summary: FluidX3D is an open-source, GPU-accelerated lattice Boltzmann CFD solver written in C++/OpenCL for fast, memory-efficient fluid simulation and visualization.
cls.what_it_does: FluidX3D implements lattice Boltzmann methods to simulate fluid flows on CPUs and GPUs via OpenCL, with features such as GPU voxelization, immersed boundary particles, multi‑GPU support and built-in visualization and export. It is used by running simulations from C++ example programs or provided demos and is notable for high performance across vendor GPUs, memory-efficient algorithms and interactive visual tools (raytracing, slices, VTK export).
cls.trl_rationale: The project has a public v1.0 release and many subsequent releases since 2022, a large user community (5k+ stars), active maintenance (recent pushes) and documented features (multi-GPU, particles, voxelization), indicating production-ready software rather than an early prototype.
prerequisites: Familiarity with CFD concepts (lattice Boltzmann method)
student_project_ideas: Compare performance and accuracy of a Reynolds‑number sweep for flow past a cylinder using FluidX3D versus a reference solver (e.g. OpenFOAM), and produce validation plots and VTK exports for visualization.

Extend FluidX3D to couple a simple heat transfer model (temperature as a passive scalar) and study natural convection in a cavity, adding automated postprocessing to compute Nusselt number and visualize temperature slices.

tools.name: OpenSC2K/OpenSC2K
tools.desc: OpenSC2K - Open Source remake of Sim City 2000 using rust and godot. Available for macOS, Windows and Linux

cls.summary: OpenSC2K is an open-source remake of SimCity 2000 built with Rust and the Godot engine for Windows, macOS and Linux.
cls.what_it_does: OpenSC2K recreates the gameplay and simulation of SimCity 2000 and provides tools for importing original game assets, mods, and extended map formats. It is distributed as prebuilt packages and can also be run from source; the project uses native Rust libraries for simulation, rendering and audio inside a Godot project and exposes scripting/modding interfaces (including a JavaScript runtime). It is notable for its extensive feature set (HD packs, larger maps, debug tools) and active cross-platform releases.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is long-lived (created 2018), has many stars (5k+), platform releases and recent activity, plus documented build and release processes; this indicates production-ready software rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: A legally obtained copy of SimCity 2000 game files

tools.name: beclab/Olares
tools.desc: Open-Source Personal Cloud OS for Always-On Agents

cls.summary: Olares is an open-source, self‑hosted personal cloud OS that runs AI agents and local LLMs on hardware you control, using Kubernetes to provide apps, storage, networking and model serving accessible from a browser.
cls.what_it_does: Olares provides a turn‑key platform to deploy and operate AI agents, local models and system apps on your own machines, with one‑click installation of apps and a marketplace for models. It is used as a self‑hosted alternative to cloud AI services, notable for GPU pooling/accelerator management, private networking and integrated system apps like Files, Vault and a model console.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is actively maintained with versioned releases (examples: 1.12.6/1.12.7), substantial community interest (many stars and forks) and recent pushes, indicating production‑ready software; the project is >2 years old and documents installers and architecture, supporting a TRL 7 judgement.
prerequisites: understanding of GPUs / accelerators for model serving
student_project_ideas: Deploy a small self‑hosted LLM on Olares and build an agent that indexes and answers questions over a shared course document folder, demonstrating secure file access and model inference.

Integrate an external sensor data stream or Raspberry Pi node with Olares to implement an edge‑to‑cloud pipeline and visualize retained telemetry in a dashboard while managing compute on a pooled GPU node.

tools.name: ArthurBrussee/brush
tools.desc: 3D Reconstruction for all

cls.summary: Brush is an open-source Rust engine that builds real-time 3D reconstructions from photo datasets using Gaussian splatting and runs on desktop, mobile and in the browser.
cls.what_it_does: Brush trains and renders Gaussian-splat 3D reconstructions from COLMAP or Nerfstudio-format datasets, allowing live, interactive training and streaming of splat viewers. It is notable for cross-platform WebGPU support (desktop GPUs, Android and WASM/browser) and for producing dependency-light binaries suitable for interactive use and web demos.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is mature and widely used: many stars (5.3/day, ~5298 stars), an active repo with cross-platform releases, a live web demo and benchmarks, indicating production-ready code rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: familiarity with WebGPU / WASM for web builds
Android SDK/NDK for mobile builds (if targeting Android)
student_project_ideas: Build a lab exercise where students capture a small scene, run COLMAP to generate poses, train a Brush reconstruction, and compare render quality and training speed between desktop and the web demo.

Integrate Brush outputs into a simple digital-twin web viewer that streams compressed .ply splat files and overlays time-series sensor data (e.g. from MQTT) to demonstrate visualization of reconstructed environments in an operational pipeline.

tools.name: geopandas/geopandas
tools.desc: Python tools for geographic data

cls.summary: GeoPandas is a mature Python library that extends pandas to store, manipulate and analyse geographic vector data (GeoSeries and GeoDataFrame).
cls.what_it_does: GeoPandas provides data structures and operations for working with geospatial vector data in Python, letting you read/write common spatial file formats, store geometries alongside attributes, perform geometric operations (buffer, intersection, convex_hull), reproject coordinate systems, and plot maps. It is used as a higher-level, pandas-friendly interface that integrates lower-level geospatial libraries (Shapely, pyproj, GDAL/pyogrio) and is notable for making GIS-style workflows accessible in Python data-science code.
cls.trl_rationale: GeoPandas is a long-lived (created 2013), widely adopted open-source project with extensive documentation, many stars/forks, active development and an ecosystem of related libraries; this demonstrates maturity and broad community use consistent with TRL 8.
student_project_ideas: Use GeoPandas to import, clean and visualise municipal infrastructure vector datasets (roads, utilities) and produce a simple spatial risk map combined with asset attribute data (pandas) and matplotlib.

Build a workflow that reads building footprints and elevation data, uses GeoPandas for spatial joins and buffering, then exports results to GeoParquet or a PostGIS table for a basic digital-twin prototype.

tools.name: frangoteam/FUXA
tools.desc: Web-based Process Visualization (SCADA/HMI/Dashboard) software
