tools.desc: AnyImage makes images a starting point for creating in Blender. Model from references, add textures, and piece together scenes.

cls.summary: AnyImage is a Blender add-on that turns reference images into usable scene assets, textures and simple 3D cutouts to speed visualisation and content creation inside Blender.
cls.what_it_does: It lets users paste images from the clipboard into Blender, create cutout meshes with thickness, convert images to depth/relief/terrain, crop and combine frames, rectify photographed surfaces and match colours. It also includes offline AI tools for background removal and 2× upscaling so artists and engineers can prepare image-based textures and quick 3D proxies without external services.
cls.trl_rationale: The README and docs show a functioning, useful Blender add-on and the project has community interest (stars), but the repository is only ~59 days old so it lacks a longer track record or stable release history, limiting the TRL to about 5.
prerequisites: basic Python knowledge to inspect/extend the add-on
student_project_ideas: Build a Blender scene for a digital-twin mockup by converting site photos into textured cutout assets and a simple terrain, then export a glTF for a web visualisation pipeline.
Compare offline upscaling and background removal quality from AnyImage with cloud-based tools by preparing textures for a CAD model and measuring effects on render quality and material appearance.

tools.name: zhuyansen/awesome-opus-5.5-video
tools.desc: Videos, motion graphics, 3D scenes and games made with Claude Opus 5.5 — original posts, prompts and sources. English / 中文.

cls.summary: A curated 'awesome' list of public videos, motion graphics, 3D scenes and game demos made with Anthropic's Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku/Fable 5.5 models, with links to posts and many example prompts.
cls.what_it_does: This repository collects and categorises thousands of publicly shared video works made with Claude family 5.5 models, linking to original posts, example prompts and some source notes so readers can play the videos and copy prompts. It is notable as a large, crowd-curated gallery and prompt collection rather than runnable software or an analysis toolkit.
cls.trl_rationale: This is a curated 'awesome' collection rather than production software; the repository is 51 days old and mainly links to external posts. It has community interest (stars/forks) but no releases or evidence of production deployment, so maturity corresponds to an early alpha curated dataset.
student_project_ideas: Perform a quantitative analysis of the collected prompts to identify common prompt templates and their relation to visual styles, then present findings in a short report.
Build a searchable web gallery that ingests the README's links and metadata to allow filtering by category, model and prompt structure (combine with a small front-end framework and CSV/JSON).

tools.name: rust-adventure/skein
tools.desc: Convert glTF extras to Bevy Components using reflection

cls.summary: Skein is a Bevy plugin and Blender addon that stores Bevy component data in glTF extras so components authored or edited in Blender are instantiated automatically when the scene is loaded in Bevy.
cls.what_it_does: Skein lets you reflect Bevy Component types, apply or edit those components inside Blender, export the scene to glTF with component data placed in extras, and then automatically instantiate those components when the glTF is loaded in a Bevy app. It is used as a Bevy plugin and a Blender extension and is notable for creating a clear asset-pipeline bridge between Blender authoring and Bevy runtime components.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has an established README showing compatibility matrices, an active repository with many stars (336) and recent commits (last push 2026-10-26), and documented version compatibility between the Bevy plugin and Blender addon, indicating production-ready maturity rather than an experimental prototype.
prerequisites: Blender user knowledge and glTF export basics
Understanding of Bevy Reflect/Component system and asset loading
student_project_ideas: Create a small interactive Bevy scene where students author component-driven behaviours in Blender (using Skein) and verify that edited values drive runtime behaviour (combine with simple physics or input systems).

Build a digital-twin style viewer that replaces materials from exported Blender glTFs with runtime materials in Bevy using Skein, and demonstrate swapping materials programmatically for scenario visualisation.

tools.name: Speedstu/CUDA-for-AMD-Windows
tools.desc: Run CUDA-targeted Windows applications on AMD GPUs with ZLUDA + ROCm/HIP.

cls.summary: A reproducible Windows compatibility stack that lets CUDA-targeted Windows applications run on supported AMD GPUs by combining ZLUDA with AMD ROCm/HIP and runtime validation scripts.
cls.what_it_does: The project provides an installer, runtime staging, and test/validation tooling to run and verify CUDA-facing Windows applications on AMD GPUs using ZLUDA and the AMD HIP SDK. It is used by cloning the repository, running the PowerShell installer which detects GPU/HIP environment and stages a compatible runtime, then launching CUDA apps through the provided wrapper and validation scripts; notable features include numerical CPU-vs-GPU probes, pinned component paths for reproducible builds, and documented hardware compatibility profiles.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very recent (65 days old) so it cannot be judged production-grade; however the README documents reproducible installers, pinned upstream components, and extensive validation on specific AMD GPUs which supports an alpha-in-use rating rather than a paper prototype.
prerequisites: AMD GPU with supported architecture (e.g. gfx1200)
Installed AMD HIP SDK / HIP Libraries and compatible drivers
Familiarity with CUDA/PyTorch or native CUDA-targeted applications
student_project_ideas: Compare numerical results and performance of a PyTorch training loop run through the CUDA-for-AMD stack versus native CUDA on an NVIDIA GPU, reporting mismatches and profiling GPU utilisation.

Package a small CUDA-targeted inference app (e.g. a trimmed llama.cpp demo) and extend the repository's validation scripts to add automated correctness and performance checks for another AMD GPU family.

tools.name: arriemeijer-creator/AeroJAX
tools.desc: AeroJAX: A differentiable, structure-preserving framework for real-time flow simulation, control, and inverse design. Architected for neural operator integration and latent-space acceleration. Built with JAX.

cls.summary: AeroJAX is a JAX-native, real-time CFD framework that supports interactive simulation, differentiable solver steps, and gradient-based inverse design for fluid flows.
cls.what_it_does: AeroJAX runs real-time Navier–Stokes (and Lattice Boltzmann) simulations that you can interact with live (move obstacles, change BCs, swap solvers) and is end-to-end differentiable so gradients can be used for inverse design and control. It is used via Python, provides a GUI (PyGame) for interactive experiments, and is notable for mixing CPU‑optimised real‑time performance with JAX differentiability and swappable pressure solvers (including neural operators).
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has many stars (334), demos and an interactive GUI which show a usable project; however it was created ~235 days ago (<1 year) so there is not yet the longer track record or wide production deployments required for TRL 7+, so TRL 6 (beta) is appropriate.
prerequisites: basic CFD and numerical PDE knowledge
student_project_ideas: Implement an adjoint-based shape optimisation workflow that uses AeroJAX gradients to minimise drag of a NACA airfoil and compare results against a finite-difference baseline.
Integrate a neural operator pressure solver into AeroJAX and evaluate runtime and accuracy trade-offs vs. multigrid/FFT on increasingly fine grids, reporting performance and stability.

cls.summary: PMetal is a Rust-based framework for running, fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) and serving large language models on Apple Silicon (GPU and Neural Engine) with Metal/MLX acceleration.
cls.what_it_does: PMetal provides command-line, TUI, GUI, Python bindings and an MCP server to train, quantize, merge and serve LLMs locally on macOS using Metal and the Apple Neural Engine. It emphasises LoRA/QLoRA family fine-tuning, packed-weight inference (NVFP4/FP8/MXFP4), speculative decoding support and Hugging Face Hub integration, and includes tools for distributed multi‑Mac training and export to GGUF.
cls.trl_rationale: The README, installation instructions (Homebrew), many features (training, serving, quantization), and active commits indicate a beta-level project with documentation and community interest; the repository is 309 days old (under one year), which limits TRL to at most 6 despite traction.
prerequisites: macOS on Apple Silicon (Metal / ANE familiarity)
basic Rust tooling and command-line experience
familiarity with LLM concepts (LoRA, QLoRA, quantization) and Hugging Face models
student_project_ideas: Fine-tune a small open LLM on a domain dataset using PMetal's LoRA/QLoRA pipeline and compare model size, accuracy and inference latency before and after quantization.

Deploy a PMetal serve instance on an Apple Silicon Mac and build a simple client that benchmarks end-to-end latency and throughput for chat completions and embeddings, comparing ANE vs GPU execution paths.

cls.summary: Kiln is an open-source JavaScript/TypeScript toolkit and local MCP server for agent-driven procedural 3D asset authoring, preview and GLB export.
cls.what_it_does: Kiln lets a coding agent write JavaScript that builds and revises procedural 3D assets using provided geometry and material helpers; it runs the programs locally (via an MCP server, CLI or SDK), returns rendered views and structural checks, and exports GLB files. It is notable for integrating a coding-agent workflow (no external model API key required), editable source with revisions, parameterised variants, and a preview pipeline suitable for game and WebGPU scenes.

tools.desc: SuperMimic-UniLab: An Independent reproduction of SuperMimic on UniLab for whole-body humanoid motion tracking.

cls.summary: UniSuperMimic is an open-source reproduction of the SuperMimic whole‑body humanoid motion‑tracking system implemented for UniLab with multiple simulation backends and end-to-end training and evaluation pipelines.
cls.what_it_does: The repository provides code to train and evaluate goal‑conditioned policies and a differentiable world model for whole‑body humanoid motion tracking using datasets (LAFAN1 and BONES‑SEED). It supports three simulation backends (mjwarp, MuJoCo, Motrix), dataset download/convert/pack pipelines, and deterministic full‑clip evaluation so researchers can reproduce large‑scale training and benchmarking on a single GPU.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is a working reproduction of a published paper with end‑to‑end training and dataset pipelines and reported runs, but the project is very new (created 26 days ago) so it lacks a long track record or wide production use—hence an alpha/in‑use TRL.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of RL and PyTorch workflows
student_project_ideas: Use the UniSuperMimic repo to train a policy on a small subset of BONES‑SEED (with --limit) and compare tracking performance across the three supported backends (mjwarp, MuJoCo, Motrix), reporting differences in speed and fidelity.

Integrate a simple state estimator (e.g., IMU + joint encoders simulated/noisy) and evaluate how sensor noise affects policy tracking and robustness, producing recommended sensor fusion or reward modifications.

tools.name: sanidhyy/3d-portfolio
tools.desc: Modern 3D Portfolio using React, Three.js and Typescript

tools.name: gilzoide/unity-sqlite-net
tools.desc: SQLite-net for Unity, supports Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, tvOS, visionOS, Android and WebGL

tools.name: brendan-duncan/wgsl_reflect
tools.desc: A WebGPU Shading Language parser and reflection library for Javascript.

tools.name: gbroeckling/padspanHA
tools.desc: Bluetooth room presence for Home Assistant. Shows which room every iPhone, Android phone, Apple Watch and tag is in, live, on a 3D floor plan of your house. Works with the ESPHome or Shelly Bluetooth proxies you already have, and runs next to Bermuda or ESPresense. Try it in your browser: padspan.traks.ca/demo

cls.summary: PadSpan is a Home Assistant integration that performs local Bluetooth-based room-level presence tracking and visualises devices on a 2D/3D floor plan of a house in real time.
cls.what_it_does: PadSpan listens to existing Bluetooth scanners (ESPHome, Shelly, ESPresense, or the HA machine) and determines which room each phone, watch, tag or beacon is in, updating sensors every ~5 seconds. It provides a floor‑plan editor, 3D/isometric multi‑floor visualisation, Kalman-filtered RSSI smoothing, room/occupancy sensors and automations inside Home Assistant, and runs locally next to other BLE proxies.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository shows an active project with a demo site, Marketplace/HACS install paths, ~300 stars and recent commits, indicating community use and polish consistent with a beta release; however the repo is 286 days old (<1 year) so it lacks the multi-year production track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: basic Home Assistant configuration and networking
student_project_ideas: Build an occupancy-driven lighting and HVAC automation lab: deploy an ESPHome BLE scanner network, install PadSpan in Home Assistant, and create automations that adjust lights and temperature by detected room occupancy while measuring responsiveness and false positives.

Compare room‑level localisation algorithms: collect RSSI traces using PadSpan and an ESP32 scanner, then implement and evaluate alternative filters (Kalman, particle filter, smoothing/windowing) to quantify room classification accuracy and latency.

tools.name: Kiamo2/YATI
tools.desc: Addon to import Tiled maps into Godot 4

tools.name: RomanSlack/jev-drone
tools.desc: Camera-only autonomous drone in MuJoCo with a small judgment model (TypeSafe Jev) in the loop at 2.5Hz

cls.summary: jev-drone is a MuJoCo-based simulated Skydio X2 quadrotor that uses classical vision + a low-rate judgment model (TypeSafe Jev) to make tactical decisions and complete a five-station obstacle course.
cls.what_it_does: The repository runs a simulated autonomous quadrotor in MuJoCo that performs perception (depth + segmentation), geometric control, and a safety reflex loop, while a small judgment model (Jev) is queried at ~2.5–3 Hz to make higher-level tactical choices (e.g. climb, gap_left/right, reacquire). It is notable because Jev is used as an advisory, typed judgement layer in the live control loop (with caching and veto by the reflex layer), demonstrating how a low-rate judgment model can enable maneuvers that a greedy baseline cannot.
cls.trl_rationale: The project demonstrates complete end-to-end demo flights and reports quantitative results (not just a notebook), and has substantial community interest (300 stars) but the repository is very new (62 days old) so there is not yet a long track record or stable releases—consistent with an alpha-in-use TRL.
prerequisites: familiarity with ROS-like control loops or robotics software structure
TypeSafe Jev access or compatible judgement-model API
student_project_ideas: Replace the Jev judgement model with an open-source classifier or a simple learned policy and compare course completion, time-in-reflex and target-visibility metrics to quantify the contribution of the judgement layer.

Integrate a real ROS2-based perception node (simulated camera -> ROS topics) and evaluate how latency and perception noise affect Jev call frequency and overall course success, producing plots of performance vs. perception latency.

tools.name: hongbo-miao/hongbomiao.com
tools.desc: A personal research and development (R&D) lab that facilitates the sharing of knowledge.

tools.name: bring-shrubbery/ml-sharp-web
tools.desc: Web playground to create Gaussian Splats using Apple's SHARP model

cls.summary: A browser-based playground that runs an exported Apple SHARP ONNX model to generate and preview Gaussian splats from a single image and export a PLY point-splat file.
cls.what_it_does: This project runs an exported SHARP predictor (ONNX + sidecar) in the browser using ONNX Runtime Web to produce Gaussian splats from a single input image, provides an interactive preview, and allows downloading the result as a .ply file. It is notable because it performs heavy model inference client-side (WASM/WebGPU) and includes utilities to export SHARP to the ONNX format and to handle the ONNX sidecar weight file.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository shows a working end-to-end browser prototype, active commits and 300 stars but is younger than one year (268 days) so lacks a longer track record and broad production use; README calls it 'working prototype / experimental'.
prerequisites: Bun (JavaScript runtime) and Node-like tool familiarity
Modern desktop browser (Chrome/Edge) with good WASM/WebGPU support
If exporting models: Python environment and Apple's ml-sharp upstream repository plus large disk space for ONNX sidecar
student_project_ideas: Build a small web lab where students compare Gaussian splats generated from different images and quantify reconstruction quality (e.g. using Chamfer distance) by combining this tool with a simple mesh/point-cloud analysis script.
Extend the viewer to stream and visualise splats from multiple images or video frames, then benchmark browser inference performance and memory usage across browsers and model sizes.

tools.name: geolens-io/geolens
tools.desc: Self-hosted geospatial data catalog with semantic search (pgvector), OGC/STAC APIs, and map builder. Built on FastAPI, PostGIS, React, and MapLibre.

cls.summary: GeoLens is a self‑hosted spatial data catalog and browser-based map builder that indexes datasets from files, databases, services and STAC catalogs and exposes them via OGC/STAC APIs and vector tiles.
cls.what_it_does: GeoLens gathers spatial datasets (files, PostGIS tables, OGC services, STAC items) into a searchable catalog with provenance and version history, provides a browser map builder for styling, analysis and story maps, and serves the same data through OGC API / STAC / tile endpoints so GIS clients and code can consume it. Notable features include semantic search using vector embeddings (pgvector), source health checking and a self‑hosted Docker Compose deployment.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is active, has a public demo, substantial stars and recent commits, and provides install docs and Docker Compose (evidence of beta readiness). However the repository is only ~8 months old so it lacks a long production track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Build a QGIS workshop where students ingest local GeoTIFFs and GeoParquet layers into GeoLens, style them in the map builder and publish an OGC API Features layer consumed back into QGIS.

Create a reproducible cataloging pipeline: write a script that harvests a remote STAC catalog, configures embeddings for semantic search, and evaluates search relevance for a set of geospatial queries.

tools.name: Dicklesworthstone/frankentui
tools.desc: High-performance terminal UI kernel in Rust across 20 crates: diff-based rendering, inline mode, RAII cleanup, 70+ widgets, resizable pane workspaces, a Bayesian intelligence layer, and in-tree web/WASM backends (WebGPU with canvas2d fallback). 45 interactive demo screens run in the browser. WIP.

cls.summary: FrankenTUI is a high-performance, Rust-based terminal UI kernel and widget framework with Web/WASM backends and a large demo showcase.
cls.what_it_does: FrankenTUI provides a disciplined runtime, diff-based renderer, inline-mode terminal behaviour, and a large collection of composable widgets to build deterministic, flicker-free terminal and browser-hosted UIs. It is consumed as a Rust workspace of ~20 crates (runtime, layout, widgets, web backends) and ships 45 interactive demo screens that run in the browser via WASM (WebGPU with canvas2d fallback).
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active (~290 days old), has many crates, 45 browser demos, a dedicated website and several hundred stars which indicate real activity and a usable codebase, but it is younger than one year so a maximum TRL of 6 is appropriate (beta: versioned builds, docs and demonstrable usage but not long-term production track record).
prerequisites: wasm toolchain for browser builds (wasm32-unknown-unknown, wasm-bindgen)
familiarity with terminal concepts and WebGPU for best integration
student_project_ideas: Build a custom monitoring dashboard that embeds FrankenTUI to display simulated telemetry from a student-built system (e.g. combine with a small MQTT broker or local data generator).
Create a WASM-hosted demo that adapts an existing command-line tool to use FrankenTUI for an inline UI and compare rendering determinism across terminal and browser backends.

tools.name: Polytoria/polytoria-game
tools.desc: Polytoria, a multiplayer gaming platform built with Godot and .NET

cls.summary: Polytoria is an open-source 3D multiplayer game platform and world/creator system built with the Godot Engine, .NET/C# and Luau scripting.
cls.what_it_does: Polytoria provides a server-client multiplayer framework and creator tools for building and publishing 3D multiplayer worlds, with state replication and Luau scripting for game logic. It is distributed as an open-source codebase alongside a web-hosted launcher and targets desktop platforms (Windows, macOS, Linux); notable points are its use of Godot and a Luau scripting layer.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active and moderately popular (~299 stars) with recent pushes, but is under one year old and lacks evidence of stable 1.0 releases or broad production adoption; this supports an 'alpha in use' rating.
student_project_ideas: Create a small multiplayer game level using the Polytoria creator and Luau scripts to demonstrate synchronized state and player interactions, comparing behaviour with a Godot-only prototype.
Extend the Polytoria server or client to add a simple analytics endpoint (player join/leave, latency) and visualise the results in a dashboard to study multiplayer performance characteristics.

tools.name: llamastash/llamastash
tools.desc: Zero-overhead, terminal-native local-LLM orchestrator. Run any engine, any model via the same proxy.

cls.summary: LlamaStash is a Rust-based terminal-native orchestrator and OpenAI-compatible proxy that runs and manages local LLM engines and models through a single CLI/TUI/daemon binary.
cls.what_it_does: LlamaStash launches, monitors and proxies different local LLM engines (eg. llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang and other OpenAI-compatible servers) behind a single, consistent CLI/TUI and HTTP proxy. It simplifies engine-specific setup (ports, flags, readiness probes) and exposes a uniform API and commands so users and agents can start, stop and query models without learning each engine's details.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, well-documented and provides install scripts and multi-platform support, indicating beyond prototype quality; however it is only ~6 months old (under one year) so a beta-level TRL (6) is appropriate rather than production-grade.
prerequisites: familiarity with command-line tools and terminals
basic knowledge of local LLM models and engines (gguf, safetensors, etc.)
student_project_ideas: Build a small offline assistant for a lab environment that runs a selected GGUF model via LlamaStash and evaluates latency and resource usage compared to running the engine directly.
Create an automated test harness that uses LlamaStash's proxy to run a set of prompt-based V&V checks on locally hosted models and logs differences between model outputs over time.

tools.name: CodeBySonu95/VoxSherpa-TTS
tools.desc: 🎙️ VoxSherpa TTS   Offline Neural Text-to-Speech Engine for Android  ⚡ Sherpa-ONNX powered   🔊 Natural voice synthesis   📱 Fully offline processing   🚀 No cloud • No limits

cls.summary: VoxSherpa-TTS is an open-source Android app that runs neural text-to-speech models entirely on-device (offline) using Sherpa-ONNX, offering high-quality and multi-speaker synthesis without cloud services.
cls.what_it_does: VoxSherpa-TTS converts text or documents to speech on Android phones by running neural TTS models (Kokoro-82M and Piper/VITS) locally via Sherpa-ONNX and ONNX Runtime. It provides model management, system TTS integration, multi-speaker dialogue tags, and export/playback features so users can generate and save audio without internet. Notable aspects are its fully offline operation, support for large multilingual models (Kokoro) and a fast lightweight engine (Piper) tuned for mobile devices.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 261 days old (<1 year) but shows active development, ~300 stars, Android app structure, and explicit integration with Sherpa-ONNX and published models; this indicates beta-level maturity with versioned app releases and real-user interest but not the multi-year track record needed for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: knowledge of ONNX and on-device inference
familiarity with mobile audio APIs and model file handling
student_project_ideas: Build an Android demo app that integrates VoxSherpa to convert IoT device logs or notifications into spoken alerts, measuring latency and CPU/memory usage across devices and comparing Kokoro vs Piper models.
Create a mini research project that modifies the app to add a custom on-device vocoder or lightweight compression for model storage, and evaluate perceived audio quality and storage trade-offs.

tools.name: opengeos/geolibre-rust
tools.desc: whitebox_next_gen geospatial tools (plus new GeoLibre tools) compiled to WebAssembly (WASI) for in-browser use in GeoLibre

cls.summary: geolibre-rust is a pure-Rust geospatial toolkit compiled to WebAssembly that provides in-browser GIS tools (raster, vector, LiDAR, projections, SAR tools and a WASI tool runner) for interactive processing without server-side GDAL or native installs.
cls.what_it_does: It packages a superset of WhiteboxTools functionality plus additional GeoLibre-authored tools as a wasm-bindgen browser library and a WASI tool runner, letting users read/write GeoTIFF/COG, run raster/vector/LiDAR and SAR processing, and execute registered tools entirely in the browser or Node. Notable features are an in-memory /work filesystem WASI runner, demo web UI, published npm/PyPI packages and Docker-distributable static demo images so tools run client-side with no server compute.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively developed, has many stars, publishes npm/PyPI packages and Docker demo images and includes a working browser demo, indicating a beta-level maturity with install/run instructions; however the repository is only ~5 months old so lacks the long track record or broad ecosystem integration needed for TRL7+.
prerequisites: npm/Node and browser familiarity for the demo
optional: Rust toolchain to build from source
student_project_ideas: Build a browser-based workflow that ingests a Sentinel-1 scene (COG), applies radiometric calibration and computes a SAR index using geolibre-rust, then visualises results in a web map.
Create a GIS pipeline that converts drone-derived GeoTIFFs into COGs, runs a slope/contour tool from geolibre-rust in the browser, and compares results to GDAL outputs for a validation report.

tools.name: simplexai-labs/linger
tools.desc: Linger is An Open-Source Personal Agent That Runs Fully on Your PC.  We aim to break Big Tech’s grip on AI by bringing powerful local AI to everyday computers through efficient model–harness co-design, so everyone can run their own.

cls.summary: Linger is an open-source personal AI agent that runs local large language models on a consumer PC to provide a proactive, memory-enabled assistant.
cls.what_it_does: Linger installs and runs large local language models on desktop hardware using an MoE inference approach so bigger models fit on GPUs with limited memory, and provides an agent framework (teams, memory, background tasks and desktop/browser automation) that keeps data on your device. It is used as a personal assistant that can read inboxes, schedule background tasks, and act proactively, notable for its PolyStrata MoE engine and an installer that selects and configures models for your hardware.
cls.trl_rationale: The README describes a feature-rich system and the project has community interest (stars), but the repository is only 7 days old so it lacks a demonstrated long-track production record; per TRL guidance that limits it to TRL 5.
prerequisites: Discrete GPU (recommendations in README e.g. 12 GB GPU) and substantial RAM (e.g. 32–64 GB)
Node.js / TypeScript runtime and basic desktop privileges for installers
Disk space for model weights (can be tens to hundreds of GB)
student_project_ideas: Build a project that connects Linger to a research group’s shared calendar and demonstrates automated meeting follow-ups and task delegation while keeping data local.
Create a lightweight plugin that uses Linger’s local LLM runtime to summarise lab notebook entries and integrates results into a Git-based project workflow.

tools.name: rokbenko/quackd
tools.desc: One CLI for all your robots. Connect them, command them, and let them work together, each with an LLM for a brain (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Grok, or local via Ollama or vLLM), VLAs for arms and decision LLMs (Jev, Laya, Kev). Drives Microduck, Open Duck Mini, LeRobot, XLeRobot, AlohaMini, ToddlerBot, or any ROS 2 base from a laptop, offboard.

cls.summary: quackd is a Python CLI that connects multiple robots (real or simulated) and gives each an LLM 'brain' so you can send high-level goals and have robots plan and coordinate actions.
cls.what_it_does: quackd registers heterogeneous robots via adapter manifests that declare each robot's body and skills, then runs an LLM pilot for each robot to select and execute skills step-by-step toward a user goal. It supports multi-robot coordination (a 'flock'), integrates with cloud and local LLMs and enforces execution contracts (allowed skills, step limits, human approval). Notable points are direct ROS 2 support, multiple commercial and local LLM backends, and tooling for running both hardware and simulated/mocked robots from one CLI.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 81 days old so age limits the TRL to about 5 despite visible demos and ~300 stars; README describes real-hardware runs and many integrations but there is limited evidence of long-term production use or stable releases.
prerequisites: familiarity with ROS 2 and robot adapters
access to LLM API keys (for cloud LLMs) or local LLM runtimes (Ollama/vLLM/llama.cpp)
student_project_ideas: Build a lab assignment where students register a simulated ROS 2 robot with quackd and implement a .duck task for 'find and fetch' to evaluate how different LLM backends (local vLLM vs OpenAI) affect plan robustness.

Integrate a low-cost robot arm (real or simulated) with quackd and extend an adapter to add a custom skill, then measure and report on verification behaviour when the LLM executes multi-step manipulation tasks.

tools.name: T-Crypt/berth
tools.desc: Berth is a lightweight GPU resource manager written in Go. It controls which applications get access to your GPU, when they get it, and how that access is handed off.

cls.summary: Berth is an open-source Go daemon that leases GPU memory to applications so multiple GPU users (LLM engines, ComfyUI, games, containers) take turns and avoid out-of-memory crashes.
cls.what_it_does: Berth brokers access to a machine's GPU memory by queuing requests with priorities, draining and unloading holders, and granting timed leases so only one engine loads at once; it supports running engines directly, in containers, and integrates with ComfyUI and model-swapping tools. It is notable for parking models to RAM or using CUDA checkpointing to speed handoffs and for surviving daemon restarts so running engines reattach.
cls.trl_rationale: The README describes alpha v0.6.0 and daily use on an RTX 4090 with testers on Windows, showing early adopters, but the repository is only 37 days old so it cannot be rated above TRL 5 despite notable interest.
prerequisites: familiarity with NVIDIA GPUs and drivers (CUDA)
student_project_ideas: Set up Berth on a shared workstation to coordinate inference workloads (vLLM, llama.cpp, ComfyUI) and measure switch times and throughput with and without parking, presenting the results as a lab report.

Integrate Berth with a containerised robotics perception pipeline to ensure an object-detection model and a simulator take turns on the GPU, implement priority policies, and evaluate latency impact during handoffs.

tools.name: puritysb/AgentDeck
tools.desc: Local dashboards and physical controls for AI coding agents — native 3D aquariums, Stream Deck, Apple/Android apps, e-ink, ESP32 and LED displays.

cls.summary: AgentDeck is an open-source local dashboard and device integration suite for monitoring and controlling AI coding agents across desktops, mobile devices and small hardware displays.
cls.what_it_does: AgentDeck observes local AI agent sessions and presents status, history and usage limits in a desktop/mobile dashboard, terminal UI and a variety of hardware surfaces (Stream Deck, tablets, e‑ink, ESP32-driven pixel displays). It is used as a monitoring and control layer for developer agents, notable for its multiple native clients (macOS/iOS/Android), daemon + CLI integration, and many supported small-device outputs including a novelty '3D aquarium' view.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively developed, has many stars, native macOS/iOS apps (App Store listing) and hardware firmware examples, indicating real usage; however the repository is under one year old so by the TRL rules it should be capped at TRL 6.
prerequisites: macOS/iOS for native Apple app builds
familiarity with agent CLIs (Claude, Codex, OpenCode or compatible agents) for full functionality
student_project_ideas: Build a lab assignment where students extend AgentDeck to monitor a simple group of local agent processes (e.g. OpenCode or a small LLM wrapper), log their activity, and display aggregate usage on an ESP32-driven pixel board.

Create a student project to add a new hardware integration (e.g. Raspberry Pi e-ink panel) that subscribes to the AgentDeck daemon and provides compact session summaries and approval controls for long-running agent tasks.

tools.name: aliaihub/awesome-hermes-usecases
tools.desc: Curated real-world use cases for Hermes Agent — the self-improving AI agent from Nous Research. Backed by primary sources.

cls.summary: A curated collection of practical workflows, starter kits and deployment guides showing how to use Hermes Agent (an agentic AI) for automation and developer workflows.
cls.what_it_does: This repository collects real-world use cases, guides and runnable demos for Hermes Agent, covering tasks from scheduled PR review and team bots to reverse engineering and local model quantization. It is used as a reference and jump‑start for deploying, configuring and extending Hermes-based agents, with links to starter kits, recipes and validated results. The collection is notable for grouping evidence-backed examples and integration notes (interfaces, hosting, memory/orchestration) rather than being a software library itself.
cls.trl_rationale: This is a curated, actively maintained collection of use cases for Hermes Agent created ~209 days ago with many community examples and demos; it documents practical workflows rather than itself being a production platform, so maturity is at an alpha/early‑in‑use level.
prerequisites: familiarity with Hermes Agent / Nous Research tooling
experience with LLMs, Docker and messaging integrations (Telegram/Discord) helpful
student_project_ideas: Build and evaluate a Hermes-based scheduled PR review bot for a course repository, measuring precision of suggested changes and automating issue creation.
Implement a team Telegram assistant using a starter demo from the repo to manage lab tasks and persistent project context across students, then report on usability and failure modes.

tools.name: mohitsoni48/TurboLLM
tools.desc: Run any local LLM engine, auto-tuned to your GPU — polished web UI + OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API. Point Claude Code at your own machine in one command. No Electron, no Python, offline-first.

cls.summary: TurboLLM runs and auto-tunes local LLM inference engines on your GPU and exposes an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API with a browser UI.
cls.what_it_does: TurboLLM launches a lightweight local daemon that probes and auto-tunes any llama-server-compatible engine (including community forks) to get best tokens/sec on your GPU, serves models over an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API, and provides a polished web UI for local use. It is notable for automatically benchmarking hardware and engine capabilities, loading engines on demand, and targeting performance without bundling Electron or Python.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active (last push recently) and has moderate community interest (≈296 stars, CLI usage documented), with install/run instructions and measured benchmarks, indicating a beta-level project; however it is only ~5 months old (158 days) so it lacks the multi-release, long-term production track record needed for TRL7+.
prerequisites: local model files (GGUF) or compatible llama-server binaries
student_project_ideas: Build a small agent that runs on a lab machine and uses TurboLLM as its local LLM backend to compare latency and throughput across different quantised GGUF models and present results in a dashboard.
Integrate TurboLLM with a simple robotics control pipeline (ROS bridge) to host a local instruction-following model and evaluate on-board inference latency and safety constraints for edge deployment.

tools.name: ANDRETRIPOL/OpenGhost
tools.desc: Open desktop AI agent for Windows, macOS and Linux, written from scratch: its own agent engine, its own browser tooling and its own drawing engine that shows what it explains.

cls.summary: OpenGhost is an open-source desktop AI agent (Electron app) that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and pairs conversational assistance with a built-in drawing/visualisation engine and a controllable browser pane.
cls.what_it_does: OpenGhost provides a desktop conversational agent that can run commands, edit files, interact with git, browse signed-in pages and produce live diagrams, charts and images alongside text answers. It is used as an interactive assistant: you chat with the agent, it can plan multi-step tasks and show the work with editable visualisations, and it ships as an Electron app with releases for major desktop OSes. Notable features are its bespoke drawing engine (over 40 kinds of drawings), an agent loop with helper tools, and an integrated browser the agent can drive.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is young (created 53 days ago) but already publishes desktop releases and a browser demo, showing early adoption beyond a throwaway prototype; age limits TRL and there is no long track record of production use or stable ecosystem yet.
prerequisites: API key(s) for LLM services (Anthropic Claude or other supported backends) unless running with a local LLM option
student_project_ideas: Integrate OpenGhost with a small local LLM (e.g. llama.cpp backend) and build a course exercise that demonstrates offline agent workflows for code-editing and automated testing.

Use OpenGhost's drawing engine to create an assignment where students prompt the agent to generate system architecture diagrams for a given requirements set, then compare and extend the generated diagrams with manual edits.

tools.name: openshaders/openshaders
tools.desc: The biggest open-source home for shaders on the web.

cls.summary: OpenShaders is an open-source collection and platform for web GPU/WebGL shaders, with a live editor and ready-to-use components for embedding shader effects in websites.
cls.what_it_does: OpenShaders collects, hosts and intends to provide an editor and registry for fragment/vertex shaders that run in WebGL and WebGPU. It is used to explore, claim, edit and embed shader code into web projects and (eventually) to install shader packages via a registry and React components. It is notable for focusing on reusable, web-ready shaders and an editorial platform rather than being a low-level engine or simulator.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (created ~72 days ago) and README describes a platform 'coming soon' with limited source code visible; there is evidence of active work and a website but no long track record or stable releases, so maturity matches an experimental prototype (TRL 3).
prerequisites: familiarity with WebGL or WebGPU and GLSL/HLSL shader concepts
React knowledge to use provided components
student_project_ideas: Create a web demo that integrates an OpenShaders effect into a three.js scene to visualise airflow or surface properties on a simple CAD model.
Build a small interactive website that lets users tweak shader parameters (colour, noise, lighting) and measure perceived performance across WebGL and WebGPU backends.

tools.name: loyal-studio/Honami-Animation-System
tools.desc: Honami Animation System is a complete, from-scratch alternative to Unity's built-in Animator. Designed for Unity 6, it gives you a powerful node-graph editor, built-in procedural rigging and seamless Timeline integration - all at zero runtime allocation cost.

cls.summary: Honami is an open-source Unity 6 package that replaces Unity's built-in Animator with a node-graph animation editor, timeline integration and an allocation-free runtime.
cls.what_it_does: Honami provides visual editors (node graph, timeline, mask and clip editors) to author states, blends, transitions and events, and drives playback via a custom PlayableGraph with zero-runtime-allocation evaluation. It is installed as a Unity package and used inside the Unity Editor to author and preview animation for characters, props and other Animator-driven objects, offering features like per-bone masks, blend trees and timeline-driven sequences.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is an active, well-starred Unity package (MIT licensed) with recent development and working editor features, but it is only ~4.5 months old (137 days) so it lacks the long track record or wide production adoption required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: Basic animation concepts (clips, bones, masks, timelines)
student_project_ideas: Build a small interactive simulation in Unity that uses Honami to author and switch character and machine animations driven by runtime parameters (e.g. speed, load), demonstrating parameterised blend trees and masked upper-body layers.

Create a timeline-driven cinematic of a robotic arm performing an assembly task where Honami's per-bone masks and clip editing are used to author precise motions and trigger events that synchronize with a physics scene.

tools.name: fengyiqicoder/awesome-fable-5.2
tools.desc: Games, 3D worlds and web pages built with Claude Fable 5.2 that you can actually open — 162 live works (every link checked) + 117 video demos, each with a GIF preview and creator credit. Updated daily.

cls.summary: A curated, regularly updated collection of live web demos, games and 3D scenes created with Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, with links, GIF previews and creator credits.
cls.what_it_does: This repository is an "awesome" style index that catalogues hundreds of playable or viewable works generated by Claude Fable 5.2, grouped by category (games, 3D worlds, tools, videos) and linked to live pages and video demos. It is used as a browseable reference and inspiration gallery for people interested in what can be produced by Fable 5.2; the listing highlights notable examples and provides prompts where available.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is very new (created 7 days ago) but already contains a large curated index and many links; that shows early adoption and usefulness as a reference but not a long track record, so an alpha-in-use TRL is appropriate.
student_project_ideas: Survey and categorise entries to identify common prompt patterns and implementation techniques used to produce playable WebGL/three.js demos, then present findings in a short report.
Pick one open example from the list, fork or reimplement it, and add instrumentation (performance profiling and simple telemetry) to study how generative code scales in a browser environment.

tools.name: U-C4N/Autocad-MCP
tools.desc: AutoCAD MCP server for AI agents (Claude, Cursor, any MCP client): 240+ tools to draw, edit and read DWG/DXF drawings. Live AutoCAD via COM, or headless with ezdxf — no AutoCAD needed. Mechanical sheets with ISO GD&T and tolerances, P&ID (ISA-5.1), floor plans, pipe and cable takeoffs.

cls.summary: AutoCAD MCP is a Python server that exposes 250+ CAD operations so AI agents can read, draw and edit DWG/DXF drawings either via a live AutoCAD COM seat or headless using ezdxf.
cls.what_it_does: It provides a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server implementing hundreds of CAD tools (draw, edit, dimension, P&ID, ISO GD&T, takeoffs) that agents can call programmatically. The server can operate live through AutoCAD COM on Windows or headless anywhere using ezdxf and ODA conversion, and includes QA, checkpoints, operation journalling and typed error envelopes for reproducible automation.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository shows a v1.8 release, extensive tests (7,583 collected), active development and 292 stars but is under one year old (~204 days), so it fits a beta-level maturity with versioned releases and active maintainers but limited long-term production track record.
prerequisites: familiarity with AutoCAD concepts (layers, handles, dimensions, DWG/DXF)
Windows/COM knowledge for live engine or familiarity with ODA/accoreconsole for DWG handling
student_project_ideas: Build an agent-based CAD assistant that takes a floor-plan description and produces a multi-sheet DXF using Autocad-MCP headless + ezdxf, then generate a parts list and area takeoff.

Integrate Autocad-MCP with a CI test suite to automatically checkpoint and verify ISO GD&T and dimensioning on mechanical part drawings after parametric changes, demonstrating automated V&V of drawing revisions.

tools.name: jegly/OfflineLLM
tools.desc: Private on-device AI chat for Android - runs any GGUF model locally via llama.cpp with ARM-optimised SIMD. Zero network   permissions, encrypted settings, biometric lock, tamper detection. + GPU Acceleration - PQC ML-DSA-87 signed releases

cls.summary: OfflineLLM is an Android app that runs GGUF-format LLMs fully on-device via llama.cpp with optional Vulkan GPU offload and a focus on privacy and performance tuning.
cls.what_it_does: OfflineLLM lets users import GGUF models and run full LLM inference locally on arm64 Android devices using bundled ggml/llama.cpp kernels and optional Vulkan GPU acceleration. It is notable for enforcing zero network permissions, per-device CPU kernel selection, advanced performance controls, and mobile-specific features like KV-cache incremental chat and tamper detection.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is an active, public Android app with signed releases, many stars and recent pushes, and clear install instructions which indicate a beta-level project; however it is younger than one year (created 2026-04-04), which limits TRL to at most 6 without longer real-world track record.
prerequisites: Familiarity with LLM model formats (GGUF) and llama.cpp/ggml concepts
student_project_ideas: Benchmark and compare on-device performance (CPU vs Vulkan) of a small GGUF model across several Android phones, reporting kernel selection, throughput and power, and present optimization recommendations.

Integrate OfflineLLM with a simple IoT app: use the Android device as a privacy-preserving inference node that accepts local sensor input, generates natural-language summaries locally, and demonstrates secure local-only operation.

tools.name: arounamounchili/linkforge
tools.desc: The LLVM for Robot Descriptions. A programmable IR engine to compose, validate, and compile URDF/XACRO/SRDF models from Python or Blender.

cls.summary: LinkForge is a programmatic robot-description engine that composes, validates and compiles URDF/XACRO/SRDF models from Python or Blender for simulation and control toolchains.
cls.what_it_does: LinkForge lets you define robot models as code (via a headless Python core or a Blender extension), performs automated physics and topology validation, and compiles validated models to standard targets (URDF, SRDF, XACRO and meshes). It is notable for its headless core suitable for CI/ML pipelines, scientific inertia calculations, safe assembly/composition of subassemblies and explicit integrations with ROS 2, MoveIt 2, Gazebo and MuJoCo.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with a published pip package, a detailed README, CI-focused headless core and integrations listed (ROS 2, MoveIt 2, Gazebo, MuJoCo), indicating beta-level maturity. However the project was created ~328 days ago (<1 year) so it lacks the multi-year track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Build a validated URDF/SRDF for a 6-DOF manipulator using LinkForge programmatically, then run simulation validation in Gazebo and implement a simple ROS 2 controller to command joint positions.

Create a Blender-to-RL pipeline: author a modular mobile-manipulator in the LinkForge Blender extension, export headless URDFs for thousands of randomized variants, and use them in a MuJoCo or Gazebo reinforcement-learning training loop to study sim-to-real robustness.

tools.name: mlslabs/MLSLabsGaussianSplattingRenderer-UE
tools.desc: A high-performance Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) plugin developed by MaLanShan Audio & Video Laboratory, designed for real-time visualization, management, and scalable rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and dynamic Volumetric Video (4DGS).

cls.summary: An Unreal Engine 5 plugin that renders high-performance 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic volumetric (4D) video in real time inside UE5 projects.
cls.what_it_does: This plugin provides a custom non-Niagara rendering pipeline for visualising millions of Gaussian splats and playback of volumetric video sequences inside Unreal Engine 5, with Blueprint and Sequencer integration. It is used by copying the plugin into a UE5 project or engine plugins folder and supports Windows, Linux and Android with DirectX12/Vulkan GPU backends, targeting high frame rates on modern GPUs.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with releases, documentation, tutorial video and performance claims; however it was created less than one year ago (281 days), so although mature for a plugin it lacks the multi-year track record required for TRL 7+, limiting it to TRL 6.
prerequisites: Windows 10/11 (64-bit) or supported Linux / Android build environments
GPU with DirectX12 (FL 12_2) or Vulkan support and familiarity with packaging UE plugins
student_project_ideas: Integrate a small robotic scene exported from a simulator into UE5 and use the plugin to visualise sensor-originated point/gaussian data as a volumetric overlay, measuring performance trade-offs between splat count and frame rate.

Create a volumetric video pipeline: convert a small multi-view capture dataset into .sog/.ply 3DGS files, import into UE5 with the plugin and evaluate compression, playback latency and visual quality on desktop and Android VR target.

tools.name: selfpatch/ros2_medkit
tools.desc: ros2_medkit - diagnostics gateway for ROS 2 robots. Faults, live data, operations, scripts, locking, triggers, and OTA updates via REST API. No SSH, no custom tooling.

cls.summary: ros2_medkit is an open-source diagnostics gateway that gives a ROS 2 robot a REST API for faults, live data, snapshots and rosbags without changing robot code.
cls.what_it_does: It monitors a running ROS 2 system, discovers nodes/topics/services/actions automatically, converts error logs, failed actions and /diagnostics into tracked faults, and provides snapshots and rosbags of incidents via a REST API. It is used by running a provided Docker image or installing the package on the robot host and then querying the HTTP API or connecting a web UI; notable features include automatic discovery, saved fault history, live streaming and OTA/update and RBAC plugins.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is a year old with active development, Docker images, documentation, examples and ~287 stars; it provides installable images and integration tutorials and is intended for deployment on robots, indicating production-ready maturity rather than a fragile prototype.
prerequisites: Docker (for quick start) or ability to build/install ROS packages
Linux / robot host network access to the ROS domain
student_project_ideas: Deploy ros2_medkit to a small ROS 2 mobile robot and implement a lab that generates faults (e.g. sensor failures) to collect rosbags and demonstrate fault diagnosis and recovery workflows.
Build an analytics pipeline that ingests rosbags and snapshots exported by ros2_medkit and applies anomaly detection or ML-based root-cause classification, presenting results in a custom dashboard.

tools.name: huawei-csl/MACaQ
tools.desc: SOTA model-agnostic quantization for GGUF, local inference and beyond. Quantize and run text, image, video and audio models with llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch.

cls.summary: MACaQ is an open-source tool for model-agnostic quantization that produces high-quality GGUF models for fast local inference of text, image, video and audio models.
cls.what_it_does: MACaQ quantizes large neural network weights into compact GGUF or backend-specific formats (2/3/4-bit, W4A4 and similar) so models can be run locally with runtimes like llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch. It provides end-to-end workflows (quantize, refine with MACaQ-R, save, and run) and claims faster calibration and lower perplexity than competing quantizers, with recipes for several model families and hardware backends.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository demonstrates a working tool with multi-backend examples, concrete recipes, and downloadable models but is very new (created 7 days ago), so there is limited real-world track record; TRL capped at 5 because of its age despite strong documentation and early community interest.
prerequisites: familiarity with Python and virtual environments
experience with model runtimes (llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers) and PyTorch
sufficient local GPU/CPU resources and knowledge of model formats (GGUF, safetensors)
student_project_ideas: Compare MACaQ-quantized and baseline FP16 models for a small text generation model to measure inference speed, memory usage and output quality using llama.cpp and report trade-offs.
Integrate MACaQ-quantized Diffusers models into a simple local image-generation web app and measure latency and visual fidelity versus an unquantized baseline.

tools.name: Arch1eSUN/Arcgentic
tools.desc: Mechanical plan/dev/self-audit/external-audit gates for AI coding agents, with a configurable role-routing topology engine, an MCP-UI live status panel, and native-tooling Claude Code V2 dispatch. Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and PyPI.

cls.summary: Arcgentic is an open-source harness layer that structures AI coding agent sessions (Codex, Claude Code) into gated engineering workflows with role routing, audit gates and a live MCP UI.
cls.what_it_does: Arcgentic wraps AI coding agents with a repeatable workflow that enforces planning, development, self-audit, optional user testing, external audit and closeout gates so work cannot silently drift. It is used as a Python CLI / plugin bundle (also published to PyPI and npm) to dispatch roles to Codex and Claude Code, maintain session state, and provide an MCP-style status panel and audit tooling.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has published releases (v2.2.1), PyPI and npm distribution, documented verification 'dogfood' evidence for specific Claude Code/Codex paths, and a non-trivial community (285 stars), indicating beta maturity; however the repository is under one year old so TRL is capped at 6.
prerequisites: experience with AI coding agents (Codex or Claude Code)
basic Python and CLI familiarity; npm/Node.js for plugin assets
understanding of software development workflows and code review
student_project_ideas: Build an experiment comparing developer productivity and defect rates when using Arcgentic-gated Codex sessions versus ad-hoc Codex prompts, measuring time-to-fix and audit outcomes.
Integrate Arcgentic with a small CI pipeline and automated tests to create a reproducible agent-driven feature delivery loop, and evaluate how its audit gates interact with automated test failures.

tools.name: crow-hq/llm-wiki-v2
tools.desc: Turn your documents into a Markdown wiki you can read, that answers with citations. Works with any LLM provider, Ollama included. CROW: 99.5% right note read vs 79%, 1.6× faster ingest, 63% fewer LLM tokens, no scaling limit.

cls.summary: LLM Wiki v2 ingests documents into a local Markdown wiki and answers questions with cited sources using any LLM provider (including local Ollama).
cls.what_it_does: It turns files (Markdown, PDF, Office, spreadsheets, etc.) into a browsable Markdown wiki and provides a question-answer interface that cites the notes used. It runs locally with a browser UI, supports multiple LLM providers (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Ollama, Claude/Codex via MCP) and includes a classifier (CROW mode) to keep the knowledge base organised and efficient as it grows.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is installable via pip, has a demo, docs and several hundred stars, showing early adoption, but the repository is only ~54 days old so it lacks a long track record; that recent age limits the TRL to alpha-in-use.
prerequisites: optional: local model runner (Ollama) or API keys (OpenRouter/OpenAI/etc.)
student_project_ideas: Build a course-specific wiki: ingest lecture notes, lab instructions and example reports into llm-wiki2 and evaluate how well its RAG answers cite and retrieve relevant course material.
Integrate a small local Ollama model with the wiki and implement an automated pipeline that files student lab submissions into the wiki and provides instructor-facing search/summary reports.

tools.name: raketenkater/ggrun
tools.desc: llama.cpp/ik_llama.cpp launcher: loads big MoE models across mismatched multi-GPU rigs by exact VRAM math.

cls.summary: ggrun is a launcher that plans and checks how a GGUF LLM will be placed across mixed GPUs and host RAM before starting a llama.cpp/ik_llama.cpp backend.
cls.what_it_does: ggrun inspects model metadata (GGUF) and the machine (CPU, RAM, GPUs, PCIe links), computes a placement and memory plan for large models across mismatched multi‑GPU rigs, and generates/validates the backend command before launching a llama-server backend. It is notable for exact VRAM accounting, bandwidth‑weighted placement on heterogeneous rigs, admission controls (cgroup containment on Linux), and built‑in installers for common platforms.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is an active, documented tool with installers, CI-like setup steps and 284 stars, but the repository is only ~8 months old so it lacks the multi-year track record and broad adoption required for TRL 7+. The README shows practical features and platform installers which support a Beta judgement.
prerequisites: familiarity with local LLM backends (llama.cpp/ik_llama.cpp) and GGUF models
NVIDIA GPU/CUDA knowledge for best results (or Vulkan/CPU fallbacks)
student_project_ideas: Install ggrun on a multi‑GPU workstation and measure how different placement policies affect throughput and latency for a large GGUF model, comparing dry‑run plans with actual performance.

Integrate ggrun with an agent harness (e.g. Claude Code or a simple OpenAI-compatible client) to evaluate session persistence, prefill/decode status reporting and failure recovery when models are partially offloaded to host RAM.

tools.name: datadrivenconstruction/OpenConstructionEstimate-DDC-CWICR
tools.desc: Open multilingual construction cost database for AI Agents - 55K+ work items, 27K+ resources, 30 regions. Semantic search via Qdrant vector DB

cls.summary: A large open multilingual construction cost database and associated pipelines (n8n, Qdrant, CAD/BIM) for automated quantity takeoff and 4D/5D estimating.
cls.what_it_does: Provides a packaged dataset of 55k+ work items, 27k+ resources and 30 region market tracks in tabular and vector formats, plus n8n workflows and pipelines to produce estimates from text, photos/PDFs and CAD/BIM exports. It is used to power semantic search (Qdrant), automated BoQ editors, and CAD/BIM to cost pipelines (4D/5D) and integrates with the OpenConstructionERP project for end-to-end workflows.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo contains a large, organised dataset, example n8n pipelines, Docker deployment notes and an integrated desktop app (OpenConstructionERP) indicating a beta-quality project; however the repository is under one year old (created 2025-12-09), so TRL is limited to 6 despite clear functionality and community interest (stars/forks).
student_project_ideas: Build an automated takeoff pipeline that ingests IFC exports, queries the CWICR catalog via Qdrant semantic search, and produces a localized BoQ and cost summary using the OpenConstructionERP API.

Create a lab exercise to compare quantity extraction accuracy from photo/PDF inputs by running the repository's photo-to-estimate workflow on a small set of annotated site images and measuring BoQ item matching and price variance across two regional tracks.

tools.name: Tencent/wave-mcp
tools.desc: Open-source, license-free MCP server for RTL waveform debug: reads FST waveforms (VCD/FSDB auto-convert) plus a SystemVerilog netlist, with 34 tools covering driver analysis, value/X tracing, pass-fail waveform diff, a browser wave viewer the agent drives, and pre-simulation static analysis.

cls.summary: wave-mcp is an open-source MCP server that lets LLM agents and engineers query and debug RTL waveforms (FST/VCD/FSDB) together with a SystemVerilog netlist and a set of waveform analysis tools.
cls.what_it_does: wave-mcp ingests simulation waveforms and RTL filelists to build a session that supports hierarchical exploration, signal/value queries, driver/ fanin analysis, X-root-cause tracing, waveform diffing and a browser waveform viewer; it is used as an MCP server (CLI, stdio or HTTP) so code agents can call its 37 tools programmatically. It is notable because it reads FST directly, auto-converts VCD/FSDB, provides static netlist analysis via pyslang, and is released as a license-free, production-validated open-source stack.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 113 days old (younger than one year) so TRL is capped; however the README documents extensive production validation on real chip projects, many tools, examples and installation instructions, and active repo activity and stars, consistent with a beta-level (TRL 6) maturity.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of RTL (SystemVerilog/VHDL) and waveform concepts (FST/VCD/FSDB)
familiarity with command-line tools and agent MCP configuration
student_project_ideas: Build an automated verification report pipeline that uses Verilator to produce FST traces, calls wave-mcp via its prepare_session and tools to detect first-failing signals and generate a human-readable debugging summary for each failing test.

Integrate wave-mcp with a simple Code Agent (e.g., Codex or an LLM client) to create an interactive assistant that answers signal queries and visually opens the browser waveform at suspicious times, and evaluate its usefulness on an open RTL design (e.g., OpenTitan IP).

tools.name: Cohenjikan/shiyun
tools.desc: 把中国三千年的诗放进一片可漫游的三维星系：每位诗人是一颗星，每首诗都有坐标，星与星之间的虚空是「一切可能的诗」。32,657 位诗人 / 933,857 首。灵感来自刘慈欣《诗云》。

cls.summary: An open-source web application that maps hundreds of thousands of Chinese poems and poets into an interactive, navigable 3D 'poetry galaxy' rendered in the browser.
cls.what_it_does: Shiyun ingests large Chinese poetry corpora and places each poet as a star and every poem at a unique coordinate in an interactive 3D scene, letting users fly, pick stars to read poems, search by line, and 'unrank' generated poems from numeric addresses. It runs entirely in the browser using React + three.js, provides offline static deployment instructions and data pipeline docs, and emphasises a reversible indexing engine implemented in TypeScript.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with many stars, complete README, demo site and tests, but it is under 1 year old (162 days) and primarily a front-end art/prototype rather than a widely adopted production library, so maturity corresponds to alpha-in-use.
prerequisites: familiarity with React, TypeScript and three.js
student_project_ideas: Extend the visualization to show temporal or stylistic evolution by augmenting the dataset with metadata (era, style) and adding animated filters and timeline controls.
Implement a metrics panel that computes network statistics (centrality, communities) of the poets' gift/response graph and visualises those analytics within the 3D scene.

tools.name: nerficg-project/faster-gaussian-splatting
tools.desc: An efficient and research-friendly Gaussian Splatting framework described in the CVPR'26 paper "Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization"

cls.summary: Faster Gaussian Splatting is a CUDA/PyTorch implementation that speeds up 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel-view synthesis and scene reconstruction, trading GPU memory for faster training and rendering.
cls.what_it_does: It implements a highly-optimised Gaussian Splatting pipeline for reconstructing and rendering 3D scenes from images, focusing on faster optimization, lower VRAM usage and extensibility. Users install the CUDA backend as a PyTorch extension or use the native implementation to train and render 3DGS models; notable features include fused backward passes, VRAM-informed pruning, and multiple research variants (dynamic 4D, fused optimizer, ablation testbed).
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is the official implementation accompanying a CVPR 2026 paper, actively maintained with multiple branches and installable CUDA/PyTorch extension; however it is younger than one year (≈280 days) so it fits a beta-stage maturity rather than long-term production proven (TRL 7+).
prerequisites: NVIDIA GPU with recent CUDA toolkit (recommended CUDA 12.8)
Linux or Windows familiarity for GPU builds
student_project_ideas: Integrate Faster-GS with a drone photogrammetry pipeline to reconstruct a small outdoor scene and compare reconstruction quality and training speed against the original graphdeco Gaussian Splatting implementation.

Modify the FasterGSFused branch to measure VRAM and training-time trade-offs when enabling/disabling specific optimisations (pruning, fused backward) and produce a reproducible performance study on different GPU types.

tools.name: alibaba/tair-kvcache
tools.desc: Alibaba Cloud's high-performance KVCache system for LLM inference, with components for global cache management, inference simulation(HiSim), and more.

cls.summary: Tair KVCache is an open-source distributed metadata manager and supporting components that coordinate multi-tier KV caches to accelerate large-language-model inference.
cls.what_it_does: Tair KVCache provides a centralized metadata plane (KVCache Manager) and supporting clients/connectors so inference engines can discover, reserve and reuse cached KV blocks across requests and nodes; it also includes HiSim for simulating inference/cache behaviour. It is used as infrastructure alongside LLM runtimes: inference services call the manager to find cache locations while the data plane performs direct transfer to/from storage backends, enabling multi-tier DRAM/SSD caching, two-phase writes, quotas and eviction policies.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is a substantial, actively maintained C++ project with clients, modules and documentation and ~283 stars, indicating early community adoption; however it was created ~323 days ago (under one year), so it fits a beta-level maturity rather than long-term production/industry-standard status.
prerequisites: distributed systems concepts (consensus, leader election, quotas, eviction)
gRPC / protobuf and basics of LLM inference architectures
student_project_ideas: Integrate KVCM with a small Hugging Face transformer inference service to measure time-to-first-token (TTFT) and throughput improvements when reusing KV cache across requests.
Use the HiSim simulator to replay inference traces and compare eviction policies (LRU, usage-proportional) and tiering strategies (DRAM/SSD) to quantify hit-rate vs cost trade-offs.

tools.name: nirholas/three.ws
tools.desc: Give your AI agent a 3D body: rigged GLB avatars from text or a photo, an LLM brain, a Solana wallet, a one-tag embed.

cls.summary: three.ws is an open-source, browser-native platform that generates rigged GLB 3D avatars from text, images or uploaded models and exposes them to AI agents via an MCP-compatible HTTP API.
cls.what_it_does: It produces textured, rigged 3D models (GLB) from text, images or sketches and provides an embeddable web viewer and an MCP server endpoint so coding agents (Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor, etc.) can request and use 3D assets. Notable features include keyless, in-browser generation/hosting, integrations for multiple MCP clients, and tooling to embed interactive 3D models in places like GitHub READMEs.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is active, has documentation, a public website and integrations, and ~281 stars which indicates community interest; the repository is ~313 days old (under one year), so while it appears beta-ready with usable demos and MCP integrations, it lacks a longer production track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: basic familiarity with three.js/WebGL and GLB/GLTF formats
familiarity with MCP-style agent integrations or LLM-based agents (helpful)
student_project_ideas: Build a simple web demo that uses three.ws Forge to generate rigged GLB avatars from class-generated prompts and integrates them into a web-based scene with interactive controls (three.js) to demonstrate embedding and runtime animation.

Create a conversational agent prototype that uses three.ws as the 3D body provider and an MCP-capable LLM (e.g., Claude Code or an open MCP client) to drive gestures/animations in response to dialogue, then evaluate usability in a human–agent interaction lab study.

tools.name: mujocolab/mjviser
tools.desc: Web-based MuJoCo viewer powered by Viser

cls.summary: mjviser is a web-based viewer that lets you run and interactively visualise MuJoCo simulations in a browser using the Viser web server.
cls.what_it_does: mjviser hosts MuJoCo simulation state in a small local web server and provides an interactive browser-based viewer with simulation controls, joint/actuator sliders, contact/force visualisation and camera tracking. It is used either from the command line (uvx or an installed console script) or from Python by passing a mujoco model and data to the Viewer API, and it is notable for exposing Viser extension points so instructors or researchers can add custom GUI controls and overlays.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active (created 2026-03, last push 2026-11) with many stars (281), examples, an API and integration notes, indicating a beta-quality project; however it is younger than one year so lacks longer production track record required for TRL7+.
prerequisites: Viser (server/client library) or the ability to install mjviser via pip
student_project_ideas: Build a controller lab where students implement different controllers (e.g. PID, PD with gravity compensation, RL policy) for a MuJoCo robot and compare performance using mjviser for playback and contact visualisation.
Combine mjviser with a data-logging pipeline (e.g. save mujoco MjData traces to files) to implement motion playback, trajectory optimisation and visualise before/after comparisons in the browser.

tools.name: khanh020905/my-office
tools.desc: Văn phòng 3D cho các phiên Claude Code · A 3D office for your Claude Code sessions

cls.summary: My Office is an open-source 3D web “office” that visualises Claude Code AI sessions as animated characters and provides a Node.js CLI/service to run and manage the environment.
cls.what_it_does: My Office maps each Claude Code session to a character at a desk in an interactive 3D office: sessions move between rooms to read files, run commands, or deploy and the UI shows machine usage and idle/forgotten developer servers. It runs as a Node.js application with a CLI installer that can install hooks into Claude Code, run as a background service, and serves a three.js-based web demo; notable features include built-in session lifecycle behaviours, telemetry options, and a demo you can run without installing.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is very new (created 20 days ago) so it cannot claim long-term production use; however the README is substantial, it provides a runnable demo and a CLI/service installer, and community interest (many stars/forks) suggests early adoption consistent with an alpha-in-use level.
student_project_ideas: Extend the My Office UI to visualise CI/CD pipeline status and link deploy events to desk animations, demonstrating how visual metaphors can communicate pipeline state to teams.

Adapt the office to simulate multi-agent workflows for a software engineering course: instrument the sessions to log resource use and evaluate scheduling or autoscaling policies (combine with a lightweight container manager).

tools.name: timoncool/dub-studio
tools.desc: Free offline AI video dubbing studio for Windows — voice cloning, translation, subtitles & on-screen-text localization. 100% local, one native .exe, zero Python.

cls.summary: Dub Studio is a Windows desktop application for fully local AI video dubbing, voice cloning, translation and subtitle/on‑screen text localisation.
cls.what_it_does: Dub Studio processes video to produce dubbed versions with cloned voices, translated captions and localized on‑screen text using local models and optional cloud fallbacks. It is used as a native Windows .exe (Rust + native C++/CUDA) that downloads and manages models, runs speaker diarization, TTS, ASR and vision stages, and provides an editor with instant preview and an MCP HTTP control interface for automation.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is a working, actively maintained native application with releases, a live demo and many stars, and it downloads and runs real models locally; however the repository is only ~149 days old so it lacks the longer track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: NVIDIA GPU recommended for local CUDA engines
moderate disk space for model downloads
student_project_ideas: Create a batch workflow that uses Dub Studio's MCP HTTP interface to automatically dub a set of lecture videos into another language and compare automated vs. human-corrected subtitles.

Evaluate and quantify lip-sync/timing quality across different local and cloud TTS engines by running the same source clips through multiple engine selections and measuring alignment and intelligibility.

tools.name: Physics-Scaling/GeoPT
tools.desc: Official Code for "GeoPT: Scaling Physics Simulation via Lifted Geometric Pre-Training" (ICML 2026) https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.20399

cls.summary: GeoPT is a Python codebase that pre-trains neural models on large-scale geometric data to improve general physics simulation performance and reduce task-specific training data needs.
cls.what_it_does: GeoPT implements a dynamics‑lifted geometric pre‑training method that generates self‑supervised trajectory data from geometric shapes and trains a unified model to predict physical dynamics across tasks. It is used by generating pre-training data (scripts provided), installing the Python requirements, and fine‑tuning the pre‑trained model on downstream simulation benchmarks; notable aspects are its large synthetic dataset generation and claims of substantial data savings and improved scaling with model/data size.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is the official code for a peer‑reviewed ICML/ICLR workshop paper, includes released pre‑training data generation code and experiment scripts, and has active development and community interest (stars, recent pushes); however it is under one year old so lacks the multi‑year production track record required for TRL 7+, hence TRL 6 (beta).
student_project_ideas: Fine-tune GeoPT on a small CFD-like dataset (e.g., flow around an airfoil from ShapeNet-derived geometries) to compare prediction accuracy and required supervised data against training from scratch.

Use the provided data_generation scripts to create a reduced synthetic dataset and evaluate how pre-training transfer improves dynamics prediction for a robotics manipulation simulation using a simple particle or mesh-based simulator.

tools.name: autonomous-ai/autonomous-grid
tools.desc: Your AI intranet: network the computers you already own for inference and training.

cls.summary: Autonomous Grid lets you network multiple local computers behind a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to route inference and training jobs to whichever machine holds the required model.
cls.what_it_does: Grid creates a local intranet that exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API and routes requests to the best machine that has a requested model installed, supporting model download, engine installation and both inference and experimental training. It is used via a CLI to start a grid host, join worker machines that run models (llama.cpp, vLLM, etc.), and point apps at the grid address; it is notable for focusing on local, self-hosted orchestration of LLM inference across heterogeneous machines.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active (created 153 days ago) with a polished README, install scripts for multiple OSes, and 278 stars indicating community interest; however it is younger than one year so there is not yet long-term production track record, so TRL is capped at 6 (beta).
prerequisites: familiarity with CLI and basic Linux/macOS/Windows administration
understanding of LLM model files (GGUF) and local model runtimes
networking basics (local IPs, ports) and OpenAI-compatible API usage
student_project_ideas: Deploy a small grid of two Raspberry Pi (or VMs) and a workstation, run a compact GGUF model on the workstation, and build a web client that sends inference requests through the grid to measure latency and throughput under different network conditions.

Integrate Grid with a data-collection service (Prometheus + Grafana) and instrument model selection and resource usage to evaluate scheduling strategies for routing inference requests across heterogeneous hardware.

tools.name: jeantimex/webgpu-water
tools.desc: A real-time water simulation using WebGPU

cls.summary: A browser-based real-time water demo that implements a GPU heightfield water simulation and advanced rendering (reflections, refractions, caustics) using the WebGPU API and WGSL shaders.
cls.what_it_does: This project ports the classic WebGL water demo to WebGPU, running a GPU-accelerated heightfield wave simulation on a 256×256 grid and rendering reflections, refractions, Fresnel, and caustics in real time in the browser.
