Integrate maplibre-gl-lidar with a small backend (Entwine EPT server) to serve tiled point clouds and implement a UI to filter by classification and export selected points to GeoJSON or CSV.

tools.name: bearlikelion/godot-box3d
tools.desc: Godot Extension to add Box3D physics

cls.summary: A GDExtension that replaces Godot 4's built-in 3D physics backend with Erin Catto's Box3D to provide an alternative physics solver inside Godot projects.
cls.what_it_does: godot-box3d integrates the Box3D physics engine into Godot 4 as a drop-in replacement for PhysicsServer3D so existing physics nodes keep working; you enable it by installing the addon and switching the project physics backend. It is notable for being a high-performance, multithreaded solver derived from Source-engine lineage (Rubikon/Box3D) and for providing benchmarked improvements over Godot's default and other backends in the author's tests.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 138 days old (younger than one year) so TRL is capped; however it has releases, documentation site, benchmarks, cross-platform builds, and 200+ stars which indicate a beta-level, actively developed project rather than a tiny proof-of-concept.
prerequisites: Familiarity with Godot 4 (project settings, nodes, scene system)
C++ toolchain knowledge for building GDExtensions if building from source
Basic understanding of rigid-body physics concepts
student_project_ideas: Compare the behaviour and performance of a fast-contact scenario (e.g. a skate/surf map or vehicle suspension) in Godot using the built-in physics, godot-jolt, and godot-box3d and report differences in stability, step time, and contact forces.

Build a small robotics simulation (a wheeled robot or manipulator) in Godot and use godot-box3d to evaluate collision response and controller stability under different solver settings, then integrate telemetry export for offline analysis in Python.

tools.name: godot-fun/gai
tools.desc: An AI coding agent built in Godot.

cls.summary: GAI is an AI coding agent implemented as a Godot app that reads, edits, runs and tests code locally with a live, GPU-driven UI and persistent plain-text memory.
cls.what_it_does: GAI runs an autonomous coding loop inside a Godot scene: it inspects a repository, searches the web or local context, edits files, runs commands/tests, shows diffs and can revert changes with Git. It is notable for running locally (GGUF/local models supported), a GPU-rendered interactive UI with animated scenes, built-in persistent `.memory/` and a framework (zfoo) for embedding agent tools and skills.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has a clear README, examples and 200+ stars which shows interest and usability, but it is only 155 days old (<1 year) so it lacks a longer track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: Python and Node.js (for dependencies and browser service)
student_project_ideas: Build a constrained-code-fix workflow where GAI is given unit-test failures in a small Godot project and students evaluate the agent's edits, rollback behaviour and test pass/fail rates.
Extend the zfoo framework skill set by adding a hardware-in-the-loop skill that uses a local serial interface (Python) so the agent can run, observe and adapt firmware tests for a microcontroller.

tools.name: heterodoxin/AbliteratedOutTheBox
tools.desc: llama.cpp fork that abliterates at inference

cls.summary: A fork of llama.cpp that modifies a model's hidden activations at inference to bypass refusals and produce content for flagged prompts without changing stored weights.
cls.what_it_does: This project reads two opposing 'directions' encoded in the prompt (refuse vs comply and disclaimer vs clean), detects when a prompt would lead to a refusal by running a short look-ahead, and applies an in-graph projection edit at a common layer to suppress refusal/disclaimer signals during generation. It is used by building the runtime, converting a model to GGUF, and running the provided binary; notable is that it performs the edit at inference time with no fine-tuning or additional files and claims a single recipe covers many model architectures.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is very new (created ~27 days ago) so it cannot show a long track record; it is a working fork with build instructions and examples (evidence of an installable prototype) but lacks demonstrated production users or stable release history, so an early-alpha TRL is appropriate.
prerequisites: CMake and a C++ build toolchain
GGUF-format LLM model (conversion uses Python with torch and transformers)
Familiarity with local LLM runtimes (llama.cpp) and command-line usage

tools.name: 5p00kyy/club-5060ti
tools.desc: Practical local LLM recipes and benchmarks for RTX 5060 Ti setups

cls.summary: A collection of reproducible local LLM presets, benchmark receipts and setup notes tuned for RTX 5060 Ti (single- and multi‑GPU) inference.
cls.what_it_does: club-5060ti provides exact, copyable presets and verified benchmark evidence for running large language models locally on RTX 5060 Ti GPUs, covering single-card, dual-card and community multi‑GPU lanes. It is used as a practical cookbook and results explorer to reproduce performance, memory and context-length behaviour with tools like llama.cpp, vLLM and NInfer, with emphasis on documented presets and reviewed evidence.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository contains structured presets, many example configs, evidence bundles and a public results explorer and has active commits and community interest, but it is younger than one year (186 days) so it fits a beta-level maturity rather than long-term production track record.
prerequisites: basic understanding of LLM runtimes (llama.cpp, vLLM) and model formats (GGUF)
student_project_ideas: Reproduce one of the published 2x‑5060Ti presets (e.g. Qwen3.8 vLLM route), measure prefill/decode throughput and memory, and compare results between vLLM and llama.cpp implementations.

Extend a preset to mixed GPU topologies (5060Ti + another CUDA card), document changes to the preset and run the benchmark protocol to produce an evidence bundle for comparison with the project's results explorer.

tools.name: zephyr4123/speakmore
tools.desc: SpeakMore：口述成文，划词即译。开源、免费的语音输入与翻译工具，支持 Mac 与 Windows：语音输入、语音翻译、划词翻译。兼容 Gemini、OpenAI、通义千问、DeepSeek、Kimi、智谱 GLM、MiniMax 及任意 OpenAI 兼容服务，语音输入亦可完全在本机运行。附 Typeless 逆向分析。

cls.summary: SpeakMore is an open-source Electron desktop app for cross-application voice dictation and inline translation on macOS and Windows, with optional on-device speech models and support for many cloud LLM/ASR services.
cls.what_it_does: SpeakMore captures user speech via a global hotkey, cleans and punctuates the transcribed text and writes it into the current input, performs speech-to-speech/text translation, and provides a selection-based (划词) inline translation card. It is used as a desktop accessibility/productivity tool and notable for offering both on-device offline ASR options and configurable connections to many cloud LLM/ASR providers.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (35 days) which caps TRL to at most 5; the README and metadata show a well-documented, installable Electron app with many features and active interest (stars/forks), but there are no stable releases or long-term production track record visible in the repo.
prerequisites: Node.js / Electron tooling for building from source (if compiling)
student_project_ideas: Compare on-device ASR accuracy and latency (metal/vulkan/cpu variants) against cloud ASR (OpenAI/Gemini/DeepSeek) for noisy and quiet environments and report trade-offs in cost, privacy and latency.
Integrate SpeakMore's CLI or hotkey-triggered transcription into a small accessibility prototype that inserts structured text into a custom web form and evaluate user workflow improvements.

tools.name: artembobkin/ImmersiveMap
tools.desc: Native Swift 6 + Metal map rendering engine for SwiftUI. Globe and flat vector-tile maps with labels, SwiftUI markers and avatars, on iOS and macOS.

cls.summary: ImmersiveMap is a native Swift + Metal map rendering engine that provides globe and flat vector-tile maps with SwiftUI integration for iOS and macOS.
cls.what_it_does: ImmersiveMap renders vector-tile maps (from built-in Protomaps PMTiles or user-provided tile archives) as either a globe or flat map using Metal, and integrates directly into SwiftUI apps with support for markers, avatars, 3D models and tour-video export. It is used as a client-side mapping/rendering library embedded in Apple apps and is notable for reading PMTiles from storage with no tile server and shipping 3D building models and biome data inside the package.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has an active repo with documentation, examples and steady development (207 stars, recent commits and a documentation site) indicating a beta-quality library; however it is younger than one year (created 2026-05-25) so lacks the multi-year production track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of Metal and vector tile concepts (PMTiles/protomaps)
student_project_ideas: Build an iOS SwiftUI app that loads a custom PMTiles file to visualise local OSM data, add SwiftUI markers and export a short tour video demonstrating navigation around the map.
Integrate custom 3D building models into ImmersiveMap and evaluate rendering performance and level-of-detail trade-offs on different Apple devices, reporting frame rates and memory use.

tools.name: open-nvr/open-nvr
tools.desc: The open platform for AI on your cameras: a self-hosted NVR (ONVIF/RTSP, recording, WebRTC) running any AI model through one open contract, with an app SDK and one-click apps. New capabilities arrive as software, not new boxes. Air-gapped or connected, audited end to end. Home Assistant built in. AGPLv3. A Frigate/ZoneMinder alternative.

cls.summary: OpenNVR is an open-source, self-hosted network video recorder and edge-AI platform that runs any vision model on your cameras, records streams, and exposes an app/adapter SDK for building camera applications.
cls.what_it_does: OpenNVR ingests ONVIF/RTSP camera streams, records and serves live video like an NVR, and routes frames to pluggable AI model adapters for detection, ANPR, captioning and other analytics. It is deployed as a Docker stack for local or air-gapped operation, provides auditing of model inferences, and offers SDKs to write apps or adapters so new capabilities arrive as software rather than new hardware.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with install instructions, Docker quickstart, SDKs on PyPI and a modest user community (206 stars), but it is under one year old (created 2026-03-30) so it lacks the longer track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Build an ANPR pipeline using OpenNVR with a custom adapter that sends plate detections to a time-series database and visualises occupancy trends in Grafana.

Create a lab exercise comparing on-device vs cloud-based object detectors by deploying two adapters (local and cloud) in OpenNVR and measuring latency, bandwidth and audit logs for a set of test scenarios.

tools.name: makermate/clarvis-ai
tools.desc: Clarvis - 3D Printing Made Easy

cls.summary: Clarvis is an open-source AI-driven 3D‑printing assistant that converts images, sketches or text into 3D models, slices them to G-code and sends prints to networked printers via chat interfaces.
cls.what_it_does: Clarvis orchestrates an end-to-end 3D printing workflow: it accepts sketches, photos or text via chat (Telegram/Discord/WhatsApp), generates or finds 3D models with AI or library search, slices with CuraEngine to produce G-code, and sends that G-code to printers using Moonraker (Klipper) or PrusaLink. It is notable because it combines AI model generation/editing, remote slicing and printer control into a single Dockerised, chat-driven stack.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo provides a complete, Dockerised stack (gateway, slicer, CLI), an interactive setup script and documented integrations, indicating a beta-quality project; however it is under one year old (created 252 days ago) so lacks the longer track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: basic 3D printing knowledge (printer network access, .3mf export)
API keys/tokens for Google (agent) and optional services (FAL.ai, Thingiverse)
student_project_ideas: Build an automated pipeline that takes student-submitted sketches and produces printable parts: integrate Clarvis with a classroom printer, evaluate print success rates and iterate slicing profiles.

Compare AI-generated models from Clarvis (via FAL.ai) with hand-modeled designs by students, then perform simple structural or printability analysis (e.g. overhangs, print time) and report differences.

tools.name: alisamsam/Solidworks-MCP
tools.desc: MCP server to automate SolidWorks using Claude AI — 22 tools for parts, sketches & features

cls.summary: A Python MCP server that lets Claude AI send natural-language commands to automate SolidWorks (create parts, sketches and features) on Windows.
cls.what_it_does: This project implements a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes 22 tools to control SolidWorks via its COM API, allowing natural-language prompts (via Claude) to create documents, sketches and parametric features. It is used by running the Python server on Windows with a licensed SolidWorks installation and connecting it from the Claude desktop app; notable features include SolidWorks 2023–2025 compatibility, robust API fallback chains, multi-unit support and JSON configuration.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is well-documented, has a modular package layout, version-aware features and 200+ stars indicating community interest; however it is only 240 days old (younger than one year) and lacks a long track record of real-world deployments, so beta (TRL 6) is appropriate.
prerequisites: Windows 10/11 with SolidWorks 2023–2025 installed and licensed
Python 3.10+ and ability to install packages
student_project_ideas: Build a parametric part generator where students design a family of mounting brackets by issuing natural-language prompts to the MCP server, then export and validate the generated STEP files using FreeCAD or a simple dimension-check script.

Create an automated feature validation tool: generate parts via Claude+MCP then run a Python script that reads the model feature list and checks for required features/dimensions as a verification exercise for CAD automation and design rules.

tools.name: Glade-tool/glade-mcp
tools.desc: Connect any MCP-compatible AI client (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) to Unity or Godot. 275+ granular tools, an editor aware system prompt, game design document project context, script semantic search, and skill calibration.

cls.summary: GladeKit MCP connects MCP-compatible AI clients to Unity and Godot editors so agents can inspect and edit projects, run verification probes and assist game/script development inside the editor.
cls.what_it_does: GladeKit MCP runs a local MCP server and editor bridge that exposes a large, editor-aware toolset (275 tools for Unity, 115 for Godot) to AI clients such as Claude Code, Cursor and Windsurf. It is used by installing the Unity UPM package or the Godot addon and configuring an MCP client; notable features include script semantic search, one-call gameplay scaffolders, a verification loop with game-view screenshots and exported build tools so agents can produce and validate editor changes.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active (created 223 days ago) with 200+ stars, documented install steps for Unity and Godot, and release assets for the Godot bridge; however it is under one year old so lacks a long track record required for TRL 7+. The README shows practical features and bridges but not multi-year production adoption evidence.
prerequisites: familiarity with Unity or Godot editor workflows
basic knowledge of MCP clients / LLM-based AI clients
C# (Unity) or GDScript (Godot) for using/editing generated code
student_project_ideas: Use GladeKit MCP with Claude Code to build an LLM-driven NPC behaviour generator in Unity that scaffolds controllers and uses the verification loop to run playability probes.
Create a Godot-based automated testbench that uses GladeKit's verification loop and screenshot probes to detect regressions in level navigation after procedural changes.

tools.name: LexianDEV/FlowKit
tools.desc: An addon for Godot that adds a visual scripting solution, inspired by engines such as Clickteam Fusion 2.5 and Construct's event sheet editors.

cls.summary: FlowKit is a Godot 4 addon that provides an event-sheet, Clickteam/Construct-style visual scripting system for creating game logic without writing code.
cls.what_it_does: FlowKit lets users author event-driven game logic inside Godot via event sheets composed of conditions and actions bound to scene nodes. It integrates into the Godot editor, stores event sheets as .tres resources, and is extensible through a provider system for custom events, conditions and actions. The notable points are its Construct/Clickteam-inspired workflow and runtime engine optimized for Godot scenes.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is a year-old, active Godot addon with a detailed README, wiki and community (205 stars, recent commits), which indicates beta-level maturity; age is under one year so TRL is limited to 6 despite visible adoption.
student_project_ideas: Build a small interactive simulation (e.g., traffic intersection or agent-based model) in Godot and implement the agents' behaviours using FlowKit event sheets to demonstrate event-driven logic without code.
Extend FlowKit by adding custom providers (actions/conditions) that interface Godot with an external system (for example a ROS bridge or MQTT client) to prototype a simple digital-twin interaction.

tools.name: Yun-0000/Anima
tools.desc: Anime characters that feel alive, right in your browser. Chat or just talk out loud: each one answers in their own voice, moves while they speak and reacts with gestures and expressions.

cls.summary: Anima is an open-source web app that renders talking, gesturing anime-style VRM characters in the browser and connects them to chat and voice services.
cls.what_it_does: Anima runs a React + three.js frontend that loads VRM character models and plays retargeted motions while a backend (FastAPI) handles chat replies, streamed speech and a separate 'director' that chooses gestures and expressions. It integrates with third‑party speech and LLM services (ElevenLabs, OpenAI/Deepseek) for live voice and conversational replies, and provides a hosted demo and easy local developer setup.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has a hosted demo, automated frontend/backend setup and several hundred stars, showing beyond a proof‑of‑concept; however it is under one year old (created ~198 days ago) so there is limited long‑term production track record, supporting a TRL of about 6.
prerequisites: Optional API keys for ElevenLabs, OpenAI/Deepseek for full functionality
Basic familiarity with WebRTC and three.js/VRM models
student_project_ideas: Extend the frontend to import a student-created VRM or glTF avatar and implement a new custom motion (using three-vrm and a motion retarget), demonstrating animation blending and lip‑sync.

Replace the director component with a simple rule-based or small LLM controller (e.g. local LLM or OpenAI with a limited budget) to evaluate how different director strategies affect perceived expressiveness and latency.

tools.name: mercurialsolo/claudectl
tools.desc: Hive compute for coding agent swarms - expand your personal compute by adding on-demand agentic swarms

cls.summary: claudectl is a Rust CLI/TUI tool that runs a local 'hive' of agentic LLM sessions to share learned behaviours and automate tool calls for Claude Code and local LLM setups.
cls.what_it_does: claudectl provides an on-device agent-orchestration system (a hive) that advertises on the LAN, shares learned policies across machines, and auto-approves or denies tool calls using a local LLM brain or built-in rules. It is used from the terminal or as a Claude Code plugin to run, monitor and coordinate parallel agent sessions, apply safety rules, and persist learning across machines; notable features include a small standalone binary, TUI dashboard, Homebrew bottle, and explicit support for local LLMs like Ollama.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 228 days old (<1 year) but has releases, detailed docs, a Homebrew bottle, many stars and active pushes; these signs indicate a beta-level, usable project rather than a fragile prototype, so TRL 6 fits the demonstrated maturity.
prerequisites: familiarity with command-line tools and terminals
basic knowledge of local LLMs (e.g. Ollama) and Claude Code plugin usage
Rust toolchain if building from source (rustc 1.88+)
student_project_ideas: Create a lab exercise that integrates claudectl with a local Ollama model to automate safe shell commands and measure how the 'brain' reduces risky operations over time.
Build a student project that uses claudectl's hive to distribute and parallelise automated test runs across multiple machines, adding a metrics dashboard to evaluate cost, speedup and failure modes.

tools.name: YuriCrystal/ai-avatar-bot
tools.desc: Live2D／VRM voice AI avatar with lip sync, knowledge base, operations dashboard, support and analytics｜可一行嵌入網站

cls.summary: A front-end embeddable Live2D/VRM voice AI avatar widget that provides live speech input/output, lip-sync, basic knowledge retrieval and an optional admin backend.
cls.what_it_does: This project provides a one-line embeddable widget (iframe) that shows a Live2D or VRM avatar which can listen (STT), speak (TTS), lip-sync and retrieve answers from a local knowledge base or an optional browser LLM. It is used by dropping the widget files into a website or referencing an embed.js and can optionally connect to serverless functions, a Clerk/Neon backend for admin, analytics and neural TTS; notable points are its pure front-end zero-key mode and support for both 2D Live2D and 3D VRM models.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 161 days old with a working demo, many stars/forks and an admin/backend option, indicating a usable beta-level project; not old enough or evidenced as production in multiple organisations to justify TRL 7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with Live2D or VRM models and three.js
basic knowledge of web audio / Web Speech API and optional WebGPU for WebLLM
student_project_ideas: Embed the avatar widget into a mock product site and connect a custom knowledge JSON to build a conversational help assistant that routes inquiries to a simple backend (Neon Postgres) for analytics.

Create a demonstration digital-customer-support prototype where the avatar triggers site actions via registerTool(), and evaluate UX and reliability when integrated with a simple simulated e-commerce backend.

tools.name: codepawl/creator-generalist
tools.desc: AI agent skills to be professional at 2D and 3D

cls.summary: An AI agent skill pack that automates production of 2D and 3D content (Blender, three.js and game engines) for short videos, assets and small game prototypes.
cls.what_it_does: This repository provides a collection of AI 'skills' that script and assemble 2D and 3D creative pipelines (character modelling, rigging, animation, scene builds, video editing and simple game greyboxes) and can output Blender scenes, three.js/web builds and playable prototypes. It's used by installing the pack and asking the agent for a job (e.g. /3dg, /2dg, /gameg) which then queries for missing details, generates a cheap preview and produces assets and exports for target tools and platforms.
cls.trl_rationale: The README shows a broad feature set (many skills, Blender/three.js/Game engine targets and QA steps) but the repository is only 11 days old, so there is no long track record or stable releases; this looks like an experimental prototype with active early development.
student_project_ideas: Use the agent to generate a low-poly rigged character in Blender, export to glTF and build a short interactive three.js scene that demonstrates animation blending and lighting.

Create a short playable greybox game prototype: ask the agent for a web playtest build, then instrument the output with telemetry (frame time, events) and produce a short QA report comparing performance across browsers.

tools.name: davidsun1234/sichuan-digital-twin-dashboard
tools.desc: A lightweight Sichuan digital twin operation dashboard with Canvas map rendering, realtime simulation and bilingual documentation.

cls.summary: A lightweight, zero-runtime-dependency web dashboard that renders a Sichuan province GeoJSON map on HTML Canvas and simulates realtime operational data for digital-twin style large-screen visualisations.
cls.what_it_does: This project provides a static-web digital twin dashboard template that draws province-level GeoJSON on a high-DPI Canvas, simulates dynamic modules (energy supply, regional load, event timelines) and supports hit-testing, labels and animated map pulses. It is used by cloning the repo and running the included dev server or deploying the static files (GitHub Pages, Nginx, object storage), and notable for having no runtime JS framework dependencies and a complete bilingual README and demo.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is well-documented, has a live GitHub Pages demo, 200+ stars and working code for local dev, indicating beta-level readiness; however it is only ~145 days old with no evidence of long-term production deployments, so TRL is capped at 6.
prerequisites: familiarity with GeoJSON and web deployment
student_project_ideas: Replace the simulated energy and load data with live values from a WebSocket or REST API (mock IoT gateway) and build a simple alerts pipeline that highlights high-load regions on the map.

Extend the dashboard to another province or city by converting public administrative GeoJSON, adding layers for transport or sensor locations, and integrating a basic time-series charting library (e.g., Chart.js) for trend analysis.

tools.name: mrdoob/draco.js
tools.desc: A small, drop-in, pure-JavaScript Draco mesh loader for three.js.

cls.summary: draco.js is a small pure-JavaScript Draco mesh decoder that loads Draco-compressed meshes directly into three.js scenes without requiring a WASM binary.
cls.what_it_does: It decodes Draco-compressed triangle meshes (including glTF KHR_draco_mesh_compression EdgeBreaker and sequential connectivity) entirely in JavaScript as a drop-in DRACOLoader for three.js, enabling smaller network payloads and simpler deployment compared with the official WASM decoder. It is notable for being very small (~18 KB gzipped), easy to ship as a single ES module (no .wasm fetch or worker glue), and delivering decode results identical to the reference decoder with comparable performance on large meshes.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is actively maintained with a live demo, clear README, and 200+ stars, showing adoption and maturity; however it is only ~167 days old (<1 year) so I limit TRL to 6 (beta) despite good documentation and usage alignment with three.js.
student_project_ideas: Build a web-based digital twin viewer that streams compressed glTF models and compares page load and decode times using draco.js versus the WASM draco3d decoder.

Create a three.js scene importer that fetches and decodes large LiDAR/mesh data (exported as glTF with KHR_draco_mesh_compression) and implements level-of-detail streaming for interactive visualization.

tools.name: siva-sub/NekoSpeak
tools.desc: Private, offline AI Text-to-Speech for Android with Kokoro, KittenTTS, Pocket-tts and Piper models.

cls.summary: NekoSpeak is an open-source Android app that runs modern neural Text‑to‑Speech models entirely on-device for offline, privacy-preserving TTS and voice cloning.
cls.what_it_does: NekoSpeak packages multiple on‑device TTS engines (Piper, Pocket‑TTS, Kokoro, Kitten TTS) behind the Android TTS API so apps can synthesize speech without internet access. It provides voice management, downloadable voice/model store, and on‑device voice cloning, optimised for mobile CPUs with an adaptive streaming approach to handle varying device performance.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is ~312 days old (<1 year) but shows multiple releases (v1.4.2), bundled APKs, dozens of releases/stars and active development (native code, JNI, technical docs), indicating beta maturity rather than long production track record.
prerequisites: basic ML model formats (ONNX) and JNI/native integration
student_project_ideas: Build an accessibility Android app that integrates NekoSpeak for custom voice cloning and evaluate user experience and latency on a range of devices.
Benchmark NekoSpeak's engines (Piper, Pocket‑TTS, Kokoro) across several phones to measure real‑time factor and implement an improved adaptive streaming scheduler or multi‑threading strategy.

tools.name: DreamyLab30/Filmimic
tools.desc: Real-time film emulation for Unreal Engine: 21 looks, grain, halation, lens effects, Blueprint controls and reusable presets.

cls.summary: Filmimic is an open-source Unreal Engine plugin that applies real-time film-style color, grain and lens effects as a post-process with presets and Blueprint controls.
cls.what_it_does: Filmimic provides 21 photographic "looks", animated grain, halation, bloom, lens artifacts and many parameterised post-processing controls as an Unreal Engine plugin; it is installed into a project's Plugins folder and controlled via an in-editor Actor, Blueprint API or preset assets. It is notable for a large set of reusable presets, detailed parameter grouping (197 parameters), four quality tiers and explicit support for UE5.8.3 and HLSL shader integration.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository publishes a labelled 1.0.0 source snapshot and a tested baseline (Unreal Engine 5.8.3 / Windows / DX12 / SM6), showing an author-quality release, but the project is only 26 days old so there is no public track record of broader adoption or long-term stability; that recent age limits the TRL to ~5.
prerequisites: C++ toolchain for the matching UE version
familiarity with Unreal Plugins, Blueprints and post-process workflow
student_project_ideas: Create a short architectural visualisation scene in UE5 and use Filmimic presets plus custom parameter animation to compare visual storytelling choices and produce before/after analysis of perceived lighting and material appearance.

Integrate Filmimic with a simple UE-based digital twin scene and implement a Blueprint-driven switcher that changes film looks based on simulated sensor conditions (e.g. time of day, exposure) to study visualisation impact on operator interpretation.

tools.name: rayl15/OpenVision
tools.desc: Open-source iOS app connecting Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses to AI — 5 backends (on-device MLX models, Apple Intelligence, OpenAI, Gemini Live, OpenClaw), on-device neural voice, face recognition & live web search. Private and offline-capable.

cls.summary: OpenVision is an open-source iOS app that connects Ray-Ban smart glasses to multiple AI backends (including fully on-device models) to provide voice+vision assistants, live video Q&A, and hands‑free productivity tools.
cls.what_it_does: OpenVision routes audio and camera frames from Ray‑Ban smart glasses to a choice of AI backends (on‑device MLX models, Apple Intelligence, OpenAI, Gemini Live, Grok/xAI, Hermes, and OpenClaw) to enable photo Q&A, continuous live video questioning, natural on‑device speech, web search and agentic task tools. It is used as an iOS app on a phone paired with glasses and is notable for supporting fully offline on‑device vision with smaller models, a multi‑backend architecture, and privacy‑focused operation.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, well-documented and used by a community (202 stars) and demonstrates multiple working backends and on‑device modes, but it is under one year old so evidence of long-term production deployments is limited; therefore TRL is capped at 6 (beta).
prerequisites: familiarity with on-device ML concepts (Apple MLX) and WebSocket APIs
access to compatible Ray‑Ban smart glasses or equivalent hardware for full testing
student_project_ideas: Build an on‑device image Q&A demo using SmolVLM2 via MLX on iPhone + Ray‑Ban frames, and evaluate latency, accuracy and privacy compared with a cloud backend (OpenAI/Gemini) using quantitative metrics.

Implement a hands‑free task (e.g. voice-controlled reminders + location tagging) that uses OpenVision's OpenClaw tools and integrates with Apple Reminders and a small backend to log and visualise usage data for an HMI/usability study.

tools.name: gogpu/wgpu
tools.desc: Pure Go WebGPU Implementation

cls.summary: wgpu is a pure-Go implementation of the W3C WebGPU API providing multiple native and browser backends for GPU rendering and compute from Go programs.
cls.what_it_does: wgpu implements the WebGPU API in Go and lets developers run GPU rendering and compute pipelines across Vulkan, Metal, DirectX12, OpenGL ES, a software backend and the browser (WASM) using a single API surface. It is used by importing the package in Go projects, selecting a backend via build tags, writing WGSL shaders (via the gogpu/naga compiler) and creating pipelines, buffers and command encoders for GPU work. Notable points are its pure-Go focus (zero CGO), multiple selectable backends, and explicit support for compute shaders and GPU→CPU readback.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is under one year old (created 2025-12-05) so TRL is limited to beta; however it has substantial README, active recent commits, multiple backends, examples and build instructions which indicate a usable beta-level project rather than a fragile prototype.
prerequisites: WGSL or shader language familiarity (naga/SPIR-V pipeline)
student_project_ideas: Implement a GPU-accelerated image processing pipeline in Go using wgpus compute shaders and compare performance to a CPU implementation.
Build a simple real-time WebAssembly demo (Go→WASM) that renders an interactive scene with WGSL shaders to demonstrate cross-backend portability between browser and native.

tools.name: red1-for-hek/portfolio-website
tools.desc: Interactive & Responsive 3D developer portfolio built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, GSAP, WebGL have AI chat & chessbot

cls.summary: A ready-to-deploy 3D developer portfolio template built with React, TypeScript and Three.js that includes smooth GSAP animations and an integrated chat/chessbot demo.
cls.what_it_does: This repository provides a complete front-end portfolio website template that uses Three.js and WebGL for interactive 3D scenes, GSAP for animations, and React + TypeScript for the UI. It is distributed as source code you run with npm/Vite and is notable for combining a polished 3D presentation with an example chat API and small bot features for demonstration.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is ~311 days old (<1 year) but shows active maintenance, a working demo, install/run instructions, and many stars indicating community interest; however it lacks a long production track record so TRL is capped at 6 (beta).
prerequisites: familiarity with Three.js/WebGL for customizing 3D scenes
student_project_ideas: Customize the template to showcase a small engineering project (e.g. an interactive CAD model or sensor data visualiser) by integrating a WebGL scene with a simple REST API that serves telemetry.

Extend the included chat/chessbot example into a course demo: build a domain-specific assistant that explains parts of a systems design shown in the 3D scene (combine with a simple knowledge base or GitHub README parsing).

tools.name: fendouai/awesome-embodied-ai
tools.desc: 2,000 curated embodied AI and robotics resources with bilingual metadata and transparent ranking

cls.summary: A large, curated and bilingual index of resources (software, models, datasets, benchmarks and hardware) for embodied AI and robotics research and development.
cls.what_it_does: This repository collects and ranks ~2,000 links to components, hardware, software, models, datasets and benchmarks relevant to embodied AI and robotics, with bilingual metadata and transparent curation rules. It is used as a discovery and reference resource to find implementations, datasets and tools and to identify candidate benchmarks and projects; its notable aspects are the scale, bilingual (English/Chinese) entries and explicit ranking/curation policy.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is an actively maintained, sizeable curated index with editorial policies and many entries, but it is a new GitHub repo (created 39 days ago) and functions as a resource list rather than production software or a validated platform, so maturity is early (readme and links present but no long track record).
student_project_ideas: Select a benchmark and dataset listed in the collection and implement a small reproduction experiment comparing two published embodied-AI policies (e.g. using MuJoCo or Isaac Gym).

Use the hardware and software lists to design a low-cost robot prototype: pick components from the hardware section and assemble a parts list with a control stack drawn from the software entries, producing a bill of materials and integration plan.

tools.name: HRuiCcc/RuiC-motion-reel
tools.desc: 一句话 brief 生成动态图形 / 动效宣传片 · Agent Skill。时长按 BPM×小节算（12–60 秒），默认 1920×1080；常规宣传片走 remotion/ 模板，特殊质感走自研引擎：2× 超采样矢量/文字、真 3D 点云、丝网印四色分色、普朗克/薄膜干涉物理配色、代码合成配乐，不用外部美术素材、不用 AE。16 张风格牌为参考库，已做过九种视觉语言（暗色科技 / riso / 纸艺 / 银盐 / 普朗克恒星 / 氰版蓝图 / 紫外光刻 / 品牌暗色 / 品牌亮色），成片见 docs/films/

cls.summary: A Python-based procedural motion-graphics engine and an Agent Skill that generates short animated promo reels (video + music) from a one-line brief without external art assets or After Effects.
cls.what_it_does: It converts a short natural-language brief into a timed film SPEC, then procedurally generates typography, 2× supersampled vector text, true 3D point‑cloud renders, procedural print-style separations, and synthesized music and mixes into a finished video using ffmpeg. It's notable because the full pipeline (layout, 3D sampling, print-style colour separations, and DSP-based music synthesis) is code-first and intended to be invoked by an encoding Agent as a 'skill' rather than by hand in a GUI tool.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (created ~50 days ago) but has extensive documentation, demo films in docs/, a runnable template and nontrivial feature set; this suggests early adopters and practical use but insufficient time or broad community for higher TRL.
student_project_ideas: Create a 24-second branded promo that integrates a small ROS/robotics data stream (e.g. pose or sensor image) into a motion-graphics sequence to visualise robot state changes as title cards and point clouds.

Extend the engine to export intermediate geometry as glTF or point-cloud files and build a simple interactive WebGL viewer (three.js) to compare rendered frames with real-time web playback and discuss offline vs real-time rendering trade-offs.

tools.name: OtoDock/oto-dock
tools.desc: The self-hosted platform for your company's AI agents. Your team builds them on Claude Code, Codex or local models, and they work in chats, on schedules, on the phone and on your own machines.

cls.summary: OtoDock is a self-hosted multi-tenant platform for building, running and scheduling company AI agents that connect to API subscriptions or local models and run on servers or paired user machines.
cls.what_it_does: OtoDock provides an on-premises environment where teams create agent 'digital employees' that use Claude, ChatGPT/Codex or local model servers, run in chats or on schedules, trigger from webhooks, and access company tools and files. It is installed as a Docker-based server with a web dashboard and supports multi-tenancy, role-based access, remote paired machines, checks/triggers and integration with external model APIs and local model servers. Notable points are its self-hosted, multi-tenant design and support for both cloud LLM subscriptions and local model backends.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 131 days old with active pushes, an install script and documentation and ~200 stars indicating early adopters; it appears to be a beta-quality self-hosted platform but is younger than one year so it fits TRL 6 rather than higher.
prerequisites: Linux (x86-64 or arm64) or macOS (Apple silicon) server
Claude / OpenAI subscription or local model server (Ollama or OpenAI-compatible API)
basic system administration and reverse-proxy/HTTPS setup
student_project_ideas: Build an autonomous agent that monitors a simulated ticketing system and automatically triages and routes tickets; deploy it on OtoDock using a local model server and evaluate performance and audit logs.
Integrate OtoDock agents with an MQTT time-series pipeline to automate alerts and maintenance tasks on a small IoT testbed, demonstrating secure remote machines and role-based access.

tools.name: jpezzulli/sglang-rtxpro6000
tools.desc: Optimized SGLang runtime for Qwen3.8-27B FP8 with DFlash2 and Qwen3.8 Flash-Next NVFP4 with FR-Spec on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB GPU (SM120): 524K context, HiCache and NIXL.

cls.summary: Penny Royal is an optimized local LLM runtime for running Qwen3.8-class models with very long contexts on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 using layered caching (GPU, RAM HiCache, NVMe NIXL) and experimental Flash-Next/DFlash2 performance features.
cls.what_it_does: It provides a highly tuned runtime (SGLang-derived) for hosting Qwen3.8-family models on an RTX PRO 6000, enabling 524k-token contexts, speculative decoding, and persistent conversation caching across GPU, system RAM and NVMe. It is used by running the provided container/binary on a suitable host and configuring HiCache/NIXL, and is notable for hardware-specific optimisations (SM120 / NVFP4 / FlashInfer kernels) and long-context persistence.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active with numbered releases, published container images and community results, showing use beyond a single demo; however it is only 85 days old so per the TRL rules its demonstrated maturity should be capped (alpha in use).
prerequisites: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) or equivalent Blackwell GPU
Linux host with Docker / container runtime and NVMe storage
Familiarity with local LLM deployment, GPU/driver configuration and large-model memory tuning
student_project_ideas: Compare end-to-end latency and token throughput for a Qwen3.8 conversation workload with and without HiCache/NIXL enabled, and visualise cache hit rates and GPU memory usage over time.
Integrate Penny Royal with a small multi-agent tool-chain (e.g. a planner and a code-execution tool) to evaluate how long-context caching affects multi-turn agent performance and resource usage.

tools.name: Zhou-Yujing114514/deepseek-harness-linux
tools.desc: First-class Linux packaging for DeepSeek Harness desktop — AppImage, .deb, .tar.gz for x64/arm64, built by native CI.

cls.summary: A community fork that produces ready-to-install Linux desktop packages (AppImage, .deb, .tar.gz) for the DeepSeek Harness Electron app on x64 and arm64, with CI-driven builds and AppImage auto-update support.
cls.what_it_does: This repository packages the upstream DeepSeek Harness desktop client for Linux, producing AppImage, .deb and .tar.gz artifacts for x64 and arm64 and providing CI workflows to build and publish them. It focuses on making the official desktop experience available to Linux users (including auto-update for AppImage) without modifying the agent core, and documents how to build and run the packages locally.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is active, provides CI workflows and release artifacts and has substantial community interest (stars/forks), but the repository is only 45 days old so it lacks the multi-release, long-term track record required for TRL 6+.

tools.name: andrewwoan/aimee-xus-papercraft-world
tools.desc: A Seasonal Papercraft Portfolio!

cls.summary: A web portfolio that presents a papercraft-style 3D scene built with Blender assets and rendered interactively in the browser using Three.js.
cls.what_it_does: This repository contains the code for a personal portfolio website that loads Blender-created models and textures and renders a stylised papercraft world in the browser with Three.js. It is used as a demonstration/tutorial project (with a published live site and a YouTube walkthrough) and is notable for its artist-focused visuals and educational value for web 3D hobbyists.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is about 11 months old with a working live site, a tutorial video and a reasonably active community (stars/forks), which indicates usable, beta-level maturity; its age (<1 year) and single-author project nature limit a higher TRL.
student_project_ideas: Adapt the scene to visualise an engineering concept (for example, turn paper models into simplified mechanical assemblies) and add UI controls to toggle components and annotations using Three.js.

Create a performance-optimised version of the portfolio that compares rendering approaches (LOD, texture atlasing, shader simplifications) and measures frame-rate and memory on desktop and mobile browsers.

tools.name: marketcalls/openalgo-charts
tools.desc: Production-grade charts built for brokers, exchanges, trading platforms, and financial portals.  Bring your own market data, plug it in, and deliver a complete charting experience without building the charting stack from scratch.  Open source. Data-agnostic. Ready to integrate.

cls.summary: OpenAlgo Charts is an open-source JavaScript/TypeScript library for embedding interactive financial charts, indicators and drawing tools into web apps using your own market data.
cls.what_it_does: The library renders candlesticks, alternative bar types (Renko, Heikin Ashi, point & figure, etc.), orderflow/footprint views, indicators, drawings and replay/alert features in the browser and offers an optional widget for a full terminal UI. It is data-agnostic (you supply market data or connect to a feed) and is designed for integration into frameworks such as React, Vue, Angular or plain JS with no runtime dependencies, using canvas/WebGL rendering.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively maintained with versioned releases (current 2.7.3), an examples gallery and documentation, and a modest user community (stars/forks). However the repository is only ~144 days old so it lacks the longer track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with browser build tools and npm
student_project_ideas: Build a small trading dashboard that streams simulated or historical market data into OpenAlgo Charts and implements a custom indicator and alerting rule for demonstration and evaluation.
Create a backtest replay tool that feeds historical tick data into the chart's replay API and compares trade entry/exit performance for two simple strategies, visualising orders and P&L on the chart.

tools.name: tmseidel/ai-git-bot
tools.desc: The self-hosted AI workflow automation platform for Git repositories.

cls.summary: AI-Git-Bot is a self-hosted platform that automates Git workflows (PR reviews, test generation, issue triage and coding agents) by connecting repository events to LLM providers.
cls.what_it_does: AI-Git-Bot listens to events in Git platforms and runs configurable AI-driven workflows such as pull-request reviews, test generation (including E2E tests), issue triage, documentation and i18n sync, and coding agents that can create PRs. It is deployed as a self-hosted Java/Spring service and notable for supporting many Git providers and AI backends (cloud and local LLMs) so teams can retain code and model control.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, has several hundred stars, recent commits and documentation describing workflows and integrations which indicate a beta-stage project; however it is under one year old (231 days) so evidence limits the TRL to 6 rather than production-ready.
prerequisites: git and familiarity with Git hosting platforms (GitHub/GitLab/Gitea/Bitbucket/Azure DevOps)
Java / Spring Boot knowledge for deploying the service
experience with self-hosting (Docker/containers, reverse proxy, credentials for AI providers)
student_project_ideas: Integrate AI-Git-Bot with a small team repository to automatically generate unit and Playwright E2E tests for incoming pull requests, measure test coverage changes, and report results back to the PR.

Extend or add a workflow that enforces a specific requirements-to-test traceability rule: detect requirement IDs in commits/issues and create or update test stubs, demonstrating automated V&V integration between issue tracking and tests.

tools.name: HoldMyBeer-gg/blenderwright
tools.desc: MCP server for Blender. Hundreds of tools for modeling, materials, rendering and more, driven by Claude, Cursor, Codex, Ollama, llama.cpp, or any MCP client.

cls.summary: blenderwright is an open-source Blender addon and local MCP server that lets LLMs control Blender to create, edit, animate and render 3D scenes via natural language and scripted tools.
cls.what_it_does: It exposes a large library of Blender operations (modeling, materials, lighting, animation, rendering, mesh checks, etc.) over a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so LLM-based assistants (Claude, llama.cpp, Ollama, Codex, Cursor and others) can drive Blender via natural language or programmatic clients. Notable features include an expert-prompt library, visual feedback screenshots, mesh quality analysis, optional restricted raw-Python execution, and a queue-based thread-safe server architecture targeted at Blender 5.2 LTS.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active, has releases, substantial test coverage (3500+ tests), 198 stars and ongoing commits, indicating community activity and polish; however it was created ~240 days ago (under one year) so it fits a beta-level TRL rather than production-long-track record.
prerequisites: basic familiarity with Blender UI and addons
familiarity with running local Python/commands for developer installs (optional)
student_project_ideas: Use blenderwright to build an automated pipeline that generates parametrised CAD-like models (e.g. mounting brackets) from text prompts, export them as STEP/glTF and evaluate mesh quality for 3D printing.

Integrate blenderwright with an LLM (e.g. local llama.cpp) to create a guided scene-generation lab where students issue high-level requirements and the system produces scenes and automated reports on geometry and render settings.

tools.name: krillclaw/KrillClaw
tools.desc: The world's smallest AI agent runtime. 49KB. Written in Zig. Zero dependencies.

cls.summary: KrillClaw is a very small AI agent runtime written in Zig that runs on microcontrollers and edge devices to orchestrate LLM calls, tools and hardware I/O.
cls.what_it_does: KrillClaw runs autonomous AI agents on constrained devices (microcontrollers or cloud) by connecting to LLM providers, executing tools/plugins, and managing message channels and hardware interfaces. It is used as a tiny runtime/agent loop with transports (BLE, Serial, HTTP, MQTT, WebSocket), a persistent KV store, scheduling and plugin bridging to external tool handlers. Its notable features are the extremely small binary size (~450 KB in README), zero runtime dependencies, and explicit support for embedded hardware integration and multiple messaging channels.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively developed, includes unit and integration tests, CI, extensive README and device targets (50+ validated targets) which support a beta judgement; however the repository is under one year old (created ~275 days ago) so TRL is capped at 6.
prerequisites: familiarity with Zig and its build/cross-compilation toolchain
basic embedded development knowledge (toolchains, flashing, SDKs like Nordic SoftDevice for BLE)
understanding of LLM provider APIs and common IoT protocols (MQTT, WebSocket, HTTP)
student_project_ideas: Build a lab exercise where students deploy KrillClaw to a low-cost microcontroller to implement a simple voice-commanded device that forwards recognized commands to an LLM via the bridge and actuates GPIO outputs.

Integrate KrillClaw with an MQTT-based sensor network to create an edge agent that aggregates sensor data, queries an LLM for anomaly interpretation, and publishes alerts; evaluate latency, resource use and reliability.

tools.name: hexianWeb/Third-Person-MC
tools.desc: Three.js web version Minecraft  in browser

cls.summary: A browser-based third-person, Minecraft-style Web3D demo built with Three.js and Vue 3 that showcases procedural voxel terrain, a third-person camera, and basic combat/interaction mechanics.
cls.what_it_does: This project provides a playable web demo implementing a Minecraft-like voxel world with procedurally generated biomes, a third-person camera that avoids clipping, character movement/animations, and basic combat controls. It is run as a client-side web application (Vite + Vue) and notable for integrating custom GLSL shaders, instanced meshes for voxel rendering, and an on-line demo to quickly try features in the browser.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is a functioning, usable web demo with an online preview, documented project structure and dev commands, and several hundred stars, indicating active interest; however it is under one year old so evidence of long-term production use or wide adoption is limited.
prerequisites: Node.js and pnpm (or npm) for local dev
student_project_ideas: Extend the procedural terrain system to add a simple resource/collection mechanic and store collected items in a Vue/Pinia-backed inventory UI.
Integrate a physics library (e.g. cannon-es) to implement destructible blocks and measure performance differences between InstancedMesh and per-mesh approaches on complex scenes.

tools.name: SergiioB/intel-arc-pro-b70-inference-cookbook
tools.desc: Pinned Intel Arc Pro B60/B70 inference recipes, engine patches and measurement records: Qwen3.8-27B EXL3 on one card (262,144 context, 63 tok/s; MTP3 measured lossy on 27% of a fixed 329-item set), Nemotron Bolt 74B, Flash-Next, dual-card routes, and a machine-checked catalog where each speculative row states whether the drafter changes the answer.

cls.summary: A community-maintained cookbook of pinned recipes, engine patches and reproducible benchmark records for running large LLMs efficiently on Intel Arc Pro B60/B70 GPUs.
cls.what_it_does: The repository collects tested inference 'recipes' (commands, images, patches and configuration) to run and measure LLMs on Intel Arc B60/B70 hardware using engines like vLLM and llama.cpp (SYCL). It is used to reproduce performance experiments, pick routes for single- or multi-card serving, and apply engine/patch combinations that the author measured; notable for machine-checked benchmark rows and detailed reproduction steps.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is well-documented, has many pinned recipes, tests and a reproducible benchmark catalog and active pushes, but it is only ~103 days old so does not yet show long-term production adoption; that age limits TRL to beta-level 6.
prerequisites: Linux (primary) or Windows for some recipes
Intel Arc Pro B60/B70 GPU and appropriate SYCL drivers
Familiarity with LLM inference engines (vLLM, llama.cpp) and model quantisation concepts
student_project_ideas: Reproduce a subset of the cookbook's benchmark catalog: run the Qwen3.8-27B EXL3-XPU recipe on a B70, validate outputs against the published bench JSON and write a short report on repeatability and sources of variance.

Implement a small inference service that uses a chosen cookbook route (e.g. llama.cpp SYCL KV optimised) and measure throughput/latency trade-offs when varying context length and speculative decoding settings.

tools.name: omnilink-tech/omnisim
tools.desc: An open-source robotics workshop for agents: simulate complete robots on high-fidelity physics, build digital twins, make the parts on CNC, laser and 3D-printer twins, connect simulation to real robots, and let AI agents program, test and debug it all, just by talking to it.

cls.summary: OmniSim is an open-source robotics workshop and high-fidelity simulator that builds digital twins of robots and manufacturing machines and lets AI agents program, test and drive them.
cls.what_it_does: OmniSim simulates complete robotic systems with high-fidelity physics, creates twins of CNC, laser and 3D-printer machines, and connects simulation to real hardware and agentic workflows (chat/agents) so robots and manufacturing processes can be designed, tested and iterated. It is used via Python commands and example 'world' files, integrates with common robotics tools (MuJoCo, ROS 2) and exposes manufacturing workflows (slicing, G-code, GRBL/Klipper) so parts and assemblies can be produced virtually and validated in simulation.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has many examples and demonstration projects and recent pushes, indicating more than an experimental prototype, but it is only 200 days old (<1 year) and the README explicitly warns that twins have not been validated on real machines, so maturity is consistent with a beta-level project (TRL 6).
prerequisites: familiarity with MuJoCo / physics simulators and ROS 2
knowledge of G-code/GRBL/3D-print slicing workflows for manufacturing twins
student_project_ideas: Create a digital twin of a small differential-drive robot in OmniSim, connect it to ROS 2, and implement and evaluate a navigation stack comparing simulated sensor models to ideal sensors.

Use OmniSim's manufacturing twins to iterate a simple robot arm bracket: generate CAD/STL, slice and 'print' it in the printer twin, measure the simulated part against the drawing, and propose design corrections for manufacturability.

tools.name: Zengkailin/parametric-topdown-pixel-architecture
tools.desc: 参数化2D topdown像素建筑 - 把参数化 3D 建筑渲染成 2D 俯视像素图的本地网页工具（Godot hd2d_scene_tools 网页移植版）

cls.summary: A pure‑frontend local web tool that procedurally generates 2D top‑down pixel images of parametric buildings and can export spritesheets, ZIPs and Godot prefabs.
cls.what_it_does: This project renders parameterised 3D building geometry into 2D top‑down pixel art in the browser (no server required) and includes a Node.js CLI for batch/agent use. It provides many built‑in styles and export options (single PNG, multi‑direction sheets, ZIP, embedded generation recipe) and a Godot plugin / prefab export path to integrate art into Godot projects.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is feature‑rich (web UI + CLI, Godot prefab export, embedded recipe metadata) and has many stars indicating interest, but it is very new (created 22 days ago) so lacks a longer track record; that limits maturity to TRL 5 (alpha in use/early adopters).
prerequisites: optional Python 3.10+ with Pillow for developer scripts
student_project_ideas: Build a pipeline that generates sets of procedural top‑down building sprites for a simple simulation or game and import them into a Godot scene using the tool's prefab export to study asset integration.

Create a small tool that converts exported recipe JSON files into a map generator that arranges multiple procedurally generated buildings into a tiled town layout and evaluates visual composition metrics (coverage, spacing).

tools.name: kstevica/captain-claw
tools.desc: Command a fleet of AI agents, on every deck, every desk, every wrist. Self-hosted multi-agent platform with memory, a coding pipeline, Flows, a team kiosk and voice devices. Any LLM, or 100% local with Ollama.

cls.summary: Captain Claw is a self‑hosted multi‑agent orchestration platform that lets you spawn, coordinate, train and deploy specialist AI agents across devices and networks.
cls.what_it_does: It provides a flight‑deck UI and backend to create teams of specialist agents, run multiple orchestration modes, chain deterministic Flows, and manage a coding pipeline so agents can plan, build and review software. It is used as a self‑hosted service (supports provider APIs or local models via Ollama) and notable for its multi‑deck federation (BotPort), per‑agent memory layers, training/examination features and many prebuilt agent archetypes.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively developed, has releases (PyPI package, release notes up to 0.9.0), a live demo and ~200 stars which indicate early adoption; however the repository is only ~9 months old so it lacks the longer real‑world track record needed for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: knowledge of LLM provider APIs or local LLM runtimes (e.g. Ollama)
student_project_ideas: Build a supervised team that automates a small engineering workflow (requirements → test specification → simple code generator) using Captain Claw and evaluate reliability across orchestration modes.
Deploy a Fleet across a Raspberry Pi and a cloud VPS to prototype edge/cloud task allocation for a simulated IoT monitoring pipeline and measure latency, failover and task handover.

tools.name: xiayu1987/noobot
tools.desc: Cheap Money-Saving Self-hosted AI agent workspace with tool calling, MCP, multi-model routing, sandboxed execution, multi-agent workflows, and LLM-authored 3D character animation rendered with Three.js.

cls.summary: Noobot is a self-hosted AI agent workspace (web + Electron) that supports tool calling, multi-model routing, multi-agent workflows and LLM-driven 3D character animation previewed with Three.js.
cls.what_it_does: Noobot provides an isolated multi-user workspace for running AI agents and chaining tools (file ops, scripts, browser automation, media tools) with model-family routing and MCP connectors; it also includes an LLM-driven 3D character animation feature using Three.js for authoring and previewing animations from natural language. It is delivered as a web app and packaged desktop clients and can be deployed self-hosted with sandboxed execution (Docker) or host mode.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 214 days old (<1 year) so TRL is capped; however it has packaged installers/releases for Windows and macOS, active commits, ~195 stars and working deployment scripts which indicate a beta-level project with versioned packages and user installs (fits TRL 6).
prerequisites: Docker (if using sandbox execution) and system admin for self-hosting
student_project_ideas: Build a lab exercise where students extend Noobot with a new tool plugin that runs a simple analysis pipeline (e.g. CSV data -> plotting -> PDF report) and demonstrate model-driven orchestration across connectors.

Create a project that uses Noobot's character-animation feature to generate simple multi-agent choreography, export the GLB/animation, and integrate it into a Three.js scene to study automated animation pipelines and evaluation of generated motions.

tools.name: w1ne/labwired-core
tools.desc: Open-source circuit and MCU firmware simulator for mixed-signal co-simulation, deterministic CI, and MCP workflows. STM32, ESP32, RP2040.

cls.summary: LabWired Core is an open-source deterministic simulator that runs real MCU firmware ELF binaries against modeled boards (CPU, peripherals, buses and sensors) to support CI gating and virtual hardware testing.
cls.what_it_does: LabWired Core loads a firmware ELF and executes it on a modeled chip and board, producing UART, GPIO and bus traces, register state and a pass/fail exit code so firmware can be tested without physical hardware. It is used from a CLI, a Python SDK for pytest, CI scripts and an MCP/Playground hosted service; deterministic runs and a published fidelity ledger make it suitable for automated gates.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is actively developed, has an installable CLI, Python SDK, a hosted Playground and release references in the README, indicating beta-level maturity; however the repository is under one year old so TRL is capped at 6 under the stated policy.
prerequisites: familiarity with embedded firmware (ELF, MCU architectures)
Rust toolchain to build from source (optional)
basic Python and pytest to use the SDK
student_project_ideas: Create a CI test pipeline using LabWired to automatically run and gate a FreeRTOS-based STM32 firmware build on GitHub Actions, asserting UART output and GPIO toggles.
Model a simple sensor-peripheral board in LabWired and validate an ESP32 firmware's I2C communication and power-sequencing behavior, comparing simulator traces with a short hardware run.

tools.name: congchuanling-dot/Cohort
tools.desc: Local-first Agent Runtime connecting LLMs to controlled tools, Chrome, desktop automation, MCP, context governance,   and verifiable memory.

cls.summary: Cohort is a local-first agent runtime that records verifiable execution traces, controls tool permissions and context, and enables replayable and forkable experiments for LLM-driven automation.
cls.what_it_does: Cohort connects LLMs to controlled tools (browser, desktop, shell, MCP) while recording cryptographic evidence of requests, responses and tool observations into replay bundles. It provides runtime governance (context/cost/caching/policy), a Time Machine for exact replay and forked counterfactual trials, and observability for auditing and improving agent behaviour.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with ~195 stars and documentation and README describes a published v1.0.0 npm distribution and multiple runtime features, indicating beta maturity; however the repo is only ~142 days old so it lacks a long track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: comfort with CLI and Node/npm tooling
basic knowledge of LLM APIs (OpenAI/Anthropic) and API keys
familiarity with Git and browser automation concepts (CDP) and macOS Accessibility for desktop automation features
student_project_ideas: Build an experiment that records an agent performing a web-based information-extraction task via Cohort's Chrome Bridge, then use the Time Machine replay to compare two different system prompts and produce a report of divergence points and success metrics.

Integrate Cohort with a small ROS 2 robot task (or simulated robot) so an LLM issues high-level commands, Cohort governs tool calls and records verifiable traces; students then analyse failure modes and design runtime policies to improve robustness.

tools.name: codepawl/viz3d
tools.desc: An AI agent skill that turns any subject into a 3D film or app

cls.summary: viz3d is an AI agent skill that generates interactive three.js-based 3D films, apps and embeds from a text subject, producing scene recipes, images and playable web apps.
cls.what_it_does: viz3d lets an LLM-driven agent research a subject, generate scaled 3D models/scenes and produce films, interactive apps, books or games as three.js web outputs or exported images/video. It is used as a plugin/agent skill (example: Claude Code plugin) that emits JSON scene recipes and can drive a WebGL2 renderer called Crucible for higher-quality renders, or run standalone to produce three.js apps and embeds.
cls.trl_rationale: The README describes a feature-rich agent-driven 3D pipeline and an accompanying WebGL2 renderer (Crucible), and the project already has notable stars, but the repository is only 27 days old so there is no long track record; that recent age limits the TRL to at most 5.
prerequisites: familiarity with three.js and WebGL concepts
Python environment and familiarity with LLM-agent plugins
understanding of scene graphs/3D assets and JSON-based scene descriptions
student_project_ideas: Build a quick prototype web app using viz3d to visualise a warehouse from a CSV of rack locations and animate a seeded simulation of forklifts, then embed it into a dashboard.
Extend viz3d to ingest a live JSON event feed (or MQTT) representing an IoT fleet and create a live embedded three.js view that updates in real time for a digital-twin demo.

tools.name: hanxiao/dataroom
tools.desc: Give a query, get a dataroom. Pi + self-hosted Qwen3.6 research harness on a single L4.

cls.summary: Dataroom is a local LLM-driven harness that autonomously gathers, cites and packages web-research into a structured dataroom (.zip) for downstream long‑horizon agents.
cls.what_it_does: Dataroom runs a small self-hosted model in a Pi agent loop to search, read, deduplicate, verify and write sourced files into a structured on-disk dataroom intended as machine-consumable context. It orchestrates tooling (jina CLI for search/embeddings, embedding dedup index, llama.cpp-hosted Qwen3.6 model) and provides a live dashboard and outcome-based stopping so the job continues until coverage goals are met.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo has an installable stack, prebuilt images, setup scripts, a live demo and moderate community interest (stars/forks), indicating a beta-level project; it is only ~170 days old so there isn't a long track record to justify TRL7+.
prerequisites: Docker (NVIDIA toolkit) or Apple Silicon with llama.cpp
NVIDIA GPU recommended (or 32GB+ Apple Silicon unified memory)
Python 3.11 and typical Python tooling for the app
Ability to download large model files (Hugging Face token for some models)
student_project_ideas: Create a dataroom tailored to a systems-engineering design problem (e.g., requirements and standards for a small UAV) and feed it to a frontier model to produce a concept design; compare results when using different dataroom completeness thresholds.

Integrate the dataroom output with an MBSE tool by converting the SUMMARY.md and sourced files into structured requirements/traceability entries, and evaluate how well the generated dataroom supports downstream verification tasks.

tools.name: thebanri/limoni
tools.desc: Terminal UI engine for Go that tests can click and AI agents can drive (MCP). Zero-allocation rendering, immediate mode + Elm architecture, 3D, images, charts, accessibility, WebAssembly.

cls.summary: Limoni is a Go terminal UI engine that provides zero-allocation rendering, a semantic widget tree for accessibility and testing, and an MCP endpoint so AI agents can drive TUIs or tests can programmatically click widgets.
cls.what_it_does: Limoni provides an immediate-mode terminal UI engine for Go with a semantic accessibility tree, fast zero-allocation rendering, 3D/model rasterisation, images, charts and session recording. It is used as a library in Go programs (or compiled to WebAssembly for the browser), and notable features include Playwright-style in-process UI tests and an MCP-compatible automation interface so AI agents can control the UI.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 103 days old (under one year) so it lacks a long track record, but the README, examples, benchmarks, docs and CI indicate versioned examples and active development; stars and templates show early adoption consistent with a beta-level project (TRL 6).
prerequisites: basic knowledge of terminal concepts (ANSI, OSC, terminal cells)
understanding of MCP/agent concepts for automation if using agent features
student_project_ideas: Build a terminal-based telemetry dashboard for a student robot or IoT sensor (Go backend) using Limoni for the UI and record automated UI tests with the built-in uitest framework.

Create an MCP-driven automated operator that performs a deployment checklist in a mock CLI app: implement the app in Limoni, expose the limoni-mcp socket, and write an agent (or scripted client) to drive and verify the workflow.

tools.name: JianouJiang/symbolic-regression-pe-closure
tools.desc: Code and data records: Combining symbolic regression and turbulence physics to develop a compact inner-layer production-dissipation closure — Jiang & Rosic, Physics of Fluids 38, 095140 (2026), Featured Article. doi:10.1063/5.0347368

cls.summary: Repository provides code, data records and runnable examples that reproduce and evaluate a compact symbolic-regression-derived turbulence production-to-dissipation closure for the inner layer of wall-bounded flows from a 2026 Physics of Fluids paper.
cls.what_it_does: This project hosts the implementation, data records and tutorial notebooks for a new turbulence closure derived by symbolic regression and physics constraints; users can reproduce the paper's diagnostics, run quick tutorials (including an executed Colab notebook) and validate the closure against DNS profiles without running CFD. It is notable because the closure is published in a peer-reviewed featured article and the repo includes ready-to-run examples and data provenance for validation.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository accompanies a peer-reviewed (featured) journal article and provides runnable examples, tutorials and data provenance which indicates beyond-prototype maturity; however it is a newly created repo (≈96 days old) with limited long-term adoption evidence so TRL is conservatively placed at 6.
student_project_ideas: Compare the repository's symbolic-regression closure to standard two-equation turbulence closures (k-epsilon, k-omega) by post-processing existing CFD results (from OpenFOAM) to quantify differences in near-wall dissipation and production profiles.

Extend the symbolic-regression workflow by training a similar compact closure on a different DNS dataset (e.g. pipe flow) and evaluate transferability, documenting changes to feature selection and physics constraints.

tools.name: iamahsanmehmood/openskp
tools.desc: Open-source SketchUp (.skp) reader, writer, and converter - parse, create, and edit .skp files; export to GLB, OBJ, STL, PLY, DXF, IFC4, and Fragments. Python, TypeScript, .NET, Dart, and C++.

cls.summary: OpenSKP is an open-source toolkit to read, write and convert SketchUp .skp files into common CAD/BIM/3D formats without using the proprietary SketchUp SDK.
cls.what_it_does: OpenSKP parses SketchUp binary files (modern VFF and legacy MFC containers), exposes geometry, materials and scene structure, and provides writers that can create and edit .skp files. It also converts SKP to multiple exchange formats (GLB/glTF, OBJ, STL, PLY, DXF, IFC4 and ThatOpen Fragments) in several languages (Python, TypeScript, .NET, Dart, C++), making it useful for CAD/BIM interoperability and downstream visualization.
cls.trl_rationale: The project provides multi-language implementations, documentation, and tagged releases (Python and C++) and claims production use, but the repository is only ~5 months old so its demonstrated track record is limited; under the age rule this supports a beta-level TRL (6).
prerequisites: basic familiarity with CAD/3D file formats (SKP, glTF, IFC, DXF)
programming knowledge in at least one supported language (Python, TypeScript, C++, .NET or Dart)
student_project_ideas: Build a pipeline that converts complex SketchUp models to IFC4 using OpenSKP, then run automated checks (geometry validity, classification) to evaluate IFC export fidelity for a BIM workflow.

Create a lightweight web viewer that uses OpenSKP's Fragments export (or glTF export) and a three.js/ThatOpen fragments viewer to demonstrate model streaming and component-level inspection for an architecture/civil lab.

tools.name: justxor/deepseek-local-guide-ru
tools.desc: 🐋 Полный гайд на русском: как установить и запустить DeepSeek локально (V4, R1) на ПК, Mac и сервере — Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM, Open WebUI, API, RAG, агенты, fine-tuning, лучшие фишки

cls.summary: A detailed Russian-language how-to guide for installing, running and configuring DeepSeek family models locally (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio, Open WebUI) including RAG, agents and fine-tuning.
cls.what_it_does: This repository is a step-by-step tutorial that explains how to run DeepSeek V4 and R1 models and their distillates on desktop and server platforms, covering tools like Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM and various UIs and APIs. It is used as a practical deployment and configuration reference (quick-start commands, hardware guidance, optimization, RAG and agent setups) and is notable for being a comprehensive, up-to-date Russian-language walkthrough focused on local/self-hosted LLM usage.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (created ~31 days ago) but contains a large, practical README with install/run instructions for many tools; evidence supports early-alpha/alpha-in-use documentation rather than long track record, so TRL ~5.
prerequisites: familiarity with LLM concepts and model sizes
basic system administration (installing services, managing dependencies)
student_project_ideas: Deploy a local DeepSeek RAG pipeline using Ollama and a vector store to provide searchable course notes, measuring latency and accuracy across different model sizes.

Compare resource use and response quality of a DeepSeek distillate run via llama.cpp versus a server setup using vLLM, documenting installation steps and optimisation tweaks for classroom reproducibility.

tools.name: wieslawsoltes/ProGPU
tools.desc: Cross-platform GPU rendering, composition, vector, text, compute, and DirectX/LibreWPF/WinUI/Avalonia interop on WebGPU and Silk.NET.

cls.summary: ProGPU is a .NET, GPU-first rendering and composition substrate that routes vector graphics, text layout and UI composition directly to WebGPU for high-performance cross-platform UI rendering and framework integration.
cls.what_it_does: ProGPU provides GPU-backed rendering, text shaping, retained scene composition and compute pipeline helpers for .NET applications, with integration adapters for Avalonia, WinUI/Uno and native hosts. It is used as a lightweight alternative to heavier UI stacks by sending vector, text and composition work directly to WebGPU (wgpu-native) and supports selecting native backends (Vulkan/Metal/DX12/GL) and browser/wasm hosts.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with many components, NuGet packaging in CI, and integration with frameworks (Avalonia, WinUI), showing beta-level maturity; however the project is only ~6 months old so it lacks the multi-year track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with Silk.NET and host UI frameworks (Avalonia/WinUI)
student_project_ideas: Build an Avalonia desktop app that uses ProGPU to render a high-performance, pan/zoom vector map with GPU-based text labels and benchmark CPU vs GPU rendering throughput.
Create a WebAssembly demo that renders an interactive technical diagram (DXF import) in the browser using ProGPU.Browser to show cross-platform WebGPU rendering and measure latency across backends.

tools.name: Qiuner/Qiuner.github.io
tools.desc: Building beautiful websites used to be gatekept. Not anymore. So I built all of them.

cls.summary: An open-source, Astro + Three.js personal portfolio that implements a shared 3D runtime and multiple lazy-loadable interactive ‘worlds’ with a static-first fallback.
cls.what_it_does: This repository is a multi-scene interactive portfolio: content is stored in a single semantic kernel and rendered by independently loadable World Modules driven by a shared 3D runtime that manages the WebGL renderer, frame scheduling, input routing, resource cleanup and quality adaptation. It is used as a static site (Astro) with Three.js worlds, and is notable for its runtime architecture (portal journeys, adaptive quality budgets) and static-first fallback so content remains accessible without WebGL.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has a complete codebase, tests, CI/deployment workflow and a user-facing static site, indicating maturity beyond a toy prototype; however the repository is only ~108 days old so it lacks a long multi-release production track record, which constrains TRL to ~6.
student_project_ideas: Extend one World to visualise time-series telemetry from a sensor (mocked or real) and evaluate adaptive frame-scheduling under different data update rates.
