tools.name: Scottcjn/ram-coffers
tools.desc: LLM infrastructure cost reduction via NUMA-aware weight banking: 147 t/s (8.8x stock llama.cpp) on refurbished enterprise POWER8. Self-hosted inference, no cloud APIs. Part of the Proof of Physical AI stack.

cls.summary: RAM Coffers is an open-source NUMA-aware LLM inference infrastructure that partitions and routes model weights across physical memory banks to reduce memory bandwidth and cost on self‑hosted servers (demonstrated on IBM POWER8).
cls.what_it_does: The project implements a conditional memory / weight-banking layer that routes query embeddings to NUMA-local memory coffers, uses prefetch and cache-warming techniques (DCBT hints, thread affinity) and selective pruning to reduce memory fetches for LLM inference. It is used as a self‑hosted inference stack (no cloud APIs) and is notable for demonstrated throughput improvements on POWER8 hardware and published benchmarking and papers.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is ~302 days old with active pushes, benchmark results, and multiple linked publications demonstrating measured throughput; however it is younger than one year and appears experimental/targeted to specific hardware so maturity aligns with a beta-stage project rather than long-term production adoption.
prerequisites: Linux systems programming and NUMA concepts
experience with LLM inference stacks (llama.cpp / ggml)
familiarity with Python and low-level performance tuning on PowerPC/ppc64le
student_project_ideas: Reproduce a simplified NUMA-partitioned inference pipeline on x86/Linux using llama.cpp and measure throughput/latency differences with and without NUMA-aware thread affinity and prefetching.

Integrate RAM Coffers' routing idea with a small-scale edge node (Raspberry Pi/ARM) to evaluate domain-partitioned weight storage and power/energy trade-offs for on‑device LLM inference (measure energy/per-token).

tools.name: bitwize-ai/Logue
tools.desc: A local-first workspace for documents, tasks and meetings on macOS — nested spaces, typed properties, relations and saved views, with transcription, Smart Minutes and an agent running entirely on-device via MLX on Apple Silicon

cls.summary: Logue is a local-first macOS workspace for notes, tasks and meetings that runs transcription and an on-device AI agent using MLX on Apple Silicon.
cls.what_it_does: Logue organises documents into nested spaces with typed properties, relations, saved views and a block editor, and records meetings with on-device transcription, diarization and automatic minutes that turn commitments into tasks. It includes an on-device agent (via MLX) that can access the workspace, calendar and files, and emphasises privacy by keeping processing local to the Mac.
cls.trl_rationale: The README and repo contain full app source, build-from-source instructions and active development with dozens of stars, indicating a usable beta; however the repository is only ~4 months old (122 days) so it lacks the long track record or releases required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: macOS (features such as SpeechTranscriber require recent macOS versions)
student_project_ideas: Create a small integration that exports Logue meeting action items to GitHub Issues or a team Kanban board, demonstrating parsing of minutes and automated issue creation.

Build a script or plugin that syncs a Logue plaintext markdown vault with a course repository (git), showing how on-disk markdown storage can be used in a student workflow and tracked by version control.

tools.name: mapleleavessssssss-wq/vivado-mcp
tools.desc: Vivado MCP server — 让 Claude Code / Cursor / Codex 驱动本地 FPGA 全流程。30 个精选工具、8 个证据驱动 Prompt、doctor 环境自检、GUI/Tcl/attach 会话，以及时序和 CRITICAL WARNING 中文诊断。

cls.summary: vivado-mcp is a local MCP server that lets AI agents drive a locally installed Xilinx Vivado flow (synthesis, implementation, timing analysis, waveform queries and bitstream checks) with structured parsing and safety checks.
cls.what_it_does: It exposes a set of 32 high-level tools and a run_tcl bridge so AI agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can control a locally installed Vivado for tasks like synthesis, implementation, timing and CDC analysis, VCD waveform queries and bitstream safety checks. It is used as a local Python MCP server that injects a TCP entrypoint into Vivado or runs headless Tcl, provides structured JSON timing/IO reports and automated diagnostics, and includes doctor checks and install/uninstall helpers to manage the Vivado injection.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is an active, installable Python package (pip installable), with CI-style commands (doctor, install), 174 stars and recent activity, indicating more than an experimental prototype; however it was created ~250 days ago (<1 year) so lacks the multi-year track record or widespread adoption needed for TRL 7+. The README documents tested Vivado versions and real tooling features, supporting a Beta-level judgement.
prerequisites: Xilinx Vivado installed and licensed on host
Familiarity with Vivado/Tcl and basic FPGA flow concepts
student_project_ideas: Build an automated regression that uses vivado-mcp to run synthesis and implementation on a small FPGA project, capture structured timing JSON, and visualise timing changes across commits using a simple web dashboard.

Create an AI-assisted debugging pipeline where an LLM-driven agent uses vivado-mcp to extract waveform slices from VCD, detect X/Z or failed handshakes, and produce a reproducible bug report that includes suggested Tcl fixes.

tools.name: sudoingX/local-ai-on-your-gaming-gpu
tools.desc: run a 27b local ai on your gaming gpu, rtx 3060 and up, radeon rx 6600 and up in beta, 8gb or more, linux and windows, one line to install

cls.summary: A one-line installer and serving wrapper that runs a 27B local LLM on consumer gaming GPUs (NVIDIA/AMD) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API.
cls.what_it_does: This project automates downloading a packaged 27B model and the appropriate prebuilt runtime for a detected gaming GPU, configures runtime flags per VRAM tier, and launches a local server with a web chat UI and an OpenAI-compatible v1 API. It is notable for supporting large (27B) ternary Qwen/Bonsai builds on mainstream consumer GPUs, providing measured performance tiers and easy install scripts for Windows and Linux.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is recent (created 59 days ago) so maturity is limited despite a detailed installer, measured benchmarks and multiple-platform support; the README documents tested cards, install scripts and Hugging Face bundles which indicates early adopters rather than long track record, so TRL=5.
prerequisites: familiarity with command line (PowerShell or bash)
installed GPU drivers (CUDA for NVIDIA or Vulkan for AMD)
sufficient GPU VRAM (8 GB+ depending on build)
internet access for large model downloads
student_project_ideas: Measure and compare inference throughput and latency of the provided 27B runtime across different consumer GPUs (e.g. RTX 3060 vs RTX 4070) and produce a report linking performance to VRAM and PCIe/bandwidth characteristics.

Integrate the local OpenAI-compatible API into a privacy-preserving edge demo: build a small agent that runs on a laptop with a GPU and validates sensor text inputs (e.g. maintenance logs) before forwarding summaries to a cloud service.

tools.name: samffprice/loopcut
tools.desc: Loopcut: an AI agent that works inside Blender. A fork of Blender (GPL).

cls.summary: Loopcut is a forked Blender build that embeds an AI agent panel to inspect scenes and run Python actions (with checkpointed scene diffs and viewport captures) to automate modelling, shading, rigging and render setup tasks.
cls.what_it_does: Loopcut places an AI agent directly inside Blender that can read the scene, propose and run Python to change objects, modifiers, materials, rigs and render presets, showing a post-run scene diff and optional viewport capture for user approval. It supports using local or hosted LLMs or user-supplied OpenAI-compatible keys and preserves safety via checkpoints and undoing conversation steps; notable features include measuring results from the live scene and attaching reference images for visual comparison.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is an active fork of Blender with downloadable builds and many stars but is only 59 days old, so while it is usable by early adopters and provides installers/releases the short track record limits it to TRL 5.
prerequisites: understanding of LLM model keys or local model runtimes (optional)
student_project_ideas: Build an automated asset preparation pipeline that uses Loopcut to standardise naming, apply scale, fix normals and export glTF assets, then validate outputs in a simple Three.js viewer.
Compare productivity: run a controlled experiment where students script the same scene changes manually and with Loopcut, measuring time saved and errors using scene diffs and viewport captures.

tools.name: Kelpekk/Juicee
tools.desc: game-feel effects for Godot 4 with a visual graph editor. Inspired by FEEL.

cls.summary: Juicee is a free Godot 4 plugin that provides a large library of game-feel visual effects (screen shake, hit-stop, squash, trails, particles, damage numbers, etc.) with a visual graph editor and an easy singleton/inspector API.
cls.what_it_does: Juicee provides 117 reusable moment/effect primitives and presets to create and coordinate game-feel effects (camera shake, squash-and-stretch, particle bursts, UI overlays, damage numbers). It is used as a Godot plugin (singleton, JuiceePlayer node, or JuiceeGraph visual editor) to trigger, sequence and combine effects at runtime and during live-tuning in the editor. It is notable for handling effect interactions robustly (combining rumbles, avoiding time_scale lockups) and for offering a visual graph workflow and inspector-based sequencing.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is an actively maintained Godot addon with a detailed README, editor integration, Asset Store distribution and recent pushes, but it is only 160 days old (<1 year) so it lacks the longer track record or wide ecosystem needed for TRL7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with Godot editor and GDScript

tools.name: liampetti/fulloch
tools.desc: Fulloch - The Fully Local Home Voice Assistant

cls.summary: Fulloch is a privacy-focused, fully local voice assistant you run in Docker to control Home Assistant, query an Obsidian vault, and pull web results via self-hosted search.
cls.what_it_does: Fulloch provides a local voice layer for home automation and personal notes: it hosts a browser dashboard, handles speech-to-text and TTS, routes natural-language commands to Home Assistant, and can semantically search an Obsidian vault or consult a self-hosted search engine. It is deployed as a Docker image, supports local and off-box LLMs, and integrates with ESP32 satellites for distributed microphone/assistant devices.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is ~298 days old with Docker images, HACS integration, published releases, active commits and ~170 stars, indicating beta-quality and real users; not yet a long-term production standard so TRL is limited to 6.
prerequisites: Docker (Desktop/Engine) and familiarity with running containers
Home Assistant (optional for full smart-home integration)
Optional: knowledge of local LLM runtimes (Ollama/LM Studio) and ESP32 device flashing
student_project_ideas: Build an ESP32-S3 satellite that captures local voice commands and forwards them to a Docker-deployed Fulloch instance, demonstrating edge device integration and secure local networking.

Integrate Fulloch with a Home Assistant testbed and create voice-driven automation scenarios, then measure end-to-end latency and reliability for different command handling paths (regex fast-path vs LLM).

tools.name: nicorobinreal/llmspeed
tools.desc: Feel how fast a local LLM runs before you buy the hardware

cls.summary: llmspeed is a static web tool that estimates and visualises how fast a local LLM will run on a given GPU/CPU/Mac and model/quantization so you can compare hardware before buying.
cls.what_it_does: llmspeed predicts token-generation speed, time-to-first-token and memory fit for local LLMs across many GPUs, Macs and CPUs using measured benchmarks, interpolations and hardware-based projections. It is used via a static website where you pick hardware and a model (or run side-by-side 'race' comparisons) and can contribute measured benchmarks via PRs to its CSV file. What makes it notable is its combination of a curated benchmark dataset, simple real-time streaming simulation and shareable configuration links for comparing hardware and quantizations.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 81 days old so recent; README and site show a working static tool with community-contributed benchmark CSV and documented measurement process, but it lacks long-term production track record or formal releases, so maturity aligns with 'alpha in use'.
prerequisites: familiarity with local LLM concepts (models, quantization, backends)
Node.js/npm if running locally or contributing
student_project_ideas: Collect and add measured benchmarks from a campus GPU lab (llama.cpp outputs) and analyse discrepancies between measured and projected speeds, producing a short report on causes (drivers, offload, quantization).
Extend the data pipeline to include automated ingestion of vLLM/ExLlama benchmark outputs and build a small web dashboard comparing backend efficiencies across models and hardware.

tools.name: 0xSero/omarchy-local-ai
tools.desc: Local AI for Omarchy: the model validated for your GPU, one button on the bar. Start serves it, any coding agent opens on it, one click shares it on your tailnet.

cls.summary: An Omarchy plugin that detects GPU/CPU capabilities, downloads a tested local LLM, runs it in Docker and exposes it as an OpenAI-compatible local gateway for coding agents and one-click sharing over Tailscale.
cls.what_it_does: Local AI automates selecting a model recipe validated for the machine's GPU or CPU, downloads pinned weights from Hugging Face, runs the model inside Docker with a keyed OpenAI-compatible gateway, and provides an Omarchy UI to start/stop models, view hardware stats and share running models on a Tailscale tailnet. It's notable for per-card validated recipes, integrated checks for RAM/disk requirements, and seamless opening of coding agents (preconfigured clients) against the local gateway without manual configuration.
cls.trl_rationale: The README is detailed and the repo has active commits and modest community interest (173 stars), but the repository is only 77 days old so it lacks the multi-release, production track record required for TRL 6+; evidence supports an alpha/in-use status (install instructions, integrations) consistent with TRL 5.
prerequisites: Supported GPU drivers (nvidia-smi or amd-smi) or x86-64 AVX2 CPU
Optional: Tailscale and Hugging Face token
student_project_ideas: Benchmark and compare throughput, latency and memory use of two pinned local models (e.g. EXL3 vs vLLM recipes) on different GPU cards using the plugin's hardware page and Docker logs.

Build a small coding-agent experiment that uses the plugin's OpenAI-compatible local gateway to evaluate code-generation quality on engineering-focused prompts and record differences when running models on CPU vs GPU.

tools.name: akdeb/OpenToys
tools.desc: Make Local AI Toys, Robots, Devices that work with a MacBook and an Arduino ESP32

cls.summary: OpenToys is a local-first Mac app and firmware ecosystem that runs speech-to-text, LLM inference and text-to-speech on an Apple Silicon Mac and connects to an ESP32‑S3 toy/device over websockets for interactive voice-enabled robots and devices.
cls.what_it_does: OpenToys provides a local voice-AI platform that performs ASR, LLM reasoning and TTS on an Apple Silicon host and communicates with an ESP32‑S3 device via websocket/USB to flash firmware and operate toys or robots without cloud services. It is used as a macOS app (Tauri + Rust + React) for development and runtime, and includes tooling to flash ESP32 firmware and manage characters/personalities for interactive experiences.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is active, has downloadable releases (a DMG), published firmware flashing flow and media coverage, indicating a beta-level product; however the repository is under one year old (created 2026-01-24, ~297 days) which limits TRL to at most 6.
prerequisites: Apple Silicon macOS (familiarity with macOS apps)
Node.js and Rust toolchain for development
Basic ESP32 hardware and serial/USB flashing experience
student_project_ideas: Build an interactive educational toy by flashing an ESP32‑S3 with the provided firmware and creating new personalities and sensor-driven behaviours in the OpenToys app.
Extend OpenToys to log interaction telemetry to a local time-series database (e.g. InfluxDB) and visualise usage patterns on a dashboard to study human-device interaction and reliability.

tools.name: Hash-7777/HashCortX
tools.desc: A local-first AI workspace : multi provider chat, a Full Harness in Hashcoder agent, 3D models, ERPs, and multi-agent swarms in one native desktop app. No backend. No telemetry. No account. MIT-licensed.

cls.summary: HashCortx is a local-first desktop AI workspace that runs multi-model chats, agent teams, a coding agent harness and a 3D CAD/ERP generator with no backend or telemetry.
cls.what_it_does: HashCortx provides a native desktop environment for using multiple LLM providers and local models side-by-side, building and running agent swarms, and running a coding agent (HashCoder) that edits real project files under an application-level harness which runs tests and proves changes. It also includes a 3D Forge that generates dimensioned solids exportable to STL/OBJ/3MF/STEP and an ERP builder; notable features are local RAG document search, a permissioned harness that constrains agents, and offline/privacy-first operation.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with a named release (v4.5.0), 173 stars and recent commits, showing an organised project and users; however it is only ~6 months old (185 days) so a beta-level TRL 6 is appropriate rather than production-grade TRL 7+.
prerequisites: local model runtimes or cloud API keys to use providers (optional)
student_project_ideas: Integrate HashCoder with a small open-source repo to implement an automated edit-and-test workflow: create tasks for the coding agent, run its diffs, and measure test pass/fail and git operations.

Use the 3D Forge to generate a parametric part (export STEP) and run a comparative study: modify the textual prompt to produce variations, then import into a CAD/FEA tool to evaluate geometry changes and manufacturability.

tools.name: rsasaki0109/visloc-rs
tools.desc: SfM, MVS, visual-inertial SLAM, 3D Gaussian Splatting and map-based localization in Rust

cls.summary: visloc-rs is a pure-Rust collection of SfM, MVS, visual-inertial SLAM, 3D Gaussian Splatting and map-based localization tools that build maps from images/IMU and localize new images against those maps.
cls.what_it_does: It turns photos or video (optionally with IMU) into camera poses, sparse/dense maps, photorealistic Gaussian-splat scenes and supports map-based localization and real-time SLAM. The project is implemented entirely in Rust, uses wgpu for GPU work, reads/writes COLMAP formats for interoperability, and provides CLI demos and ROS 2 / Python bindings for integration. Notable points are the benchmarked comparisons to COLMAP, several real-data evaluations (EuRoC, ETH3D, LaMAria) and an end-to-end photos→splat+mesh pipeline without external tools.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is actively developed with many benchmarked results, ROS 2 and Python integration examples, and CI-quality documentation, indicating a beta-level project; however it is younger than one year (created 196 days ago) so it lacks the longer production track record needed for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: GPU drivers and wgpu-compatible GPU (for GPU pipelines)
familiarity with SLAM/SfM datasets (EuRoC, ETH3D, COLMAP) and ROS 2 if using integration
student_project_ideas: Use visloc-rs and a small RGB-D or stereo rig to build a map of a lab area, then implement ROS 2-based map-localization on a mobile robot and measure localization accuracy and runtime.

Run the photos→3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline on a small photographic dataset, compare the resulting model and reconstruction time against a COLMAP+nerf or COLMAP+mesh pipeline, and report quantitative and visual differences.

tools.name: mschneider456/worldmesh
tools.desc: [ECCV 2026] WorldMesh: Generating Navigable Multi-Room 3D Scenes via Mesh-Conditioned Image Diffusion

cls.summary: WorldMesh is a research implementation that generates large, navigable multi-room 3D scenes by conditioning image-diffusion generation on an underlying mesh and human-provided masks.
cls.what_it_does: WorldMesh produces synthetic multi-room 3D scenes in a two-phase pipeline: it first renders structure images for mask creation via a Gradio UI, then uses those masks and mesh-conditioned image diffusion to generate full scene imagery and extract 3D objects. It is notable because it integrates mesh guidance, SAM-based object extraction, and NeRF/nerfstudio-style outputs to produce navigable scenes and provides a released dataset and ECCV 2026 paper.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is the official ECCV 2026 implementation with a paper, project page and released dataset and has active development and many stars, indicating a research-grade, usable codebase; however it is under one year old and primarily a research prototype rather than a widely deployed production tool, so TRL 6 (beta) is appropriate.
prerequisites: experience with Python and model checkpoints
student_project_ideas: Create a pipeline that generates themed interior scenes with WorldMesh and evaluates layout plausibility by extracting semantic object placements and comparing them to a human-labelled dataset (combine with a simple scene graph evaluator).

Integrate WorldMesh outputs into a Nerfstudio viewer and measure rendering/navigation performance and storage trade-offs for different export formats, reporting suitability for a lightweight digital-twin viewer.

tools.name: WenyiWU0111/RSIGame
tools.desc: RSIGame: Autonomous agentic game development with recursive self-improvement

cls.summary: RSIGame is an open-source framework that uses autonomous LLM-driven agents to iteratively generate, playtest, diagnose, repair and verify video games (Godot and Phaser) using a recursive self-improvement loop.
cls.what_it_does: RSIGame automates game development by running agent loops that explore an executable build, collect evidence (logs, screenshots, metrics), prioritise issues, apply code/content edits, and re-verify changes to preserve improvements. It is notable for its explicit local (explore-diagnose-improve-verify) and global (quality monitor, checkpoint preservation, saturation detection) loops and for internalising successful edits into the generator to improve later generations.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very recent (created ~50 days ago) but shows active work, a paper / Hugging Face listing, installs and examples; however it lacks long-term production track record so TRL is limited to an 'alpha in use' level.
student_project_ideas: Reproduce a single GameCraft-Bench task using RSIGame to measure how the local loop affects bug-fix rate, and compare results when using two different generator models (one open and one commercial).

Extend the verification agent to add automated regression tests (unit-like scripted playtests) for a Godot mini-game and measure whether integrating those tests into the Global Quality Monitor reduces regressions over development rounds.

tools.name: ultralytics/yolo26
tools.desc: Ultralytics YOLO26 quickstart for detection, instance and semantic segmentation, depth estimation, classification, pose, OBB, and tracking.

cls.summary: YOLO26 is a PyTorch-based computer vision model suite for object detection, segmentation, depth estimation, pose and tracking intended for training and deployment in Python/CLI workflows.
cls.what_it_does: YOLO26 provides pretrained model weights and a Python/CLI interface to run detection, instance/semantic segmentation, depth estimation, classification, pose estimation, oriented bounding boxes and tracking. It is used by installing the ultralytics package, loading a model (e.g. yolo26n.pt) and running inference or training; notable points are multi-task support (segmentation, depth, pose, OBB, tracking) and built-in export workflows for deployment.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is only ~5 months old so by the project's age it is limited to TRL 5; however the README points to the canonical ultralytics package and downloadable pretrained weights, indicating it is more than a minimal proof-of-concept but lacks the long track record or stable multi-release evidence for TRL 6+.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of computer vision and deep learning
student_project_ideas: Build a ROS node that uses YOLO26 detection and pose outputs to detect and track objects on a mobile robot and publish bounding boxes and poses to downstream planners.
Compare depth estimates from YOLO26-depth with stereo or LiDAR data on a small mobile platform: collect synchronized data, run inference, and quantify errors for mapping/localisation tasks.

tools.name: formiat/px4-ros2-drone-nav
tools.desc: Autonomous UAV navigation in GNSS-denied indoor spaces with no prior map: stereo VIO (MSCKF) and lidar-inertial odometry with map-based relocalization (SLAM), 3D occupancy mapping, D* Lite path planning and GPU MPPI obstacle avoidance. PX4 + ROS 2 + Gazebo SITL, DARPA SubT Urban.

cls.summary: A ROS 2 + PX4 simulation stack that demonstrates autonomous GNSS‑denied indoor UAV navigation using stereo VIO or LIO, 3D occupancy mapping, D* Lite planning and GPU MPPI local avoidance in Gazebo SITL.
cls.what_it_does: The repository provides a complete ROS 2 workspace and simulation environment to develop and test autonomous quadrotor navigation in GNSS/GPS‑denied indoor and underground scenarios. It runs stereo visual‑inertial or lidar‑inertial odometry with relocalization, builds a 3D voxel occupancy map, plans persistent D* Lite paths and performs GPU MPPI obstacle avoidance, all integrated with PX4 SITL and Gazebo for end‑to‑end simulated flights. Notable elements are the focus on map‑based relocalization without global pose graph optimisation, a GPU MPPI local planner, and ready scripts to build and run the full PX4+Gazebo simulation using Docker and NVIDIA runtime.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is an active, functioning simulation stack with tagged releases (v0.7.0), demo video and scripts to reproduce full PX4+Gazebo SITL scenarios, indicating beta maturity. The repository is only ~4.5 months old so despite good artifacts and community interest it lacks the multi‑year track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Integrate a custom perception module (e.g. learning‑based depth estimator) into the workspace and compare localisation and mapping performance against the provided stereo MSCKF VIO in Gazebo SITL.

Replace the GPU MPPI local planner with a CPU‑only MPC or sampling planner and evaluate safety/braking contract tradeoffs and computational cost across different obstacle densities in the supplied urban environment assets.

tools.name: open-subs/opensubs
tools.desc: Subtitle any video without uploading it. Whisper, translation, styling and burn-in — all local, in the browser, on the desktop, or from the command line.

cls.summary: OpenSubs is an open-source tool that creates, styles and burns subtitles into videos locally in the browser, via a desktop app, browser extension or CLI without uploading the video.
cls.what_it_does: OpenSubs transcribes speech from video using local speech models (Whisper-family), optionally translates text, applies styling presets and burns subtitles into the picture; it can run as a web app (WASM), browser extension, desktop Tauri app or command-line tool. It is notable for running models locally in-browser or on-device (privacy-first), sharing a single Rust subtitle engine compiled to native and WASM so all front ends generate consistent output.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is new (created 68 days ago) which limits TRL; however the README shows multiple working front-ends (web, extension, desktop, CLI), published web app and tests, indicating early alpha/alpha-in-use capability rather than a paper prototype.
prerequisites: ffmpeg for burning subtitles on desktop/CLI
student_project_ideas: Create a lab assignment that records a short lab demonstration video, uses OpenSubs CLI to generate subtitles, and evaluates ASR accuracy for domain-specific vocabulary (compare model choices and preprocessing).

Extend the OpenSubs pipeline to add speaker diarization and visual speaker cues (e.g. bounding boxes from a face detector) in the burned-in subtitles and measure usability improvements for accessibility.

tools.name: shadcn-labs/shadercn
tools.desc: Beautiful shader components, built on vgpu and TypeGPU. 100% Free, Zero config, one command setup.

cls.summary: A collection of ready-to-use, TypeScript React shader components that render GPU-powered effects in the browser using WebGPU.
cls.what_it_does: shadercn provides copy-pasteable React components that run GPU shaders in the browser via WebGPU and TypeGPU, with typed props for uniforms and zero-config setup. It is used to add live shader-based visual effects and interactive GPU-driven previews to web UIs and documentation, and is notable for being TypeScript-first and compatible with shadcn/ui.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is young (created 81 days ago) so it cannot be judged as production-proven; the README shows a usable component library and integration with vgpu/TypeGPU and shadcn/ui, but there is no evidence of broad production adoption or stable releases, so TRL is limited to 'Alpha in use'.
student_project_ideas: Create a web dashboard that visualises time-series simulation data by feeding values into shadercn components to show GPU-accelerated animated heatmaps or waveforms.
Design and implement a custom shadercn component that visualises LiDAR or point-sensor data in a browser UI and integrates with a simple WebSocket data stream from a robot.

tools.name: cybergis/rs-embed
tools.desc: One line code to get any remote sensing foundation model embeddings for any place and any time

cls.summary: A Python library that fetches remote-sensing imagery (or accepts user imagery) and produces foundation‑model embeddings for any place and time to support geospatial analysis and downstream ML.
cls.what_it_does: rs-embed downloads or accepts user-provided remote sensing image patches, preprocesses bands and time ranges, and runs a variety of remote‑sensing foundation models to produce vector embeddings. It is used as a simple API (get_embedding, batch exports, or get_embedding_from_data) to create consistent representations for tasks like classification, clustering or change detection, notable for supporting many published RS foundation models and both cloud (Google Earth Engine) and local data inputs.
cls.trl_rationale: The project has documentation, examples, an arXiv paper, versioned releases and active commits, and a modest user community (170 stars), indicating beta maturity; however the repository is under one year old so TRL is limited to 6 by age and short track record.
prerequisites: basic remote sensing concepts (bands, CRS, time series)
optional Google Earth Engine account for provider fetches
student_project_ideas: Use rs-embed to create embeddings for a regional time-series of Sentinel-2 data and build a classifier to map crop types, comparing classification performance using different foundation models.

Combine rs-embed embeddings with a change-detection pipeline (e.g., difference-in-embeddings plus clustering) to detect land-cover change after a natural disaster and produce a simple dashboard of affected areas.

tools.name: eblanshey/HistoryWorkbench
tools.desc: A FreeCAD workbench to track CAD model history and review changes using 3D and tree comparisons.

cls.summary: A FreeCAD add-on that tracks CAD project history and lets you review changes with 3D geometry and document-tree diffs.
cls.what_it_does: History Workbench integrates with FreeCAD to snapshot projects, show colourised 3D geometry differences and tree/property diffs between iterations, and manage a local iteration timeline. It is used as a workbench inside FreeCAD (installed via the Addon Manager) and uses Git under the hood while presenting CAD-focused terminology and workflows. Notable features include multi-document support, per-property change inspection, and workflows to review/save/restore iterations without rewriting history.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository has clear documentation, an installable FreeCAD addon, active development and 169 stars, indicating beyond early prototype; however the project is under 1 year old (created 2026-05-05, ~196 days) so there is limited long-term production track record which constrains TRL to Beta (6).
prerequisites: basic git installed (optional for advanced workflows)
familiarity with FreeCAD document tree and parametric modelling
student_project_ideas: Use History Workbench in a CAD lab to show how small parametric changes propagate through an assembly and build an automated report that links property diffs to failed design checks (combine with a simple Python script that flags dimension rule violations).

Create a student project that integrates History Workbench snapshots with a CI pipeline (Git) to automatically run geometry validation scripts and visualise diffs for each iteration, demonstrating a lightweight PLM/digital thread for a small assembly.

tools.name: PrimeFoldTools/Andon
tools.desc: Stop hooks that stop AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) from claiming "done" without proof. A Lean quality system: every defect becomes a permanent countermeasure. Built by a manufacturing operator.

cls.summary: Andon is an open-source collection of hooks and lightweight operating practices that catch and record recurring AI agent defects (for example, false 'done' claims) and make countermeasures enforceable.
cls.what_it_does: Andon provides file templates, command-line hooks and plugin integrations that detect common agent failure modes (e.g. falsely claiming completion), require verification evidence, and record defects as durable countermeasures. It is used by copying templates into a project and running the Python hooks or installing the Claude Code / Codex plugin; notable features include claim-check hooks, a pipe-guard that prevents hidden-failure test commands, and a structured MEMORY.md approach to durable facts.
cls.trl_rationale: The repo is recent (created ~146 days ago) but shows an active codebase, tests, CLI examples and plugin install instructions (Claude Code / Codex), suggesting a beta-level project with versioned behaviour and community interest; its age (<1 year) prevents rating above TRL 6.
prerequisites: familiarity with running CLI tools and pytest
access to the target agent environment (e.g. Claude Code or Codex) to install plugins
student_project_ideas: Extend the claim-check hook to add a deterministic evidence verifier for a chosen CI tool (e.g. integrate with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI) and demonstrate catching a fabricated 'done' claim in an automated pipeline.

Create a small engineering workflow that uses MEMORY.md plus the Andon pipe-guard to manage repeated test-run failures in a student software project and measure how many recurring defects the hooks catch over a semester.

tools.name: jungang/alumnet
tools.desc: AlumNet - AI-powered intelligent school history exhibition & alumni management system | AI 智能校史展示系统 — 校友星图

cls.summary: AlumNet is an open-source full‑stack system for creating an AI‑powered touch‑screen school history exhibition and alumni management dashboard.
cls.what_it_does: AlumNet provides a kiosk frontend with immersive Three.js visuals and a management dashboard, backed by an Express/TypeScript API, PostgreSQL and a vector search (Qdrant) for RAG-based natural language queries. It is used to deploy museum‑style exhibitions and alumni databases quickly (Docker Compose available) and is notable for combining 3D interactive displays with AI search over alumni data.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with Docker deployment, a complete tech stack and user-facing features, and has modest community interest (167 stars); however it is under one year old (created 199 days ago) so lacks a long track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Extend the kiosk by adding a new Three.js interactive exhibit (e.g. a timeline or network graph) that pulls enriched alumni data from the backend and deploy it with Docker Compose.

Build a small RAG demo: ingest a CSV of alumni records into PostgreSQL and pgvector, index vectors in Qdrant, and create example natural‑language queries to evaluate retrieval quality and explainability.

tools.name: tradoor-terminal/tradoor
tools.desc: Open-source crypto trading terminal in the browser: charts, DOM, footprint, TPO market profile, liquidations and order flow from 14 exchanges, your own indicators in Frost Script, a journal and paper trading. Rust, WebAssembly, WebGL2.

cls.summary: Tradoor is an open-source browser-based crypto trading terminal with charts, order‑flow/DOM views, market profile, footprints, a scripting language (Frost Script), backtesting and paper trading.
cls.what_it_does: Tradoor streams market data from multiple crypto exchanges into a high‑performance browser client drawn by a Rust WebAssembly engine (WebGL2 on an OffscreenCanvas). It provides synchronized multi‑chart workspaces, order book (DOM), tape/footprint views, session TPO market profiles, a small indicator language (Frost Script) with in‑browser backtests and a paper trading/journal feature; it can be self‑hosted via Docker.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is functional and feature‑rich (charts, multi‑exchange streams, Frost Script, Docker image) and has community interest (stars/forks), but the repository is very new (created 24 days ago), so there is limited demonstrated long‑term production use.
prerequisites: familiarity with Rust/WASM if modifying the engine

tools.name: HeinrichZ/CloudField
tools.desc: First browser-based interactive cloud microphysics & aviation weather simulation tool for low-visibility decision support (WebGL2, cloud seeding, METAR/TAF/RVR, LES pre-processing, DE/EN/ZH). 首个面向民航低能见度气象研判的浏览器端云微物理交互仿真工具

cls.summary: CloudField is a browser-based interactive sandbox for cloud microphysics, aviation weather diagnostics and LES pre-processing that runs in WebGL2 and links microphysical parameterisations with METAR/TAF decision metrics and export for CFD/LES tools.
cls.what_it_does: CloudField simulates and visualises three-dimensional cloud microphysics (1‑moment and 2‑moment schemes) and related aviation weather metrics (visibility/RVR, METAR/TAF inversion, icing, seeding effects) in a browser using WebGL2. It is used as an offline sandbox to compare microphysical parameterisations, test cloud seeding scenarios (WBF process), compute remote‑sensing observables and export inflow/fields for LES/CFD tools; notable is the combination of real‑time 3D volume rendering with aviation operational diagnostics and LES pre‑processing in a zero‑dependency frontend.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (24 days) so it cannot show long track record; README documents many advanced capabilities and there are community stars, but age and short history limit demonstrated maturity to early 'alpha in use' (TRL 5). Also the 'All Rights Reserved' license statement restricts reuse which reduces practical readiness.
prerequisites: basic atmospheric science / cloud microphysics knowledge
student_project_ideas: Compare the simulated visibility/RVR outcomes for Kessler, KK2000 and ICON‑SB06 microphysics in CloudField for a given sounding, export inflow fields and run a small LES case in OpenFOAM or a toy LES to assess sensitivity of runway visibility forecasts.

Implement an METAR/TAF ingestion lab where students invert observed METARs into boundary‑layer profiles in CloudField, simulate the effect of a targeted AgI seeding trench and quantify predicted runway visibility improvements and aircraft icing index changes.

tools.name: CaviraOSS/Akashic
tools.desc: Akashic is an open-source Palantir alternative for connecting, exploring, and analyzing complex data. Fully self-hosted, privacy-first, and requiring no API keys.

cls.summary: Akashic is a self‑hosted geospatial intelligence workspace that combines live public data (aircraft, satellites, seismic, weather, radio, infrastructure, etc.) into a single interactive map for exploration and correlation without requiring API keys.
cls.what_it_does: Akashic ingests a variety of public upstream data sources and presents them as layered, inspectable entities on a map or globe so users can explore, correlate and investigate events and infrastructure. It runs a server with upstream adapters and a browser UI that streams results (including a 'recon' mode for public identifier sweeps), emphasising live exploration rather than passive dashboards.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (created ~128 days ago) but has active development, a substantive README and 167 stars indicating interest; however it lacks a long production track record and is younger than one year so TRL is limited to mid‑alpha/early‑use (around 5).
prerequisites: basic web mapping knowledge (tiles, layers, projections)
familiarity with Docker or self-hosted deployment
student_project_ideas: Build a course lab that deploys Akashic in Docker, configures an additional upstream (e.g. a local ADS‑B feed or a public USGS seismic feed), and creates a short report correlating aircraft/satellite tracks with seismic or weather events.

Extend Akashic with a custom layer that ingests municipal open‑data (e.g. traffic sensors or air quality monitors) and implements a simple alerting rule to visualise possible infrastructure stress points on the map.

tools.name: camilleroux/genart-skill
tools.desc: Generative art skill for Claude Code — deterministic, hash-seeded, onchain-ready

cls.summary: A Claude Code plugin providing authoritative reference sheets and a spec for verifying deterministic, hash-seeded generative-art sketches (no runtime code shipped).
cls.what_it_does: genart is a Claude Code 'skill' that encodes best-practice guidance for creating deterministic, hash-seeded generative art (traits/rarity, resolution independence, export for screens/pen-plotters and on‑chain platforms). Rather than shipping runnable sketch code, it supplies Markdown reference sheets and a precise Playwright-based verification spec that Claude will write into your project to test repeatability and export builds.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is recent (created 81 days ago) and contains well-written reference material, CI link-checking and an established author, but it ships no runtime code and shows no long track record or broad production use; age limits TRL to at most 5.
prerequisites: access to Claude Code plugin usage
student_project_ideas: Use the repository's verification spec to write a Playwright harness that proves same-machine reproducibility for a p5.js sketch and integrate that check into CI.
Adapt a deterministic generative sketch following the genart sheets to export pen-plotter-ready SVGs and create a batch renderer that produces an edition with measured rarity statistics.

tools.name: joeynyc/spark-doctor
tools.desc: Local diagnostic CLI for NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10). Detects power caps, UMA pressure, thermal risk, CUDA 13/SM_121 wheel mismatches, Docker issues, and validates vLLM/Ollama/llama.cpp/SGLang recipes.

cls.summary: Spark Doctor is a local command-line diagnostic tool that collects system and GPU signals on NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems and applies platform-specific rules to explain likely causes and next steps.
cls.what_it_does: Spark Doctor runs read-only probes (nvidia-smi, /proc pressure, dmesg, docker info, Python runtime checks etc.), evaluates DGX Spark-specific rules for power, thermal, memory/UMA pressure, CUDA/PyTorch compatibility and local-LLM recipe issues, and generates a concise diagnosis with evidence and remediation suggestions. It is used as a CLI on the host to scan a system, save and re-run diagnoses, validate model runtime recipes, and export reports; notable for targeting GB10/DGX Spark quirks and for validating vLLM/Ollama/llama.cpp environments.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is actively maintained, has a detailed README, CLI, and 166 stars indicating adoption, but it was created ~207 days ago (under one year) so it lacks a long track record or multiple stable major releases; this matches a beta-level maturity.
prerequisites: Linux host with NVIDIA drivers (DGX Spark / GB10)
Python 3.11+ and familiarity with virtual environments
Basic knowledge of CUDA, Docker and local-LLM runtimes (vLLM/Ollama/llama.cpp)
student_project_ideas: Build a lab exercise that uses Spark Doctor to diagnose deliberately misconfigured Docker/CUDA environments on a DGX-like VM image and produce a remediation checklist that students must apply and verify.

Extend Spark Doctor with an additional rule that detects and visualises model KV-cache memory pressure across multiple containers, and validate the extension by running a multi-backend vLLM workload (vLLM + Ollama) on a GPU node.

tools.name: ahtx/kindi
tools.desc: Kindi 0.6: fast local LLM inference on low-cost GPUs and CPUs. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (552B) at 18.7 tok/s on one RTX 3060 12 GB with a dual-Xeon DDR4 server. Ternary Bonsai 2B-27B, AH-Nanbeige4.3-33B, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B. NVIDIA from the Quadro K420 to the RTX 50 series, AMD Radeon graphics, Windows and Linux. OpenAI-compatible server.

cls.summary: Kindi is an open-source inference engine that runs large language models locally on low-cost GPUs and x86 CPUs and exposes an OpenAI-compatible server.
cls.what_it_does: Kindi provides a fast runtime for running several large LLMs (ternary Bonsai family, AH-Nanbeige, Nemotron, DeepSeek) on a wide range of consumer and workstation GPUs and on CPUs, with features like speculative decoding, prompt caching and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API. It is used by installing the project (native or Docker) and running the server, letting existing OpenAI-compatible clients or scripts connect to localhost to make chat/completion requests. It is notable for targeting very low-memory cards and for benchmarked performance claims versus llama.cpp.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is very new (created 28 days ago) which limits demonstrated maturity; however the README shows a packaged installer, benchmark data and substantial community interest (165 stars) indicating early alpha/alpha-in-use status rather than a paper prototype.
prerequisites: familiarity with local GPUs (CUDA/ROCm) and drivers
access to model files and sufficient system memory
student_project_ideas: Benchmark Kindi against llama.cpp and ggml on an 8 GB GPU to measure latency, throughput and memory trade-offs, and report results with reproducible scripts.
Integrate Kindi's OpenAI-compatible server with a simple robotics simulator or ROS node to prototype a local natural-language interface for robot tasking without cloud APIs.

tools.name: YoKONCy/infOS
tools.desc: 基于操作系统思维构建的AI Agent底座：用长记忆引擎造就「陪伴」；用精美客户端打造「体验」；用深度拓展探索「无限边界」。只为打造最懂你的AI伙伴

tools.name: jaskirat1616/Splatline
tools.desc: Convert 2D videos and photos into interactive 3D scenes using Gaussian splatting backends (VGGT, LongSplat, DepthSplat, SHARP, TripoSplat), Rerun, and the SuperSplat editor.

cls.summary: Splatline converts photos and videos into interactive 3D scenes using Gaussian-splatting reconstruction backends and provides both desktop and web viewers for smooth splat rendering.
cls.what_it_does: Splatline runs a pipeline that converts 2D video or image inputs into dense Gaussian splat representations (3DGS) using multiple pluggable backends (SHARP, TripoSplat, VGGT, DepthSplat, LongSplat). It provides viewing and editing via a Rerun integration, a browser SuperSplat editor, an Electron desktop player with GPU-accelerated splat compositing, and a FastAPI backend for job control and streaming progress.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository shows a mature feature set (multiple backends, v2.0.0, Electron player, FastAPI server), active development and community interest (165 stars) but was created ~312 days ago (<1 year) so evidence supports a beta-level TRL (6) rather than long-term production maturity.
prerequisites: familiarity with running ML models and installing Python dependencies
macOS recommended (README notes macOS support and no CUDA requirement)
student_project_ideas: Build a small pipeline that captures short smartphone video, runs Splatline's LongSplat backend to produce a temporally coherent scene, and measures reconstruction stability across different frame rates and lighting conditions (combine with simple metrics computed in Python).

Integrate Splatline's output into a web-based viewer and overlay GIS/coordinate metadata to create a simple as-built visualization for a small civil site, demonstrating registration between the splat model and ground survey points.

tools.name: notoriouslab/vault-curate
tools.desc: Find, connect, rediscover your notes — a local-first second brain for Obsidian. Semantic search with strong Chinese/CJK, relation graphs and semantic paths for connections you never drew, Hot/Cold rediscovery of forgotten notes. Desktop builds the index; phones and tablets search it. No API keys.

cls.summary: Vault Curate is an Obsidian plugin that provides local-first semantic search, relation-graph discovery and rediscovery workflows for personal markdown notes with strong Chinese/CJK support.
cls.what_it_does: Vault Curate builds a local semantic index of an Obsidian vault (desktop) and lets you search that index from desktop or mobile without sending data to cloud services by default. It offers merged keyword/semantic/fuzzy search, Canvas relation-graph generation, Hot/Cold rediscovery and optional AI-assisted curation, and emphasizes a compact bundled model (≈110 MB) plus integrations with local or chosen LLM services.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active (created 2026-04-04, last push 2026-10-30) and has a detailed README, desktop & mobile builds and a public user base (164 stars), indicating beta-level maturity; however it is younger than one year so lacks the longer track record or broad production adoption required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: Obsidian (desktop for indexing; mobile for searching)
Basic familiarity with Obsidian plugins and vaults
Node.js / typical TypeScript build toolchain for building from source (if compiling)
student_project_ideas: Evaluate and quantify Vault Curate's Chinese semantic search accuracy by building a labelled test set of Chinese notes and comparing retrieval metrics between Vault Curate, a cloud LLM (Ollama/OpenAI) and Obsidian's native search.

Integrate Vault Curate with a literature manager (e.g. Zotero) to create a project that automatically discovers and links notes to referenced papers and visualises the semantic neighbourhood on an Obsidian Canvas.

tools.name: RobLe3/cc-blender-skill
tools.desc: Claude Code skill plugin: drive Blender 5.x like a senior 3D artist via natural language. 10 chain-loadable skills (modeling, materials, lighting, cameras, rendering, animation, export, wireframe-to-3d, pro-workflow). Validated on 6 scene classes.

cls.summary: A Blender add-on that provides a pack of natural-language 'skills' so agent hosts (Claude Code, Codex) can drive Blender 5.x workflows — modelling, materials, lighting, animation, export and validation — via MCP.
cls.what_it_does: cc-blender-skill exposes ~30 chain-loadable skills that translate high-level text prompts into Blender Python executed through an MCP backend, automating tasks such as procedural modelling, materials, lighting, camera setup, rendering and export workflows. It is installed as a Blender plugin and works with Blender Lab MCP or an alternative MCP implementation, with built-in validation and export checks for pipelines like Unreal FBX/GLB.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository shows versioned releases (v1.4.0), integration test reports, CI-like validation and active maintenance with community PRs; however it is <1 year old (created 204 days ago) so maturity is consistent with a beta-level project rather than long-term production adoption.
prerequisites: An MCP host (Blender Lab MCP or ahujasid blender-mcp) and an agent host (Claude Code or Codex)
student_project_ideas: Build an automated asset-generation pipeline that accepts a dataset of scene prompts, uses cc-blender-skill via a local MCP to generate glTF exports, and measures geometry validity and UV coverage statistics for integration into a simple digital-twin viewer.

Compare manual Blender modelling versus agent-driven outputs by creating a quality-evaluation experiment: feed identical prompts to cc-blender-skill and a human student, then use objective metrics (mesh manifoldness, polycount, bake correctness) and a short usability survey to analyse differences.

alternatives_to: procedural Blender add-ons (e.g., Tissue, ANT Landscape)

tools.name: harry7557558/vksplat
tools.desc: Code for paper "VkSplat: High-Performance 3DGS Training in Vulkan Compute"

cls.summary: VkSplat is an open-source implementation for training 3D Gaussian Splatting models using Vulkan compute with Python bindings, aimed at high-performance, cross-vendor 3D reconstruction and rendering.
cls.what_it_does: VkSplat implements training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models using a Vulkan compute backend exposed to Python via a pybind11 extension. It solves high-performance, memory-efficient reconstruction and rendering of 3D scenes (tested across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs), and is notable for achieving multi-fold speedups and large-model memory efficiency compared to the original GSplat implementation.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository implements code tied to a 2026 Eurographics paper, includes tested examples, multi-vendor testing and user feedback, and has a detailed README and build paths; however the project is under one year old (created ~225 days ago) so it lacks long-term production track record required for TRL 7+.
student_project_ideas: Reproduce the paper's benchmark: run VkSplat and GSplat on a chosen scene and measure training speed, memory use and image metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), documenting differences and tuning shader compile flags.

Integrate VkSplat into a small photogrammetry pipeline (images -> SfM -> VkSplat) to produce and visualise a reconstructed scene, and compare quality and runtime against a neural radiance field (e.g. Instant-NGP).

tools.name: OpenIGI/OpenIGI
tools.desc: A clean-room reimplementation of the Project I.G.I. and I.G.I. 2 engine in C#/.NET 10. It plays the original missions faithfully, with a modern renderer (D3D12, Vulkan, WebGPU, ray tracing, DLSS), co-op, mods and a launcher.

cls.summary: OpenIGI is an open-source reimplementation of the Project I.G.I. and I.G.I.2 game engine written in C#/.NET that runs original game data with a modern renderer, launcher and modding support.
cls.what_it_does: OpenIGI reimplements the original game engine so users can run their retail copies of Project I.G.I. and I.G.I.2 with faithful gameplay, a deterministic simulation and a modern renderer. It is used by building or installing the launcher, pointing it at your game files, and optionally creating mods or content packs; it supports Direct3D12, Vulkan and WebGPU backends and can run in desktop and browser environments. Notable features include a vanilla regression mode, hardware ray tracing support, optional NVIDIA DLSS/Reflex components and a moddable C# API.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is young (created 45 days ago) which caps maturity; README and releases show an active project and usable builds, significant stars and platform support indicate early adopters but not a long track record, so TRL ~5 (alpha in use).
prerequisites: A legal retail installation of Project I.G.I. or I.G.I. 2 (game data)

tools.name: LucasJRamos/spritekiln
tools.desc: Animated pixel-art sprites (8-direction top-down or side view) from procedural 3D models in YAML, built to be driven by coding AIs. Exports to Godot, Unity, MonoGame or any engine.

cls.summary: SpriteKiln is a Python CLI that generates animated pixel-art spritesheets from small YAML procedural 3D character specs and exports them for game engines.
cls.what_it_does: SpriteKiln turns a compact YAML description of a character (skeleton, primitives, materials, animations) into pixel-art sprites in multiple directions or side view, producing timed frames, events, sockets, normal and emissive maps and engine-ready exports. It is used as a command-line tool and can be driven by coding AIs (an MCP-style assistant workflow) to iterate specs automatically; notable points are its AI-oriented workflow, text-spec driven procedural generation, and multi-engine export (Godot, Unity, MonoGame or generic Aseprite-compatible sheets).
cls.trl_rationale: The README and install instructions are complete, the CLI and AI integration features are documented and there are many stars, but the repository is only 27 days old so it lacks the longer track record and stable releases that would justify TRL 6+.
prerequisites: basic familiarity with command-line tools and YAML
student_project_ideas: Create a small Godot demo that uses SpriteKiln-generated character specs to procedurally produce multiple NPCs and implement simple AI-driven editing (e.g. change costume or animation timing and re-render at runtime).
Build a pipeline that converts SpriteKiln exports into an Aseprite-compatible workflow, then add a benchmarking script to compare visual consistency and file sizes across different style settings.

tools.name: sergiovirahonda/cortex
tools.desc: ESP32-S3 flight controller for DIY quadcopters: real-time PID stabilization, DShot ESCs, nRF24 radio, telemetry downlink. Pairs with Synapse TX.

cls.summary: Cortex is an open-source ESP32‑S3 flight controller firmware that provides real‑time PID attitude stabilization, DShot ESC output, radio telemetry and blackbox logging for DIY quadcopters.
cls.what_it_does: Cortex runs on an ESP32‑S3 and reads IMU, barometer, LiDAR and other avionics to stabilise a quadcopter using real‑time PID control while driving DShot ESCs and handling radio commands (nRF24). It includes telemetry to a matching Synapse transmitter, blackbox logging to microSD, and modular adapters so optional sensors can be omitted. Notable points are its dual‑core task separation for a ~1 kHz flight loop, native DShot via RMT, and PlatformIO build support.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 295 days old (<1 year) with a detailed README, hardware wiring, tuning guide, PlatformIO integration and active development (stars and forks indicate community interest), consistent feature set and examples so it meets a beta maturity; not enough evidence of widespread production use for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: experience with PlatformIO or ESP32 toolchains (ESP-IDF/Arduino)
basic electronics, soldering and RC/drone safety procedures
student_project_ideas: Build a small X‑frame quad using the Cortex firmware and Synapse transmitter, then measure and tune PID gains, document flight performance and safety procedures.
Add or compare an alternative sensor fusion (e.g., replace MPU6050 with an ICM‑20948) and evaluate impacts on stability and blackbox log analysis using logged flight data.

tools.name: drawthingsai/local-code-community
tools.desc: Source code of Local Code, a private AI agent for Mac, iPad and iPhone. Runs DeepSeek 4.1 on device, with Python, Node.js and a shell built into the app.

cls.summary: Local Code is an on-device AI coding agent for macOS, iPad and iPhone that bundles an LLM inference engine, a coding/runtime harness (Python, Node.js, shell) and an agent runtime to operate on files and projects inside a sandboxed workspace.
cls.what_it_does: Local Code runs quantized LLMs on Apple Silicon (or optionally cloud models) and provides an agent runtime with built-in Python, Node.js, a shell and other tools so the agent can analyze data, generate charts, edit documents, run build/test commands and author software inside a per-project sandbox. It is notable for on-device inference of very large mixture-of-experts models with streaming-from-disk of experts, resumable generation, long-term context caching and an app-level sandbox that constrains file and network access.
cls.trl_rationale: The README and repository show a working, feature-rich application with model downloads and example skills, but the repo is only 27 days old so there is little public track record; this supports an alpha/in-use rating rather than mature or widely adopted.
prerequisites: Apple Silicon Mac or iPad/iPhone (for on-device models)
large local storage for model checkpoints (hundreds of GB) if using biggest models
student_project_ideas: Build an automated code-review agent that runs inside Local Code to lint, run unit tests and summarize failing tests for a small Python project, comparing on-device and cloud model results.

Create a data-analysis skill that ingests CSV sensor logs, runs preprocessing and plots summary charts with the bundled Python environment, and evaluates how well the agent documents its processing steps for reproducibility.

tools.name: WayneChou-bot/WareTwin
tools.desc: Real-time 3D digital twin of an autonomous warehouse — 20 AMRs, deterministic simulation, explainable fleet scheduling, failure injection, VLM camera perception, AI Ops Copilot and what-if scenarios. React Three Fiber + FastAPI.

cls.summary: WareTwin is an open-source, browser-native 3D digital twin that simulates an autonomous warehouse fleet (20 AMRs), deterministic robot state machines, explainable fleet scheduling, failure injection and what‑if experiments.
cls.what_it_does: WareTwin provides a real-time digital twin of a warehouse that runs a deterministic simulation engine (100 ms tick) for robot FSMs, A* navigation, battery and conveyor models and a Fleet Manager with explainable scoring. It pairs a FastAPI Python backend with a React Three Fiber frontend to visualise the twin in the browser, supports scenario injection and offline what-if experiments, and includes an AI copilot and VLM perception modes.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository contains a complete frontend/backend implementation, live demo and runnable quick‑start (evidence of early adopters and usability), but it is very new (created 87 days ago) so it lacks a longer track record or stable releases required for TRL 6+.
prerequisites: familiarity with TypeScript, React, and basic Python web services
student_project_ideas: Extend the Fleet Manager with a new task-assignment policy (e.g. reinforcement learning or priority queues), compare KPIs across the built-in what-if framework, and visualise results in the React Three Fiber frontend.

Integrate a lightweight ROS 2 bridge that translates WareTwin twin state to ROS topics and use a real or simulated controller on a small mobile robot to validate end-to-end task assignment and safety behaviours.

tools.name: ektogamat/threejs-conference
tools.desc: Walk through a rainy cyberpunk alley powered by WebGPU, Three.js, and TSL (Three Shading Language). Neon billboards, wet pavement, GPU rain that respects rooftops and props, cinematic post-processing, and first-person exploration with BVH collision.

cls.summary: A WebGPU-powered Three.js demo scene that renders a walkable, rainy cyberpunk alley with GPU rain, TSL post-processing and BVH-based collision for first-person exploration.
cls.what_it_does: This repository implements a real-time WebGPU scene using Three.js and TSL (Three Shading Language) that showcases GPU-driven rain, cinematic post-processing, and BVH collision for first-person walking. It is used as a demo and workshop project (live demo available) and is notable for combining WebGPU compute shaders, a reusable TSL render pipeline, and three-mesh-bvh for efficient collision and scene traversal.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is a mature demo used in a 2026 TSL workshop, includes a live demo, detailed README, and active commits, but the repository is only ~4 months old and primarily demonstrates techniques rather than widespread production deployment, so TRL is limited to Beta (6).
student_project_ideas: Modify the GPU rain compute shader to model different particle behaviours (splash, wind) and measure performance trade-offs across device profiles, reporting FPS and memory usage.
Integrate a simple sensor-data stream (simulated IoT telemetry) to drive billboard content and validate update latency and visual coherence in the WebGPU render loop.

tools.name: HybridAIOne/hybridclaw
tools.desc: Enterprise-ready self-hosted AI assistant runtime with sandboxed execution, secure credentials, approvals, and memory

cls.summary: HybridClaw is a self-hosted, enterprise-orientated AI assistant runtime that runs sandboxed multi-agent assistants with encrypted secrets, approval workflows and connectors to common business services.
cls.what_it_does: HybridClaw provides a local runtime and gateway for running LLM-powered assistants and multi-agent workflows with sandboxed execution, credential separation, approval tiers and audit trails. It is used as a self-hosted service (CLI, macOS app, or container) to connect assistants to services like CRM, cloud, email and chat platforms while keeping secrets out of model context. Notable features include multi-agent A2A encrypted envelopes, structured onboarding/hatching, and built-in production skill helpers validated on smaller models.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is under one year old (created ~266 days ago) but shows evidence of a managed installer, a signed macOS app release, CLI packages and documentation which indicate beta-level maturity; however it lacks the long track record and large community required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: familiarity with LLM/agent concepts and basic system administration
experience running containers or installing CLI tools
student_project_ideas: Build a small team of HybridClaw agents that automate a simple workflow (e.g. ingesting CSV sales leads, enriching them via an API, and drafting outreach) and evaluate audit trails and approval controls; compare robustness using a local small LLM and a hosted model.

Integrate HybridClaw with a simulated IoT data pipeline (MQTT -> SQLite -> HybridClaw) to prototype an alerting assistant that generates and routes incident summaries to Slack/Email with approval gating and secret-protected connectors.

tools.name: rongxinzy/RongxinAI
tools.desc: Open-source desktop AI agent: built-in free model, local GGUF models via llama.cpp, dispatch tasks from WeChat/Feishu/DingTalk. Files, browser & MCP tools. | 开源桌面 AI 智能体：内置免费模型，llama.cpp 本地 GGUF 模型，微信/飞书/钉钉直接派任务。

cls.summary: ZhiYuan Agent is an open-source, local-first desktop AI agent that runs built-in or GGUF local models (via llama.cpp), automates tasks (files, commands, browser) and accepts tasks from chat platforms like WeChat, Feishu/Lark and DingTalk.
cls.what_it_does: ZhiYuan provides a desktop agent that can run a built-in free model or locally-hosted GGUF models (llama.cpp), execute tool actions (file I/O, shell commands, Playwright browser automation) and receive tasks from messaging platforms. It is packaged as an Electron desktop app with installers for Windows, macOS and Linux and includes an extensible plugin/skill system and MCP-style dispatching for remote connectors.
cls.trl_rationale: The project publishes installers for Windows/macOS/Linux, has active commits and a modest community (stars/forks) which indicates a beta-level, usable product; the repository is ~190 days old so it lacks a longer track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: Optional Python and C/C++ toolchain for native deps
Local GGUF models and sufficient CPU/GPU to run them
student_project_ideas: Build a task automation workflow where the agent receives a document-processing request from a WeChat test account, downloads a model locally via llama.cpp, extracts data from the document and generates a summarized report (combine ZhiYuan Agent, Playwright and a local GGUF model).

Extend the agent with a custom Skill that performs automated test-run orchestration for a small robotics simulation: accept commands via a chat connector, run scripts to start simulators and collect logs for verification (combine ZhiYuan Agent, a simulator/ROS node and logging analysis).

tools.name: cocel-postech/genz-lio
tools.desc: GenZ-LIO: SOTA robust LiDAR-inertial odometry (IEEE T-FR 2026)

cls.summary: GenZ-LIO is an open-source LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO) system designed for robust pose estimation across confined and open environments and transitions between them.
cls.what_it_does: GenZ-LIO fuses LiDAR point clouds and IMU data to produce robust, real-time odometry and pose estimates for mobile platforms. It can be run from a Python CLI or integrated with ROS/ROS2, includes experiment/config YAMLs and a visualiser, and provides pip-installable wheels that include compiled C++ extensions. It is notable for targeting generalisability across indoor/outdoor boundary conditions and providing benchmark reproductions from the authors' paper and dataset.
cls.trl_rationale: The project is backed by a recent peer-reviewed paper and provides runnable code, dataset links and pip wheels, but the repository is very young (55 days) so it lacks a long track record or broad adoption; this matches an 'alpha in use' TRL.
prerequisites: Familiarity with LiDAR/IMU data and ROS/rosbag (recommended)
C++/systems programming background for deeper integration
student_project_ideas: Evaluate GenZ-LIO robustness by comparing its trajectory estimates to LIO-SAM and LeGO-LOAM on a handheld indoor-outdoor dataset, and quantify failures during confined–open transitions.
Integrate GenZ-LIO with a small mobile robot (ROS) and implement a short navigation stack to test online mapping and loop closure behaviour in a constrained indoor environment.

tools.name: tt-a1i/MiroFish-local
tools.desc: MiroFish的免费本地运行版本 | Graphiti+Neo4j替代付费Zep | 简易便捷本地跑通

cls.summary: MiroFish-Local is a local-first multi-agent social-simulation engine that builds knowledge graphs and runs parallel agent-based simulations using local Graphiti + Neo4j instead of cloud memory services.
cls.what_it_does: It lets users construct structured knowledge graphs from seed texts, generate agent personas, and run large-scale parallel multi-agent simulations to predict social, market or policy dynamics. The project is used locally (Docker + Neo4j + Python/Node stack) and notable for replacing a cloud memory backend (Zep) with a fully local Graphiti + Neo4j option to keep data on-premises.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is a working, documented fork with install scripts, Docker Compose and a demo, and has attracted community interest (161 stars). However it is under one year old (created 2026-01-06) so there is limited track record of broad production use, which constrains the TRL to Beta (6).
prerequisites: LLM API key (OpenAI-compatible) and familiarity with LLM usage
student_project_ideas: Build and compare two scenario simulations (e.g. misinformation spread vs controlled correction) using MiroFish-Local with different Neo4j graph structures and quantify propagation metrics.
Integrate a local small LLM (Ollama or similar) with the Graphiti backend to evaluate privacy-preserving entity extraction accuracy and token cost versus using a cloud LLM.

tools.name: Khalidabdi1/factory
tools.desc: A live isometric world in the browser: a seaside town, a new city, a farming village and a Starship launch site, all simulated in real time. Built with Claude Opus 5.5, three.js, TypeScript and Next.js.

cls.summary: A browser-based, isometric real‑time city and logistics simulation built with three.js and Next.js that runs as a static site and shows traffic, vehicles and animated day/night behaviour.
cls.what_it_does: Factory Yard renders an isometric seaside town, a new city, countryside and a starship launch site in the browser and simulates moving actors (trucks, trains, people, boats) and time of day. It's delivered as a Next.js app that builds to static HTML/JS and uses a custom engine (yard/) for iso projection, routing and the simulation loop. It is notable for a compact, self-contained WebGL/three.js implementation of an isometric, event-driven world that can be hosted as a static site.
cls.trl_rationale: The repository is active, has a clear code structure and examples and builds to a static site, but it was created only 44 days ago so there is no long track record or stable release history; functionality appears complete enough for demos (early alpha).
student_project_ideas: Extend the simulation to instrument and visualise logistics KPIs (throughput, dwell time) by exporting vehicle events to a time-series CSV and building a dashboard (combine with a simple Node/Express endpoint or static CSV analysis).

Modify the engine to add a simple traffic control policy (e.g. adaptive signals or priority for buses) and compare metrics in experiments, visualising results in the scene and plotting summary statistics with a charting library.

tools.name: Orchis-ai-LLC/Konnect-EDA
tools.desc: AI-assisted PCB design for KiCAD 10: downloads and issue tracker. Commercial, closed source, free during the beta.

cls.summary: Konnect-EDA is an AI-assisted plugin that lets an AI edit KiCad 10 schematics and PCBs and export production files while running locally on the user's machine.
cls.what_it_does: Konnect-EDA connects AI assistants (Claude, Codex and others) to KiCad 10 via the Model Context Protocol so the AI can place components, wire schematics, lay out and route PCBs, run ERC/DRC checks and export manufacturing files. It is delivered as a native KiCad plugin (single Rust binary) with a catalog of AI tools and skills, real-time IPC-driven edits with undo/redo integration, and optional autorouting and parts-search features.
cls.trl_rationale: The README states 'beta' and the repo is only 24 days old, so while the core toolchain is described as tested and working and there are release assets and active pushes, it lacks a long track record; age and short history limit maturity to TRL 5.
prerequisites: basic PCB design and schematic knowledge
familiarity with using AI assistants that support MCP (Claude/Codex) is helpful
student_project_ideas: Use Konnect-EDA to implement and autoroute a simple STM32-based development board in KiCad, then export Gerbers and verify DRC/ERC results; compare a human layout versus AI-assisted layout for routing quality and manufacturability.

Build a workflow that integrates Konnect-EDA with a parts database (e.g. JLCPCB snapshot) to automatically suggest component substitutions and produce a BOM, then evaluate cost and part-availability trade-offs.

tools.name: ziv/raytiles
tools.desc: 3D Geospatial engine for Raylib

cls.summary: Raytiles is a lightweight C/C++ geospatial streaming and rendering engine for raylib that renders any location on Earth with adaptive LOD, terrain heights, lighting and background tile caching.
cls.what_it_does: Raytiles streams map and terrain tiles from configurable providers, constructs a float-based 3D terrain with normals, lights and shadows, and exposes a C++ API plus a C wrapper so you can embed real-world scenes inside raylib applications. It is designed for real-time use cases such as UAV/flight simulation, lightweight GIS visualisation and digital sand tables and focuses on efficient LOD, on-disk caching and cross-platform builds.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is 195 days old (<1 year) but shows a well-structured README, runnable sandbox/demo, cross-platform builds and active commits; these indicators support a beta-level maturity though it lacks a long production track record required for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: basic knowledge of map tile providers (e.g. Mapbox) and build tools (CMake/compilers)
student_project_ideas: Build a simple UAV flight simulator scene by integrating Raytiles with a basic vehicle dynamics model (e.g. simple physics loop) to test collision detection and waypoint navigation over real terrain.
Create a GIS analysis tool that streams a region with Raytiles and computes slope and aspect maps from the ground-truth altitude queries, then visualise hazard zones in the rendered scene.

tools.name: enclavum/otaku
tools.desc: LLM frontend for roleplay and creative writing

cls.summary: Otaku is an open-source local LLM frontend focused on roleplay and creative writing, providing web and terminal UIs and tools to manage long-story context and character information.
cls.what_it_does: Otaku hosts local or cloud LLM models and offers chat/story modes, automatic summarisation of long conversations, character management, and a web and terminal interface for interactive storytelling. It is used by installing the Python package or running a Docker compose and selecting a local backend (llama.cpp, KoboldCpp, Ollama, etc.) or an API provider.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is active with demos, install scripts, Docker support, and regular releases but is only ~5 months old (157 days) so it shows beta-level maturity (usable with docs) but lacks the long track record needed for TRL 7+.
prerequisites: local LLM backend (llama.cpp, KoboldCpp, Ollama) or API key for a cloud provider

tools.name: peonist-ai/halogen-server
tools.desc: The fastest way to run Qwen3.8 27B on Strix Halo (gfx1151)

cls.summary: Halogen is a highly optimized local inference engine for running the Qwen3.8-27B model on a single AMD Strix Halo GPU, delivered as a container with an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint.
cls.what_it_does: Halogen provides a GPU‑optimized runtime specifically written for the AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151) to run Qwen3.8-27B with higher effective precision and faster end-to-end throughput than other published implementations. It is deployed as a container (Podman/Docker) that serves an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API and can fetch model weights from Hugging Face or use locally mounted checkpoints. The project is notable because every kernel is hand-tuned for this GPU+model pairing, trading portability for raw performance and precision.
cls.trl_rationale: Repository is very new (created 83 days ago) so it lacks a long track record; README and container images, performance numbers and example usage indicate it is beyond a minimal prototype and used by early adopters, consistent with TRL 5 (alpha in use). Age limits a higher TRL.
prerequisites: AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151) / compatible ROCm driver stack
Container runtime (Podman or Docker) with GPU device access
35.9 GB Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint and tokenizer (Hugging Face or local copy)
Linux host with ROCm/hip support and necessary device permissions
student_project_ideas: Measure and compare inference latency/throughput and energy use of Qwen3.8-27B across halogen and q38rocm on a ROCm-capable machine, and produce a report analysing trade-offs between precision and speed.

Build a small OpenAI-compatible service that routes requests to halogen or a smaller CPU/GPU model based on prompt length and realtime load, demonstrating deployment decision logic and simple autoscaling in containers.
